title_old: LLM inference service unavailable causing pipeline failure
title_new: AI reading service unavailable, stopping patient record processing
hazard_old: External LLM service (OpenAI / Anthropic / AWS Bedrock) experiences outage or rate limiting
hazard_new: The external AI service that interprets clinical notes becomes unavailable or too busy to respond. This can happen due to a service outage or because too many requests are sent at once.
hazardous_situation_old: Pipeline step requiring LLM inference (disambiguation, interpretation) fails because the LLM service is unavailable, blocking pipeline completion for affected patients
hazardous_situation_new: The AI workflow cannot finish processing a patient's record because the AI service does not respond. The system cannot complete the steps needed to classify the patient's clinical episode. Affected patients are not processed until the service recovers.
harm_old: Pipeline processing delayed; audit reporting timelines may be affected
harm_new: Processing of the patient's record is delayed. Audit reports that rely on completed episode classifications may not be ready on time. Patient care is not directly affected because a clinician must review all results before they are used.
mitigation_new: First, the system shows clinicians only the results from steps that finished successfully before the failure. This means partial work is not lost and clinicians can see what has been processed so far. The development team sets this up and it runs automatically every time the AI workflow runs (DI-CB07829F). Second, a human-review gate stops any unreviewed episode classifications from being used in audit reports. A clinician must approve each result before it counts. This check runs on every patient record processed by the system (DI-BD696225). Third, the system is designed to process a single patient record within ten seconds for most cases. The development team monitors this performance target continuously so that slowdowns caused by a struggling AI service are spotted quickly (DI-620FE631). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Neo4j database unavailable causing system outage
title_new: Patient database becomes unavailable, stopping the audit tool from working
hazard_old: Neo4j Patient or Coding database experiences outage or performance degradation
hazard_new: One or both databases that store patient records and clinical codes stop working or slow down severely. This means the audit tool cannot access the information it needs to run.
hazardous_situation_old: Core system functionality is unavailable because one or both Neo4j databases cannot be reached, preventing pipeline processing, data access, and user interactions
hazardous_situation_new: When the database is unavailable, the audit tool stops completely. Clinicians cannot view patient records, run audits, or take any action through the tool. The AI workflow halts and no results are produced.
harm_old: System downtime affecting all users; audit processing halted
harm_new: All clinicians lose access to the audit tool at the same time. Audit reviews are paused. Patients whose care depends on timely audit findings may experience a delay in follow-up. Because a human reviewer must approve all results before they are acted on, no incorrect information reaches clinical records during the outage.
mitigation_new: Patient data and clinical code data are stored in separate databases. This means a fault in one does not automatically bring down the other (DI-84F44836). The system is set up so that each organisation using the tool has its own dedicated patient database, reducing the risk that one failure affects all users at once (DI-AF5A1668). A human reviewer must approve all audit findings before they are used in clinical care. This gate remains in place even after the system recovers, so no unreviewed results can reach patient records (DI-BD696225). The system is designed to complete all processing for a single patient within ten seconds under normal load, which helps the team detect when performance is degrading before a full outage occurs (DI-620FE631). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter. Additional controls are being identified.

title_old: MedSpaCy NLP model produces incorrect clinical entity extraction
title_new: AI tool produces wrong clinical information from patient notes
hazard_old: MedSpaCy model is undertrained, overfitted, or degraded, producing incorrect NER results
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes has not been trained well enough, or its accuracy has fallen over time. It starts identifying the wrong clinical information from patient records.
hazardous_situation_old: MedSpaCy model used for entity extraction produces systematically incorrect results across a category of clinical text, and the error is not detected before deployment
hazardous_situation_new: The AI tool that reads notes produces the same type of error repeatedly across a group of patient records. Nobody spots the problem before the tool is used in live clinical work. As a result, audit data drawn from those records is wrong for every patient affected.
harm_old: Systematic extraction errors could affect audit data quality across all patients processed with the faulty model
harm_new: Widespread errors in audit data could mean patients with a particular condition or medicine are missed or wrongly included in clinical reviews. This could delay care or trigger unnecessary clinical action across a large group of patients.
mitigation_new: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool records a confidence score and a full history of where each piece of clinical information came from. This lets reviewers trace and check any result the tool produces (DI-31126C6C). Second, the AI tool follows a fixed set of clinical rules when linking pieces of information together. This limits the types of error it can make (DI-3EA60D5A). Third, the audit programme is set up and tested using real patient data before any results go live. This catches systematic errors early, before they affect patients (DI-CD931485). Fourth, error categories can be updated at any time without stopping the system. The team responsible for the tool reviews and updates these categories whenever a new type of error is found (DI-770FD74A). Fifth, a versioned list of known errors is kept, with three clear categories and a defined fix path for each. The development team uses this list to resolve errors in a structured way (DI-990C0AFA). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Malicious or unexpected content in encounter text causes LLM misbehaviour
title_new: Hidden instructions in patient notes cause the AI to produce wrong clinical codes
hazard_old: Clinical encounter text contains content that manipulates LLM behaviour through prompt injection
hazard_new: Patient notes sometimes contain text that the AI mistakes for instructions. This can make the AI behave in unexpected ways instead of reading the notes normally.
hazardous_situation_old: Encounter free text contains strings that are interpreted as instructions by the LLM, causing it to produce incorrect coding, skip entities, or leak system prompt content
hazardous_situation_new: When the AI reads a patient's free-text notes, it may treat certain phrases as commands. This can cause it to assign wrong clinical codes, miss important clinical findings, or behave unpredictably.
harm_old: Incorrect coding output or information disclosure; mitigated by human review and structured output validation
harm_new: If wrong clinical codes are saved to the patient record, the patient's problem may be recorded incorrectly. This could affect future care decisions. The risk is low because a clinician checks all AI output before it is saved.
mitigation_new: First, the AI workflow only uses structured, bounded facts when deciding the clinical meaning of a finding. This stops free-text phrases from changing how the AI interprets clinical information. The development team built this in by design and it runs automatically on every case (DI-69C29EEF). Second, a coding correction review checks that all clinical codes are valid and consistent before they are saved. This is carried out by the system automatically and flagged for clinician review where needed (DI-1B8AC856). Third, role-based access controls mean only authorised clinicians can review and approve AI output before it is saved to the patient record. This is enforced by the system on every action (DI-E83828A9). Fourth, the AI uses a precise position-tracking method to make sure each finding it pulls from the notes is matched exactly to the right piece of text. This reduces the chance of a finding being misread or misplaced (DI-A0C90595). Fifth, the AI preserves clinical qualifiers such as whether a condition is current, past, or possible, so that clinical codes remain as specific and accurate as possible (DI-6A0B55A4). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and any flagged cases every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Data loss occurs when synchronising data between pipeline stages
title_new: Information is lost when the AI workflow passes data between steps
hazard_old: Sync operation fails mid-way, leaving data in an inconsistent state
hazard_new: A step in the AI workflow stops before it finishes. This leaves some patient data updated and some not, so the record is incomplete.
hazardous_situation_old: A pipeline sync operation fails partway through, resulting in partial data updates that leave the system in an inconsistent state
hazardous_situation_new: The AI workflow fails part-way through processing a patient record. Some steps complete and some do not. The system holds a mix of old and new data for that patient. A clinician reading the record may see incomplete or mismatched information.
harm_old: Partial data loss requiring re-processing; no patient safety impact as re-run is safe
harm_new: The affected patient record is incomplete until the workflow is run again. The workflow can be safely re-run without risk to the patient. Any harm is minor and temporary. No clinical decision should be made from an incomplete record before it is corrected.
mitigation_new: First, the system checks that all links between steps in the AI workflow stay intact from start to finish. This means a gap or break in the chain is detected before it can cause an incomplete record (DI-08DE2CF3). The clinical safety team reviews these checks at each software release. Second, before any new workflow setup goes live, the team runs a test pass to confirm the configuration works correctly end to end. This dry run is carried out by the technical team before every activation (DI-ACB587DD). Third, the system shows the results of each completed step as soon as that step finishes, even if the overall job has not yet ended. This means a clinician or reviewer can see which parts of the record are ready and which are not (DI-CB07829F). Fourth, the system is designed to complete a full single-patient workflow within ten seconds for most patients. This limits the window during which a record could be in an incomplete state (DI-620FE631). Fifth, any updates to clinical guidelines go through independent checks before they enter the workflow, reducing the chance that a faulty update triggers a failure mid-run (DI-F3EFEA88). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and re-run rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: LLM token usage or pricing miscalculated leading to unexpected costs
title_new: AI tool usage costs calculated incorrectly, leading to unexpected charges
hazard_old: Token counting or pricing calculation contains errors
hazard_new: The AI tool may count usage or calculate charges incorrectly. This could cause the system to report the wrong costs for each organisation using it.
hazardous_situation_old: LLM cost tracking reports incorrect values, leading to budget overruns or incorrect cost attribution
hazardous_situation_new: The system reports incorrect costs for AI tool usage. An organisation may be charged too much or too little without knowing. Budget planning becomes unreliable. There is no direct effect on patient care.
harm_old: Financial impact from unexpected costs; no clinical or patient safety impact
harm_new: An organisation may face unexpected charges or incorrect billing. This is a financial risk only. There is no risk to patient safety or clinical care.
mitigation_new: The system tracks AI tool usage separately for each organisation and applies agreed commercial rates. The clinical safety team reviews this tracking at each release (DI-19B08FFC). Pricing rules are set up with adjustable margins and discounts for each organisation. A cap prevents discounts exceeding 100%. Every pricing change is recorded permanently and cannot be altered. The finance team reviews the pricing log monthly (DI-F407CC45). The AI tool operates within set cost and usage limits for each task. If a limit is reached, the task stops automatically. The system support team checks these limits are working at each deployment (DI-54D00E21). The clinical safety committee reviews all three controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: spaCy or MedSpaCy SOUP update introduces NER regression
title_new: A software update causes the AI tool to miss or misread clinical terms in notes
hazard_old: Update to spaCy or MedSpaCy library introduces regression in named entity recognition accuracy
hazard_new: When the AI tool that reads clinical notes is updated, the new version may become less accurate at spotting clinical terms such as diagnoses or medicines. This can happen without any obvious error message. The problem may affect every patient record the tool processes until someone notices.
hazardous_situation_old: A SOUP component update degrades NER accuracy without detection, causing systematic extraction errors across all processed encounters until the regression is identified
hazardous_situation_new: The AI tool reads notes less accurately after an update. It misses or misreads clinical terms across all patient records it processes. No alert is raised. The errors build up silently in the audit data before anyone detects the problem.
harm_old: Degraded audit data quality from undetected NER regression
harm_new: Patient records and audit data contain systematic errors. Clinicians or audit teams may act on incomplete or wrong information. This could lead to patients missing follow-up care or being placed on the wrong clinical pathway.
mitigation_new: First, the system records a confidence score and full source details every time the AI tool pulls a clinical term from a note. This means each result can be traced back to its origin and checked (DI-31126C6C). The clinical safety team reviews these records as part of routine quality checks. Second, the system continuously monitors coding quality and sends an alert if accuracy drops (DI-1126FFD1). The safety team reviews these alerts as they arise. Third, the system tracks how often each type of clinical term is coded and flags unusual changes against a set threshold (DI-37315D03). The safety team reviews drift reports regularly. Fourth, audit programme settings can be adjusted in response to quality signals without needing a new software release (DI-CD931485). The safety team or audit lead makes these adjustments when needed. Fifth, when a software update is applied, the system automatically tests accuracy on a sample of records. If accuracy falls below the agreed level, the system halts and rolls back to the previous version without manual intervention (DI-7D710C52). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Bio_ClinicalBERT model update changes embedding space, degrading vector search
title_new: An update to the AI reading tool changes how it searches past encounters, making results less accurate
hazard_old: Update to Bio_ClinicalBERT model changes embedding vectors, invalidating stored embeddings and degrading vector similarity search
hazard_new: The AI tool that searches past encounters uses a scoring method to find relevant records. If the AI tool is updated, the stored scores from before the update no longer match the new version. This means the search may return the wrong encounters or miss important ones.
hazardous_situation_old: Encounter shortlisting using vector similarity returns incorrect results because stored embeddings are incompatible with updated model embeddings
hazardous_situation_new: After an update to the AI tool, the system searches past encounters using mismatched scores. It may return irrelevant encounters and miss ones that matter. A clinician reviewing the shortlist could overlook a relevant past encounter when making a clinical decision.
harm_old: Degraded encounter shortlisting recall, potentially missing relevant encounters
harm_new: A clinician may not see a relevant past encounter. This could lead to an incomplete picture of the patient's history. Any harm is likely to be minor, as other information sources remain available.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the system uses three different ways to search past encounters: keyword search, full-text search, and AI-based scoring. If the AI-based scoring is unreliable, the other two methods still return results. This means a single update cannot disable all search methods at once (DI-143F69EB). The clinical safety team reviews this design at each major update. Second, before any update goes live, the system must correctly find at least 95 in every 100 relevant encounters when tested against a set of encounters checked by an expert clinician. If it fails this test, the update is blocked (DI-10BB41E9). The technical team runs this test before every release. Third, the system stores accuracy figures for every version of the AI tool in a central log. The clinical safety team can compare figures before and after an update to spot any drop in performance (DI-CE0A08E5). This log is reviewed at each release and at quarterly safety meetings. Fourth, when a keyword search returns a strong match, the system uses that result directly and does not rely on AI-based scoring at all. This protects against poor AI scoring for clearly relevant encounters (DI-7A7BFA0C). This behaviour is tested as part of every release check. The clinical safety committee reviews all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: SNOMED CT terminology update introduces new concepts or changed relationships that break resolution
title_new: A routine clinical coding update breaks how the AI tool matches terms to clinical codes
hazard_old: UK SNOMED CT Clinical Edition update adds, retires, or restructures concepts used by the terminology resolver
hazard_new: The UK clinical coding system (SNOMED CT) is updated several times a year. Each update can add new codes, retire old ones, or change how codes relate to each other. The AI tool that reads notes and assigns clinical codes may not handle these changes automatically.
hazardous_situation_old: Updated SNOMED CT content causes the terminology resolver to return incorrect results, fail to resolve known terms, or match to retired concepts
hazardous_situation_new: After a coding update, the AI tool may assign the wrong clinical code, fail to assign any code, or use a code that has been retired. This can happen silently, without any alert to the clinician. The error may affect many patients before it is noticed.
harm_old: Degraded coding accuracy until terminology configuration is updated
harm_new: Patient records may carry incorrect clinical codes for a period of time. This could affect how patients are identified for recalls, audits, or care pathways. The risk is minor because a clinician reviews the record before any clinical decision is made.
mitigation_new: First, when a new coding update is released, the system automatically compares the new codes against the ones it currently uses and pauses any affected coding until a review is done. The technical team runs this check with every scheduled coding release (DI-B193C816). Second, the AI tool is designed to handle cases where two or more codes overlap or compete, reducing the chance of a wrong match after an update. The technical team maintains this as part of the AI workflow (DI-DC61F5B6). Third, before any updated coding rules go live, the AI tool must achieve a minimum accuracy score on a set of records checked by a clinical expert. The clinical safety team approves the results before release (DI-12015DBC). Fourth, when a coding correction is made, the system checks that all related codes and updated coding rules are consistent before saving changes back into the patient record. The technical team carries out this check at each release (DI-1B8AC856). Fifth, the AI tool that reads notes preserves important clinical detail, such as whether a condition is confirmed, suspected, or ruled out, so that the correct specific code is chosen even after an update changes code relationships. The technical team maintains this as part of the AI workflow (DI-6A0B55A4). The clinical safety committee reviews audit reports of coding accuracy after each SNOMED CT release to confirm all controls are working.

title_old: Known security vulnerability (CVE) discovered in a SOUP dependency
title_new: A known security weakness in a third-party software component could be exploited
hazard_old: A SOUP component has a known security vulnerability that could be exploited
hazard_new: The system uses third-party software components. One of these components may have a known security weakness that has not yet been fixed.
hazardous_situation_old: An attacker exploits a known vulnerability in a SOUP dependency to gain unauthorised access, escalate privileges, or exfiltrate data
hazardous_situation_new: An attacker finds and uses a known weakness in a third-party component. This could let them access the system without permission, gain higher-level control, or copy patient data.
harm_old: Data breach, system compromise, or service disruption depending on vulnerability severity
harm_new: Patient data could be stolen or exposed. The system could be damaged or taken over. Clinicians could lose access to the tool when they need it. Any of these could delay or disrupt patient care.
mitigation_new: Four controls are in place to reduce this risk. First, the system enforces strict rules about which versions of third-party components are allowed to run, blocking outdated or unsafe versions automatically (DI-F1A768AE). This control is built into the system and runs every time the software is deployed. Second, a review process checks that all third-party components and clinical codes used in the AI workflow are valid and up to date (DI-1B8AC856). The clinical safety team runs this review at each software release. Third, the AI tool that reads notes displays which third-party components it relied on during any coding suggestion, so reviewers can spot outdated components quickly (DI-4221A226). Clinicians and the safety team can see this information during routine coding review. Fourth, a dedicated system component records a full audit trail of all activity, giving the safety team a way to investigate any suspicious access without exposing patient records directly (DI-09E26C1D). The safety team can query this audit trail at any time and must review it at least monthly. The clinical safety committee reviews all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Incorrect milestone detection leads to wrong pathway duration calculations
title_new: Wrong milestone dates cause incorrect waiting time calculations
hazard_old: Anchor detection algorithm assigns wrong dates to clinical milestones or misidentifies milestone type
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads clinical notes assigns the wrong date to a key point in a patient's care pathway, or identifies the wrong type of milestone altogether.
hazardous_situation_old: Incorrect milestone dates cause pathway duration calculations to show false breaches or mask real breaches of national waiting time targets
hazardous_situation_new: The wrong milestone date causes the system to calculate pathway waiting times incorrectly. It may show a breach of national waiting time targets that did not happen, or hide a real breach that did happen.
harm_old: Inaccurate pathway metrics could misdirect quality improvement or mask genuine performance issues at population level
harm_new: Clinicians and managers see inaccurate waiting time figures for groups of patients. Real performance problems may go unnoticed. Quality improvement effort may be directed at the wrong areas. Patients who have waited too long may not be identified and helped.
mitigation_new: First, the system only uses milestone dates that a reviewer has checked and accepted before any waiting time calculation runs. This human review step stops wrong dates from reaching the final figures (DI-EE4E6477). The clinical safety team checks this gate is being applied at every quarterly review. Second, the system runs automatic checks on each patient episode, looking for unusual pathway durations, missing milestones, and steps that appear in the wrong order. These checks flag suspicious data before it affects reports. The team responsible for data quality reviews flagged episodes daily (DI-1206D9E8). Third, the system applies quality checks before promoting any new version of the AI model that detects milestones. Only models that meet the required accuracy threshold are used in live calculations (DI-80BD2F86). The clinical safety committee reviews model promotion decisions each quarter. Fourth, the system calculates waiting times and flags breaches of national targets using a configurable rules engine. Clinicians can adjust target thresholds to match current national guidance (DI-F3FD2B63). The team responsible for pathway configuration reviews these settings at least every six months. Fifth, pathway figures are shown at organisation, primary care network, and integrated care board level alongside national benchmarks, making unusual patterns easier to spot (DI-B9109EF5 and DI-BA2C8F3E). Clinicians and managers review these dashboards monthly. The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Safety-net system fails to flag patients at risk of delayed cancer diagnosis
title_new: Safety-net system fails to flag patients who may have cancer and need follow-up
hazard_old: Electronic safety-netting logic fails to detect patients with cancer-relevant symptoms who lack expected follow-up
hazard_new: The safety-net system does not spot patients who have reported possible cancer symptoms but have not been referred or investigated. The system misses the gap in their care.
hazardous_situation_old: A patient who presented with cancer-relevant symptoms but was not referred or investigated is not flagged by the safety-net system, losing an opportunity for early intervention
hazardous_situation_new: A patient reports symptoms that could indicate cancer. No referral or investigation is arranged. The safety-net system does not raise an alert. No one follows up. The chance to catch the cancer early is lost.
harm_old: Missed safety-net alert could contribute to delayed cancer diagnosis at population level through incorrect audit data and missed quality improvement opportunity
harm_new: Without a safety-net alert, the patient's lack of follow-up goes unnoticed. Their cancer may be diagnosed later than it should be. At a practice level, audit data is wrong and the team cannot see or fix the gap in care.
mitigation_new: The system uses a configurable follow-up time window. If a patient with possible cancer symptoms has no recorded response within that window, the system adds them to a worklist for review by the clinical team. The team checks this worklist regularly (DI-4C73DC01). When a clinician records a confirmed clinical response using the correct clinical code, the system automatically removes the alert from the worklist. This stops unnecessary alerts for patients who have already been managed (DI-0E215ADE). The worklist can be filtered by how serious the finding is, how many days it has been outstanding, and which group of patients it covers. This helps the clinical team prioritise the most urgent cases (DI-520A8674). The audit programme can be updated to reflect new clinical priorities without needing a software deployment. This means the safety team can act quickly if a gap in care is identified (DI-CD931485). Every action taken on a safety-net alert is saved permanently with the clinician's name and the date and time it was recorded. This creates a clear record that can be reviewed at any time (DI-B46AD5CE). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Guideline compliance checker produces incorrect deviation alerts
title_new: Guideline compliance checker gives wrong alerts about care quality
hazard_old: Guideline compliance rules incorrectly classify encounters as compliant or non-compliant with clinical guidelines
hazard_new: The compliance checker uses rules to decide whether a patient's care followed clinical guidelines. Sometimes it gets this wrong. It may flag care as a problem when it was fine, or miss care that genuinely fell short of guidelines.
hazardous_situation_old: False positive alerts create unnecessary work and erode trust in the system; false negative alerts fail to identify genuine guideline deviations that should be investigated
hazardous_situation_new: When the checker wrongly flags good care as a problem, clinical audit teams waste time investigating cases that need no action. This erodes trust in the tool. When the checker misses genuine problems, real gaps in patient care go uninvestigated and unresolved.
harm_old: False negatives could mask genuine quality issues; false positives waste clinical audit resource and erode system trust
harm_new: Missed problems mean genuine quality issues stay hidden. Patients may continue to receive care that falls short of guidelines without anyone noticing. Wrong alerts waste audit resource and make clinicians less likely to act on future alerts, including real ones.
mitigation_new: First, the system automatically checks each coded patient encounter against guideline rules and records a clear pass or fail result for every episode. The audit team can review these results at any time (DI-2AFF691F). Second, the rules engine lets the clinical team configure each rule and stores a pass, fail, or needs-action result alongside a suggested next step for every episode. This means no result is lost and every gap has a clear recommended action (DI-FC80B65A). Third, all patient record data enters and leaves the system through a single, standardised system component that follows an agreed data format. This reduces the risk of data being lost or misread before the rules are applied (DI-1795254D). Fourth, when a clinician reviews a flagged case and decides the deviation was clinically justified, they can record their reason without blocking their workflow. The system logs this rationale and shows which other patients in the same group were flagged for the same reason. This creates an auditable record of every decision (DI-6079EC71). Fifth, the AI tool that reads notes produces a structured summary for each patient, drawing on coded encounters, where the patient is in their care pathway, and any safety alerts. Clinicians can use this summary to quickly sense-check whether an alert looks right before acting on it (DI-30D9CC61). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs, alert accuracy rates, and clinician feedback every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Patient data from one organisation visible to users from another organisation
title_new: A user from one organisation can see patient records belonging to another organisation
hazard_old: Multi-tenancy isolation failure allows data from one organisation to be accessed by users of another organisation
hazard_new: The system keeps each organisation's patient data in a separate database. If that separation fails, a user from one organisation could see, search, or download patient records that belong to a different organisation.
hazardous_situation_old: A user authenticated to Organisation A can view, query, or export patient data belonging to Organisation B due to a tenancy isolation failure
hazardous_situation_new: A user who has logged in to Organisation A is able to view or export patient records held for Organisation B because the system has not correctly enforced the boundary between the two organisations' data.
harm_old: Cross-organisation patient data breach with severe regulatory and reputational consequences
harm_new: Patients' private health information is seen by people who have no right to see it. This breaches patient confidentiality, may cause distress to patients, and is likely to trigger a serious regulatory investigation and significant reputational damage to both organisations.
mitigation_new: Two controls protect against this risk. First, each organisation's patient data is stored in its own completely separate database, and the system sets this up automatically when a new organisation joins (DI-AF5A1668). This means a failure in one organisation's data store cannot spread to another. Second, every time a user runs a search or query, the system checks that the user's login token matches the correct organisation before allowing any data to be returned (DI-87CCCB18). This check is built into the system's core design so it cannot be bypassed. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and test results for both controls every quarter to confirm they are working correctly. Additional controls are being identified.

title_old: Incorrect pipeline or programme configuration causes erroneous processing
title_new: Wrong setup of an audit programme causes the AI workflow to process patient data incorrectly
hazard_old: Administrator configures a pipeline or programme with incorrect parameters (wrong value sets, incorrect milestone definitions, misconfigured guideline rules)
hazard_new: An administrator sets up an audit programme with wrong settings. This could include wrong patient groups, wrong clinical milestones, or wrong guideline rules.
hazardous_situation_old: A programme is configured with incorrect clinical domain definitions, causing the pipeline to systematically include or exclude the wrong encounters, apply wrong guideline rules, or calculate durations between wrong milestones
hazardous_situation_new: Because the programme is set up incorrectly, the AI workflow consistently looks at the wrong patients or applies the wrong clinical rules. It may count the wrong appointments, measure time between the wrong events, or flag the wrong patients as meeting or missing a guideline.
harm_old: Incorrect audit results for the affected programme, potentially misdirecting quality improvement
harm_new: The audit produces wrong results for the affected programme. Clinicians and managers act on those wrong results. Quality improvement effort is directed at the wrong areas, and real problems in patient care may be missed.
mitigation_new: First, before any new programme setup goes live, the system runs a dry-run check to test whether the settings produce sensible results. The administrator reviews the output before the programme is activated (DI-ACB587DD). Second, all programme setup must be done through the system's own screen-based interface. If a test-mode check fails, the system blocks the administrator from moving the programme to live use without a deliberate override step (DI-F2C18D2E). Third, programme settings such as patient groups and clinical criteria can be changed directly in the system without needing a software release. This means errors can be corrected quickly by the administrator as soon as they are spotted (DI-CD931485). Fourth, when settings are updated, the changes take effect automatically at the next scheduled run without any system restart. This reduces the window in which wrong settings could affect results (DI-702F4583). Fifth, the guideline rules applied to each programme can be updated directly in the system by the administrator without a software release, allowing fast correction if a rule is found to be wrong (DI-AA8014F9). Sixth, the system automatically checks whether patient encounters carry the correct clinical codes before applying guideline rules. This catches cases where wrong codes would cause a patient to be incorrectly included or excluded (DI-2AFF691F). Seventh, the thresholds that decide whether an audit result is flagged as complete or suppressed are set at programme level and can be reviewed and adjusted by the administrator without a software release (DI-0D7DCC52). The clinical safety committee reviews audit outputs and configuration logs every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Autonomous coding mode operates without human review gate
title_new: The AI codes clinical information automatically, with no clinician check before saving
hazard_old: In autonomous mode, the system codes clinical entities into SNOMED CT without a human reviewer validating each coding decision before persistence
hazard_new: When the system runs in automatic mode, it assigns clinical codes to information found in patient notes. No clinician reviews or approves each coding decision before the code is saved to the patient record.
hazardous_situation_old: Autonomous mode auto-codes entities based on NLP extraction and terminology matching. If the tier classifier, consensus verification, or terminology match is incorrect, miscoded entities are persisted directly to the patient graph without human interception
hazardous_situation_new: The AI reads clinical notes, identifies conditions and findings, and assigns clinical codes automatically. If the AI misreads the notes, picks the wrong code, or applies the wrong rules, an incorrect code is saved directly to the patient record. No clinician sees the decision before it is saved, so the error is not caught at the point it is made.
harm_old: Systematic miscoding in autonomous mode could distort audit datasets for multiple patients before the error is detected through monitoring or audit review, potentially misdirecting clinical quality improvement activities
harm_new: If the AI saves wrong clinical codes across many patient records before anyone notices, the data used for clinical audit and quality improvement becomes unreliable. Clinicians and managers making decisions based on that data may focus effort in the wrong areas, missing real problems or acting on false ones.
mitigation_new: First, a human-review gate stops any AI-generated clinical code from being saved to the patient record until a clinician has reviewed and approved it. This control applies in all modes where patient data could be affected. The clinical safety team checks this gate is active and working at every deployment (DI-604767B1). Second, when a clinician corrects a code, the system checks that the replacement code is valid, current, and consistent with related information already in the record. This check runs automatically every time a correction is made (DI-1B8AC856). Third, the AI preserves important clinical detail, such as whether a condition is current, historical, or suspected, when it reads notes and assigns codes. This reduces the chance of a code being saved with the wrong meaning. The AI workflow applies this rule on every note it processes (DI-6A0B55A4). Fourth, before any replacement code is accepted during a correction, the system confirms the code is current and has not been retired or replaced in the clinical coding system. This check runs automatically at the point of correction (DI-26CBDB16). Fifth, the AI follows a defined set of rules when identifying clinical relationships in notes, such as linking a medicine to the condition it treats. This reduces the chance of incorrect associations being coded. The rules are applied by the AI on every note it processes (DI-3EA60D5A). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: Overly broad suppress rule causes systematic under-coding of a clinical term
title_new: A rule set too broadly stops a clinical term from being coded at all
hazard_old: A reviewer creates a post-processor suppress rule for a clinical term without a context phrase, suppressing the term globally rather than only in the specific non-codeable context (e.g. 'awaiting appointment', 'hypothetical').
hazard_new: A reviewer creates a rule that tells the AI workflow to ignore a clinical term everywhere in the notes. The rule should only apply in specific situations, such as when a patient is awaiting an appointment or when the term is used hypothetically. Because no limiting phrase is added, the rule removes the term from coding in every situation, including when it is genuinely present.
hazardous_situation_old: The suppress rule silently removes all future mentions of the term from the coding queue -- including clinically valid, present-tense mentions -- before any human reviewer can see them. The systematic gap in coding is not immediately visible because the entity no longer appears in the review queue; it is simply absent from the data.
hazardous_situation_new: The rule silently removes all future mentions of the term before any clinician sees them. The term simply stops appearing in the review queue. No one is alerted. The gap in coding is invisible because there is nothing missing to notice.
harm_old: Systematic under-coding of a clinical condition (e.g. biopsy, hypertension, diabetes check) distorts audit data, producing artificially low prevalence or activity figures. Quality improvement decisions made on this data may misdirect clinical care for future patient populations.
harm_new: A clinical condition such as hypertension (high blood pressure), diabetes review, or a biopsy result is consistently not coded across many patients. Audit figures show artificially low numbers of cases. Decisions about service planning and quality improvement are based on this incomplete data. Future patients may receive the wrong level of care as a result.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce the chance of this harm reaching patients. First, the AI tool that reads notes and the AI tool that decides whether something is present, absent, or possible are compared automatically after every processing run. If their results disagree for a given clinical term, the system flags the difference for review by the clinical informatics team (DI-F298AE65). Second, the system flags any clinical term it is not confident about, and it also flags when two coding decisions within the same patient episode contradict each other. A clinician reviewer checks these flags daily (DI-C7A810AA). Third, the AI workflow tracks how often each type of clinical term is coded over time. If the coding rate for any term drops below a set threshold, the system raises an alert to the clinical safety team. The safety team reviews these drift reports at least weekly (DI-37315D03). Fourth, all rules that control how the AI codes terms are held in a monitored registry under clinical change control. Any change to a rule must be approved before it goes live, and the full context of any alert is recorded. The clinical safety officer oversees this process and reviews the registry monthly (DI-ED3A89F5). All corrections made by reviewers in the unified review queue are stored as structured examples to improve future AI behaviour (DI-890BE989). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all four controls are working every quarter.

title_old: UI use errors from unconfirmed destructive actions, silent error swallowing, and accessibility barriers
title_new: Clinician makes an accidental or missed action in the coding review screen due to unclear warnings, hidden errors, or access barriers
hazard_old: The clinical coding review UI presents multiple interaction patterns where a reasonable user could take an unintended destructive action, miss a system failure, or be unable to access critical functionality due to accessibility barriers.
hazard_new: The coding review screen lets clinicians remove clinical codes, dismiss suggestions, or reset all work with a single click. There is no confirmation step before these actions take effect. When the system fails to load data, the screen looks the same as when there is genuinely nothing to review. Some clinicians using a keyboard may trigger actions by accident.
hazardous_situation_old: (1) A reviewer accidentally clicks 'Remove' on a clinical code, 'Create ignore rule', 'Dismiss', or 'Reset all' without a confirmation step, immediately executing an irreversible or difficult-to-reverse action. (2) Dashboard and operations workspace silently swallow API failures, showing empty data indistinguishable from 'no data available', causing reviewers to believe the system is healthy when it is not. (3) A keyboard user triggers 'reject' by pressing R while focused
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician clicks Remove, Dismiss, Create ignore rule, or Reset all without meaning to. The action happens immediately and is hard to undo. Separately, the system fails silently: the review queue appears empty, but this is because the system has not loaded properly, not because there is nothing to review. A clinician using only a keyboard may press a shortcut key by accident and reject a suggestion without intending to.
harm_old: (1) Accidental deletion of correct clinical codes or creation of overly broad suppress rules could cause under-coding that distorts audit data. (2) Silent API failures could cause reviewers to skip the review queue, believing it is empty when the system has actually failed to load. (3) Accidental re
harm_new: A correct clinical code may be deleted by accident. A broad ignore rule may be created, causing the system to suppress correct codes in future. Clinicians may skip the review queue believing it is empty, when in fact the system has failed to load outstanding work. Any of these errors could lead to clinical codes being missed or removed from patient records, distorting the clinical picture and audit data, and potentially affecting patient care decisions.
mitigation_new: Role-based access control limits which clinicians can take destructive actions such as removing codes or creating ignore rules. Only authorised users can finalise or change AI suggestions. The system enforces this automatically on every action (DI-E83828A9). When a clinician corrects a suggestion, the system resets the confirmation step and requires the clinician to actively re-confirm before the change is saved. This stops accidental single-click changes from taking effect without a second check (DI-5ADEC3D1). When the system fails to load data, a dedicated failed-encounter list shows the clinician which records could not be loaded and why. A one-click option lets the clinician re-queue those records immediately, so a failed load is never mistaken for an empty queue (DI-69CE20C1). When a system component returns an error, the system records a structured error code rather than showing a blank screen. This means failures can be detected and investigated rather than going unnoticed (DI-6654FB0E). All review actions are recorded in a full audit trail. The safety team can check this trail to see whether accidental actions have occurred and whether failed loads were detected and resolved (DI-09E26C1D). The review screen shows how often a clinical code has been used historically. This gives the clinician a prompt to pause before removing an unusual or infrequent code, reducing the chance of accidental deletion (DI-22F4E3CE). The clinical safety committee reviews audit trail reports and failed-encounter logs every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: LLM infers a diagnosis from a lab value instead of coding the observation
title_new: The AI tool infers a diagnosis from a lab result instead of recording the test value
hazard_old: The LLM extraction step interprets a lab result (e.g. eGFR 69 mL/min) as evidence of a disorder (e.g. CKD stage 1) rather than coding only the observable entity and its numeric value
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes can misread a lab result as a diagnosis. For example, it may see an eGFR of 69 mL/min and suggest chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 1. It should only record the test name and number, not decide what disease the patient has.
hazardous_situation_old: A lab result line such as 'eGFR using creatinine (CKD-EPI) per 1.73 square metres (XacUK) 69 mL/min' is processed by the extraction pipeline. The LLM returns a disorder entity (e.g. chronic kidney disease stage 1) inferred from the numeric value, and the terminology resolver matches it to a SNOMED disorder concept. The inferred diagnosis is then presented to the clinician as a coding suggestion or, in autonomous mode, persisted directly to the patient graph
hazardous_situation_new: A lab result line is processed by the AI workflow. The AI tool decides the number means the patient has a specific disease. It then matches that disease to a clinical code. The suggested diagnosis is shown to the clinician as a coding option. In fully automated mode, it is saved directly into the patient record without a clinician checking it first.
harm_old: A false diagnosis is attributed to the patient. In HITL mode this wastes reviewer time and erodes trust. In autonomous mode the false diagnosis enters the clinical record and could influence care decisions, audit outcomes, and quality measures
harm_new: The patient receives a false diagnosis in their record. If a clinician reviews it first, they waste time correcting it and may trust the tool less. If the record is updated automatically, the false diagnosis could affect the patient's care, clinical audits, and quality targets.
mitigation_new: The AI workflow follows strict rules about what it is allowed to extract from notes. It is designed to record clinical observations and their values only, not to infer diagnoses from them. This reduces the chance of a lab result being turned into a disease label (DI-3EA60D5A). The AI tool is also designed to preserve the exact clinical detail from the original notes, so a test result stays a test result rather than becoming a diagnosis (DI-6A0B55A4). Before any coding suggestion enters the final record, a clinician must review and approve it individually. The system will not save a suggested code without that decision (DI-4247C7E5). If a coding suggestion does need correcting, the review process checks that the correction is clinically valid and that related codes are also reviewed for consistency (DI-1B8AC856). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of coding suggestions and corrections every quarter to check these controls are working.

title_old: Adversarial prompt injection via clinical text causes LLM to deviate from its coding task
title_new: Hidden instructions in patient notes cause the AI tool to give wrong clinical codes
hazard_old: Clinical encounter text processed by the LLM pipeline contains embedded text that looks like instructions, role definitions, or special tokens (e.g. "ignore all previous instructions", "[INST]...[/INST]", "<|im_start|>system..."). When this text is inserted into an LLM prompt without sanitisation, a sufficiently capable LLM may follow the embedded instructions rather than its assigned clinical coding task.
hazard_new: Patient notes sometimes contain text that looks like instructions to an AI tool. For example, someone might type phrases such as 'ignore all previous instructions' into a free-text field. When the AI tool reads these notes without checking for such phrases first, it may follow those hidden instructions instead of doing its coding task.
hazardous_situation_old: The disorder verifier, coding escalation engine, and candidate picker all embed raw clinical text (entity_text, encounter_text) into LLM user messages. If a malicious actor inserts injection payloads into a patient record — or if a GP system API returns encounter text that already contains such patterns — those payloads reach AWS Bedrock and Azure OpenAI without filtering. The LLM may then: (a) return an incorrect verdict that bypasses the clinical coding gate, or (b)
hazardous_situation_new: The AI tool reads raw patient encounter notes to check diagnoses and suggest clinical codes. If a malicious person adds hidden instruction phrases to a patient record, or if the GP system sends notes that already contain such phrases, those phrases reach the AI tool unfiltered. The AI tool may then return a wrong verdict on a diagnosis, or reveal information about how the system works internally.
harm_old: (a) A disorder entity is incorrectly classified (e.g. UNCERTAIN instead of ACTIVE_DIAGNOSIS, or vice versa), causing a false negative or false positive diagnosis in the patient record. (b) Confidential system information (prompt structure, model endpoints) is disclosed, enabling further attacks. (c)
harm_new: The AI tool may wrongly mark an active diagnosis as uncertain, or wrongly confirm a diagnosis that is not present. This incorrect clinical code could be saved into the patient record. A clinician reading that record may then miss a real condition or act on a false one. Either outcome could delay or misdirect the patient's care.
mitigation_new: First, the AI workflow replaces all patient-identifying details with neutral placeholders before any notes reach the AI tool. This is done automatically by the system every time notes are processed, with no way to bypass it (DI-F66A7239, DI-250F32EC). This reduces the risk that harmful phrases are linked to real patient data. Second, if the AI tool fails to return a valid verdict for any reason, the system automatically records a GATE_FAILED result and stops the coding process. This fail-closed design is built into the system and runs on every single coding attempt (DI-9D967259). Third, each coding decision is logged with a full record of what the AI tool did and why. Reviewers can see which part of the notes the AI tool used to reach its verdict. The clinical safety team checks these logs to spot any unusual or unexpected results (DI-09E26C1D, DI-E81545BE). Fourth, patient notes and clinical reference data are held in completely separate databases, so a compromised note cannot affect the coding reference data (DI-84F44836). Fifth, all data passing between system components is encrypted so it cannot be read or altered in transit (DI-155BB31E). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and system performance every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Privileged user creates malicious clinical rules causing systematic entity suppression or mislabelling
title_new: An admin user creates harmful clinical rules that cause the AI tool to wrongly mark conditions as absent or suppress them entirely
hazard_old: Authenticated users with platform-admin privileges can create, update, and deactivate ConText rules (which determine entity assertion context) and post-processor rules (which suppress, rewrite, or relabel coded entities). A malicious or mistaken admin could create rules with overly broad match criteria, pathological regex patterns (ReDoS), or incorrect category assignments that systematically distort all future coding decisions made by the pipeline. catego
hazard_new: Users with admin access can create and change the rules that the AI tool follows when deciding whether a condition is present, absent, or possible in a patient's notes. They can also change rules that remove or relabel conditions after the AI has read the notes. An admin who makes a mistake, or acts with harmful intent, could create rules that are far too broad. This would cause the AI tool to wrongly handle every patient record processed after that point.
hazardous_situation_old: (a) A ConText rule with a common clinical phrase (e.g. "patient has") is assigned the NEGATED_EXISTENCE category and direction BIDIRECTIONAL. Every future encounter containing that phrase has its disorders marked as absent, suppressing them from the coding queue permanently and silently. The suppression is not visible in the review queue because the entities never appear -- they are classified as absent before reaching the HITL stage. (b) A po
hazardous_situation_new: Scenario one: an admin creates a rule linking a very common phrase in clinical notes to a setting that marks all nearby conditions as absent. Every future patient record containing that phrase has its conditions silently removed before a clinician sees them. The conditions never reach the review queue, so no clinician knows they have been missed. Scenario two: an admin creates a badly formed text pattern that causes the AI workflow to lock up and stop processing records, blocking all coding work.
harm_old: (a) Systematic under-coding: a disease, procedure, or clinical finding present in encounters is never coded, distorting prevalence and quality-of-care audit data for all patients processed after the malicious rule is created. (b) Pipeline denial-of-service: a ReDoS regex brings the coding worker to
harm_new: In scenario one, conditions that are genuinely present in patient records are never coded. This distorts disease prevalence data and quality-of-care audit results for every patient processed after the harmful rule is created. Clinicians and commissioners make decisions based on incomplete information. In scenario two, the AI workflow stops working entirely. No records are coded until the fault is found and fixed, causing delays to care pathway decisions that depend on coded data.
mitigation_new: The AI tool checks whether its own decision about a condition being present or absent matches the decision made by the separate rules-based step. It does this automatically for every record processed. A mismatch triggers a flag for review (DI-F298AE65). Every coded condition in the review queue shows the clinician the exact phrase from the notes that led to the decision, so a clinician can spot if conditions are being wrongly marked as absent (DI-375C7EB1). Every clinical statement keeps a permanent link back to the original encounter and the source notes, so the safety team can trace any pattern of missing codes back to a specific rule change (DI-740BE510). The guidance rule review queue requires a clinician to make an active decision before any rule change takes effect, and every change is linked to the records it affects (DI-F94EB13F). The clinical safety committee reviews flagged mismatches and rule change logs every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Clinical text (PHI) exposed to multiple external LLM providers without confirmed Data Processing Agreements
title_new: Patient information sent to external AI services without confirmed data agreements
hazard_old: The dual-model consensus engine sends clinical encounter text (entity_text + encounter_text, up to 2200 characters per call) to AWS Bedrock and Azure OpenAI in parallel. When the two providers disagree, a third call is made to AWS Sonnet. This means up to three external API calls per clinical entity per encounter, each carrying patient-identifiable information from NHS GP records.
hazard_new: The system uses two AI services at the same time to check clinical notes. When the two services disagree, a third AI service is asked to decide. Each of these calls sends text from the patient's GP record to an external cloud service. This means patient-identifiable information may be sent to up to three external services for a single piece of clinical information.
hazardous_situation_old: (a) The encounter text sent to LLM providers may contain residual PHI that the de-identification pass (libs/deid) did not catch (GAP-008: known regex gaps for uncommon PHI formats). This PHI is transmitted to up to three external cloud services: AWS Bedrock in eu-west-2 (London, UK — domestic, no transfer) and Azure OpenAI in Sweden Central (international transfer, lawful under UK adequacy regulations for EEA). No data is transmitted to the United
hazardous_situation_new: The system tries to remove patient-identifiable information before sending notes to the AI services. However, there are known gaps in this process: some unusual formats of patient-identifiable information may not be caught and removed. Text that still contains patient details may then be sent to external cloud services. One service is based in the UK (AWS, London). Another is based in Sweden (Azure), which is lawful under UK data transfer rules for the European Economic Area. If a valid data processing agreement is not in place with each provider, this transfer may breach UK data protection law.
harm_old: (a) UK GDPR Article 35 non-compliance: processing special category health data without a completed DPIA is a regulatory violation subject to ICO investigation and potential fine. (b) Patient confidentiality breach: PHI transmitted to external LLM providers without adequate contractual protection cou
harm_new: A patient's confidential health information could be shared with an external company without proper legal agreements in place. This could breach the patient's right to confidentiality. It may also break UK data protection law (UK GDPR), which requires a completed Data Protection Impact Assessment before processing sensitive health data. The Information Commissioner's Office could investigate and issue a significant fine.
mitigation_new: The system can be set to use only one AI service instead of two or three, reducing how many external services receive patient data. The clinical safety team can switch to single-service mode at any time (DI-80DD8A47). The system uses secure, time-limited access tokens to connect to each external service, so only authorised connections are made (DI-4DBE1A18). A separate test environment uses its own credentials and never handles real patient data, keeping live patient information away from testing activity (DI-2E40F292). The system flags data quality problems, including gaps in information removal, and records whether each check passed or failed so the team can review issues (DI-FC80B65A). Clinicians must actively confirm they have seen any warnings about data gaps before the system continues, creating a pause point if a problem is detected (DI-00E16F9E). Every clinical statement the system produces is linked back to the original source text in the patient record, so reviewers can check exactly what information was used (DI-740BE510). Reviewers can also select and highlight the exact section of the note the AI used, making it easier to spot if sensitive details were included (DI-E81545BE). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter. Additional controls are being identified.

title_old: Pipeline codes treatment recommendations or safety-netting advice as present clinical findings
title_new: The AI tool wrongly codes treatment plans or safety-netting advice as confirmed clinical findings
hazard_old: The LLM extraction step assigns assertion "present" to entities extracted from treatment recommendation text (e.g. "consider starting metformin"), safety-netting instructions (e.g. "if develops chest pain, call 999"), or hedged diagnostic language (e.g. "consistent with migraine"). These entities then bypass the tier classifier's hypothetical/possible gates and may auto-code in autonomous mode.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes can misread sentences about future plans or warnings. For example, 'consider starting metformin' or 'call 999 if chest pain develops' describe things that have not happened yet. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible may label these as present findings. Those findings can then be saved into the patient record as if they were confirmed.
hazardous_situation_old: A clinical encounter contains treatment plans, safety-netting advice, or speculative diagnostic statements. The LLM extracts entities from these sentences with assertion "present" rather than "hypothetical" or "possible". In autonomous mode, these entities pass the tier classifier's Tier 1/2 gates and are persisted to the patient graph as confirmed clinical findings. In HITL mode, they appear as coding suggestions that waste reviewer time and erode trust.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinical note contains treatment plans, safety-netting advice, or uncertain diagnostic statements. The AI tool reads these sentences and wrongly marks them as confirmed present findings. In the fully automated setting, the system saves these directly into the patient record without a clinician checking them. In the setting where a clinician reviews suggestions, the wrong suggestions still appear and waste the reviewer's time.
harm_old: (a) A planned medication is coded as actively prescribed, creating a medication safety risk if the patient has not actually started it. (b) Safety-netting symptoms are coded as present findings, creating false positive diagnoses in the patient record. (c) A speculative diagnosis is coded as confirme
harm_new: A planned medicine may be coded as already prescribed. This creates a medicine safety risk if the patient has not yet started it. Safety-netting symptoms, such as chest pain to watch for, may be coded as findings the patient already has. This creates false diagnoses in the patient record. A speculative diagnosis may be coded as confirmed, leading to incorrect clinical decisions and potential patient harm.
mitigation_new: The system uses rules to exclude treatment recommendations and diagnostic uncertainty from being coded as confirmed findings. These rules are built into the AI workflow and are reviewed by the clinical safety team at each software release (DI-A3107424). The system automatically suppresses alerts for safety-netting advice once a confirmed clinical response has been coded. This runs without manual input every time a record is updated (DI-0E215ADE). The system shows clinicians a plain-language summary of any coded finding before it is saved. This gives the reviewing clinician a clear chance to spot and reject incorrect suggestions at every review session (DI-66F1B177). A character-level locator ties each AI-extracted finding back to the exact words in the original note. This lets the reviewing clinician see the source sentence and judge whether the finding is real, every time a suggestion is made (DI-A0C90595). A configurable follow-up time window flags outstanding findings and places them on a worklist. The clinical team reviews this worklist at agreed intervals to catch any incorrectly coded items before they affect patient care (DI-4C73DC01). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: LLM-generated surface form alias accepted by admin causes false-positive NER coding
title_new: An AI-suggested text alias causes the system to wrongly flag a clinical term in patient notes
hazard_old: The suggest-aliases endpoint (POST /terminology/concepts/{id}/suggest-aliases) uses a small LLM (Claude Haiku via AWS Bedrock) to propose additional text aliases for a SNOMED concept. The LLM operates on concept metadata only (FSN, semantic tag, existing aliases) — no patient data is transmitted. However, if the LLM suggests an alias that is ambiguous (e.g. "SOB" for "Shortness of Breath" when it could also mean "Son of a Bitch" in UK clinical notes, or "BP"
hazard_new: The system uses an AI tool to suggest extra text aliases for a clinical code. For example, it might suggest 'SOB' as an alias for 'Shortness of Breath'. But 'SOB' can mean something else entirely in UK clinical notes. If an administrator accepts an ambiguous or overly broad alias, the system will treat that phrase as a match for the clinical code whenever it appears in any patient's notes.
hazardous_situation_old: An administrator uses the Settings → Surface Forms interface to suggest aliases for a SNOMED concept using the AI button. The LLM returns a phrase that is clinically ambiguous or overly generic. The administrator accepts the suggestion. Subsequent encounters containing that phrase are flagged by the NER pipeline and may be auto-coded (Tier 1) or routed to review (Tier 2/3).
hazardous_situation_new: An administrator opens the terminology settings screen and uses the AI button to suggest new text aliases for a clinical code. The AI tool returns a phrase that is ambiguous or too generic. The administrator accepts it without realising the risk. From that point on, the AI tool that reads notes treats every occurrence of that phrase as a match for the clinical code. In fully automated mode the system may save that code directly to the patient record. In review mode it sends the match to a clinician for checking.
harm_old: (a) False-positive NER hit in autonomous mode causes an unintended clinical code to be written to the patient graph, degrading clinical coding accuracy and potentially inflating disease prevalence metrics used for population health management. (b) In HITL mode, spurious suggestions enter the review
harm_new: If the system saves the wrong clinical code directly to a patient record, that patient's record becomes inaccurate. This could distort disease registers and population health figures used to plan care. Even in review mode, clinicians waste time checking false matches, and there is a risk that a busy reviewer accepts a wrong code without noticing the error.
mitigation_new: First, before any clinical code is saved to a patient record, a reviewer must individually approve it. No code is saved automatically without this step (DI-4247C7E5). This check is carried out by a trained reviewer for every proposed code, every time. Second, when the AI tool reads notes and finds a match, it records a confidence score and shows exactly where in the notes the match was found. This helps reviewers spot weak or unlikely matches (DI-31126C6C). Third, the system is tested regularly against a set of examples checked by an expert. It must reach a minimum accuracy level before it is used in practice. This test is run by the technical team before each release (DI-12015DBC). Fourth, the review screen shows the reviewer the context around each match, including whether the term was recorded as present, absent, or possible. This helps the reviewer judge whether the match makes clinical sense (DI-375C7EB1). Fifth, the review screen also shows which text alias triggered the match and flags any known issues with that alias. This lets the reviewer or administrator remove a problem alias quickly (DI-4221A226). Sixth, a coding correction review step lets a clinician challenge and correct any code that has been saved in error, with full checks against the terminology list (DI-1B8AC856). Seventh, the AI tool that suggests aliases is restricted to producing aliases only within the correct clinical category for each code. This reduces the chance of a wildly inappropriate alias being suggested (DI-C899D282). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Terminology resolver accepts entity with wrong semantic tag — silent miscoding
title_new: AI tool matches clinical text to the wrong type of clinical code — error not flagged
hazard_old: The LLM extraction step assigns an entity label (e.g. "finding", "disorder", "procedure") to extracted clinical text. The terminology resolver then maps the text to a SNOMED concept. If the resolver's top candidate has a semantic tag that disagrees with the entity label (e.g. text "pain" labelled "disorder" but matched to 22253000 | Pain (finding)), the mismatch is accepted silently and the entity is coded against a concept of the wrong clinical category.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes gives each piece of clinical text a category label, such as 'finding', 'disorder', or 'procedure'. A separate part of the AI workflow then matches that text to a clinical code. Sometimes the clinical code it picks belongs to a different category than the label. For example, the word 'pain' is labelled as a 'disorder' but matched to a 'finding' code. The system accepts this mismatch without raising an alert.
hazardous_situation_old: A clinical encounter containing the text "pain" is processed. The LLM labels it as "disorder". The terminology resolver returns 22253000 | Pain (finding) with high confidence. Without cross-validation, the system accepts the match, coding a finding concept as if it were a disorder. In autonomous mode this incorrect coding enters the patient graph; in HITL mode it appears as a correctly-coded item and may be accepted without scrutiny.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinical note contains the word 'pain'. The AI tool labels it as a 'disorder'. The AI workflow finds a high-confidence 'finding' code for pain and accepts it without checking that the categories match. In fully automated mode, this wrongly categorised code is saved directly into the patient record. In review mode, the code appears correct on screen and the reviewing clinician may approve it without realising the category is wrong.
harm_old: (a) Incorrect SNOMED coding: entities are mapped to concepts of the wrong semantic category, distorting clinical coding accuracy. (b) In autonomous mode, miscoded entities enter the patient record and may affect quality measures, disease prevalence statistics, and clinical decision support. (c) In H
harm_new: First, clinical codes in the patient record are assigned to the wrong category. This reduces the accuracy of the patient's coded record. Second, in fully automated mode, these wrong codes enter the patient record and may affect quality measures, disease statistics, and any alerts or decision support tools that rely on correct coding. Third, in review mode, a clinician may approve the wrong code because the error is not visible, meaning the patient's long-term record contains inaccurate information that could influence future care.
mitigation_new: The AI workflow applies separate confidence thresholds for each clinical code category. It combines the category label confidence with the code-matching confidence before accepting a result. If either score is too low, the match is rejected automatically (DI-F0B8A7B0). A disorder-specific check runs as a final step. If this check fails, the system records a clear failed verdict and does not pass the code forward (DI-9D967259). The AI tool that reads notes records a full confidence score and source information for every code it proposes, so reviewers can see exactly how confident the system was and where the text came from (DI-31126C6C). Each coding proposal on the review screen shows the AI tool's context label and the supporting text, so the reviewing clinician can see why the code was suggested (DI-375C7EB1). All coding proposals must be individually approved by a reviewer before they are saved to the final record (DI-DI-4247C7E5). The system is tested against a set of examples checked by an expert before release. It must reach a minimum accuracy score of 0.85 on clinical coding before it can be used (DI-12015DBC). When a reviewer corrects a code, the system checks that the correction is valid and consistent with related codes before saving it (DI-1B8AC856). The AI tool uses a two-model approach where both models must agree before a code is accepted, reducing the chance of a single model making an unchecked error (DI-80DD8A47). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data on coding category mismatches every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Agentic auditor tool-use loop generates unbounded cloud API costs
title_new: AI audit tool enters a runaway loop and generates unexpected cloud computing costs
hazard_old: The Opus orchestrator enters a repeated tool-use loop, requesting terminology lookups iteratively without converging on a verdict. Each iteration incurs input and output tokens for Opus (expensive) and Haiku (cheaper), plus HTTP calls to the Terminology API. Without hard limits, a single record could generate hundreds of tool calls.
hazard_new: The AI audit tool can get stuck in a repeating loop when checking patient records. Each loop adds more computing costs. Without a firm limit on how many loops are allowed, a single patient record could trigger hundreds of repeated checks.
hazardous_situation_old: During a batch audit run of hundreds or thousands of TrainingLabel records, the agentic loop runs without a hard iteration cap or cost budget. Opus requests multiple tool calls per entity and multiple entities per record trigger pass 2. The cumulative token cost across the batch exceeds the authorised cloud budget, causing unexpected AWS Bedrock invoice charges and potential service disruption due to rate limiting.
hazardous_situation_new: When the AI audit tool checks a large batch of patient records, it may run without any limit on how many times it repeats its checks. This can happen across hundreds or thousands of records at once. The total computing cost can far exceed the approved budget. This may cause unexpected charges and could slow down or stop other clinical services that share the same system.
harm_old: Financial harm from unexpected cloud API charges. Potential Terminology API resource exhaustion affecting production services that depend on it. Delayed training data quality improvement due to run failure or budget suspension.
harm_new: Unexpected and potentially large financial charges from cloud computing use. Other clinical services that rely on the same system component may slow down or become unavailable. Improvements to the quality of examples used to teach the AI may be delayed if the process is stopped due to overspend.
mitigation_new: The AI audit tool has a built-in limit on how many times it can repeat a check, and a cost cap that stops it spending beyond an approved budget. The team configures and monitors these limits (DI-54D00E21). The audit programme settings, including these limits, can be adjusted at any time without a full system redeployment, so the team can respond quickly if costs rise unexpectedly (DI-CD931485). A quality report checks that enough safety-critical records have been reviewed before the audit run is accepted; this acts as an early warning if a run has failed or been cut short (DI-AE477327). All audit activity is recorded in a log that the team can review to spot runaway loops or unusual cost patterns (DI-09E26C1D). Patient record data is handled through a standard, controlled system component, which limits the volume of data that can be sent into the AI tool in a single run (DI-1795254D). The clinical safety committee reviews cost reports and loop-limit breach logs every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Haiku sub-agent returns incorrect SNOMED recommendations that are incorrectly applied to training labels
title_new: AI tool suggests wrong clinical code, which could enter the teaching examples used to train the system
