hazard_old: The Haiku sub-agent, when calling the Terminology API on behalf of Opus, may interpret API results incorrectly or hallucinate concept information not present in the API response. Opus, relying on these results, may produce a confident but incorrect SNOMED recommendation for a training label entity.
hazard_new: The AI workflow uses two AI components working together to suggest clinical codes for patient record labels. The smaller AI component looks up codes and passes results to the larger one. The smaller component may misread the lookup results or invent code information that was not there. The larger component may then accept this wrong suggestion with high confidence.
hazardous_situation_old: During pass 2 of the agentic audit, Haiku misinterprets terminology API results and returns a recommendation pairing an incorrect SNOMED concept with the entity. Opus accepts the recommendation at high confidence. If a subsequent code change were to relax the READONLY_FIELDS constraint, or if a human reviewer approves the proposal without adequate verification, the incorrect SNOMED code could enter training data and ultimately bias the production NLP pipeline toward incor
hazardous_situation_new: During a routine check of patient record labels, the smaller AI component returns a wrong clinical code pairing. The larger AI component accepts it confidently. If a reviewer approves this without checking carefully, or if a future software change removes the protection that stops automatic edits, the wrong clinical code could be saved into the examples used to teach the AI. This would teach the AI to code similar records incorrectly in future.
harm_old: Incorrect clinical coding in production NLP pipeline output, potentially affecting downstream clinical audit metrics and pathway coding accuracy for primary care patients.
harm_new: The AI tool that reads clinical notes could learn to apply wrong clinical codes to patient records. This could distort audit results and pathway coding for primary care patients. Clinicians and managers relying on those coded records could make decisions based on inaccurate information.
mitigation_new: An automated audit checks all teaching-example labels and flags problems for human review rather than fixing them automatically (DI-CFA65509). This runs continuously as part of the AI workflow. Any suggested change to a clinical code is always sent to a human reviewer and can never be applied automatically (DI-922114AE). The clinical safety team sets and monitors this rule. The AI workflow has strict limits on how many steps it can take and how much resource it can use, preventing runaway or unchecked activity (DI-54D00E21). These limits are configured by the technical team and reviewed regularly. All AI suggestions, including clinical code changes, go into a single review queue where reviewers can correct them, and those corrections are stored to improve future performance (DI-890BE989). Reviewers manage this queue as part of normal working. A separate check confirms that labels with multiple codes are recorded correctly (DI-EE80C271). This check runs automatically on each update. Before any update to the AI tool goes live, it must achieve at least 85 per cent accuracy on a set of labels checked by an expert clinician (DI-12015DBC). The clinical safety team runs this quality gate before each release. The system logs how often reviewers change or override AI suggestions, and the clinical safety officer has a dedicated view to spot signs that reviewers are accepting suggestions without adequate scrutiny (DI-22D862B0). The clinical safety committee reviews these metrics every quarter to confirm all controls are working as intended.

title_old: ODS API unavailable — nightly sync completes silently with no data freshness checks
title_new: Organisation data becomes out of date when the nightly update fails without raising an alert
hazard_old: The NHS ODS FHIR API becomes temporarily unavailable during the nightly sync window. Without a circuit breaker, the sync job could silently succeed (zero orgs checked) while LEO continues to use stale ODS data, unaware that organisations may have changed name, type, or closure status.
hazard_new: Each night, the system contacts NHS Digital to refresh the list of GP practices, PCNs, and other organisations. If that connection fails, the system may record the update as successful even though no new data was downloaded. Clinicians and managers then continue working with organisation information that could be weeks out of date, including organisations that have since closed or merged.
hazardous_situation_old: During the 02:00 UTC nightly sync, the ODS API returns connection errors for all requests. The sync job logs no errors and marks the run as complete. Practitioners continue to use LEO with org data that may be weeks old, including potentially organisations that have since been decommissioned or merged.
hazardous_situation_new: During the scheduled nightly update, the NHS Digital organisation service is unavailable. The system receives errors for every request but records the update as complete and raises no alert. The next morning, clinicians use the system without knowing that organisation names, types, and closure statuses may no longer be correct.
harm_old: Clinical audit records may be attributed to incorrect or decommissioned organisations, leading to inaccurate pathway coding metrics and misdirected clinical governance reports.
harm_new: Clinical audit records may be linked to the wrong organisation, or to one that no longer exists. This produces inaccurate pathway performance figures and sends clinical governance reports to the wrong team, delaying oversight of patient care quality.
mitigation_new: The system records a full audit trail showing which organisation data was used for each audit result and when it was last updated. The clinical safety team can review this trail to spot gaps in data freshness (DI-09E26C1D). Pathway performance figures are built from the NHS Digital organisation hierarchy, so any mismatch between stored and current organisation data becomes visible when metrics are reviewed at practice, PCN, and ICB level (DI-B9109EF5). The system exports audit results through a standard clinical data interface, and the receiving system can flag records that carry stale organisation details (DI-1795254D). A continuous quality monitoring process tracks coding accuracy and raises an alert if figures fall outside expected ranges, which can indicate that organisation data is wrong (DI-1126FFD1). The deployment status panel shows the outcome of recent system updates, allowing reviewers to see whether the last nightly organisation update completed correctly (DI-6EA84931). The clinical safety committee reviews these controls and their effectiveness every quarter.

title_old: Surface-form auto-correction applies incorrect SNOMED code
title_new: Auto-correction picks the wrong clinical code for a term
hazard_old: Automated correction may pick the wrong concept when terminology candidates are close.
hazard_new: When the AI tool that reads notes tries to fix a clinical term, it may choose a code that looks similar but means something different. This can happen silently, with no alert to the person reviewing the work.
hazardous_situation_old: The auto-correction engine selects a near-match SNOMED concept for a SurfaceForm entry, silently replacing the correct code. Downstream GoldLabel records inherit the wrong concept, degrading NER model training data quality without operator awareness.
hazardous_situation_new: The AI workflow automatically corrects a clinical term and links it to the wrong clinical code. The correct code is replaced without any warning. The expert-checked examples used to teach the AI then carry this wrong code. The team does not know the error has happened.
harm_old: Incorrect coding in gold labels reduces NER training quality.
harm_new: The AI learns from examples that contain the wrong clinical code. Over time, its accuracy falls. It may then pull incorrect information from patient notes, which could lead to a patient's condition being missed or wrongly recorded in their record.
mitigation_new: First, the system shows reviewers every clinical term alongside the codes that depend on it, so they can spot mismatches during the coding correction review. A trained clinician or coder carries out this check each time a correction is made (DI-4221A226). Second, each coding correction goes through a structured review that checks both the linked terms and the clinical code itself against the approved code list. A trained reviewer completes this check before any correction is saved (DI-1B8AC856). Third, the AI workflow must reach a minimum accuracy score on expert-checked examples before any updated coding is accepted. The clinical informatics team runs this quality gate before each model update (DI-12015DBC). Fourth, the interface for adding or changing clinical terms shows how often each term appears and blocks duplicate entries. Any person making changes uses this interface, and the system enforces these rules automatically at the point of entry (DI-30D95132). Fifth, an automated check reviews all expert-checked training examples, flags any that look wrong, limits how many can be auto-fixed at once, and places the rest in a queue for human review. The clinical informatics team monitors this queue on an ongoing basis (DI-CFA65509). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: TrainingCandidate or GoldLabel includes patient or encounter linkage
title_new: Teaching examples stored with patient-identifying details
hazard_old: Learning-loop data may contain identifiers enabling data-subject re-identification.
hazard_new: The AI tool learns from examples taken from real patient records. If those examples keep details that identify a patient — such as a patient number, visit reference, or organisation code — someone with access to the teaching data could trace the information back to a real person.
hazardous_situation_old: TrainingCandidate or GoldLabel nodes stored in the Knowledge Graph retain patient_id, encounter_id, or org_id fields. A data export or researcher access to the KG enables re-identification of clinical text to individual patients.
hazardous_situation_new: Examples used to teach the AI, and the expert-checked examples used to test it, are stored in the system's knowledge store. These records may still contain a patient number, a visit reference, or an organisation code. If a researcher or developer exports this data, they could link the clinical text back to an individual patient.
harm_old: GDPR breach and regulatory non-compliance.
harm_new: A real patient could be identified from data they did not consent to share in this way. This would be a serious breach of patient confidentiality and UK data-protection law, and could cause significant distress to the patient.
mitigation_new: Two controls reduce this risk. First, a patient-identifier detection check runs automatically every time teaching data is exported. If any patient number, visit reference, or organisation code is found, the export is stopped immediately and the attempt is logged for review. This check runs without any human action being needed (DI-452D4303). Second, the research export tool is designed so that a single action produces a structured export that contains method details but no patient identifiers. The tool enforces this by design, so identifiers cannot be included accidentally (DI-58988BF2). The clinical safety committee reviews the export logs and checks both controls are working every quarter. Additional controls are being identified.

title_old: SurfaceForm knowledge graph stores user identifiers
title_new: Patient record exports may include staff email addresses
hazard_old: created_by/approved_by fields expose operator identity in shared/exported KG artifacts.
hazard_new: The system stores the email address of the staff member who created or approved each clinical entry. If a record or data file is exported or shared, those email addresses travel with it.
hazardous_situation_old: SurfaceForm and MAPS_TO nodes in the Knowledge Graph contain created_by and approved_by fields with operator email addresses. If the KG is exported, shared with research partners, or queried by a broader user base, operator identities are exposed.
hazardous_situation_new: Each entry in the clinical knowledge store holds the email address of the staff member who created or approved it. When a clinician or researcher exports data, shares it with a partner organisation, or runs a broad query, those email addresses are included in the output without any warning.
harm_old: Personal data leakage for platform users and governance non-compliance.
harm_new: Staff email addresses are personal data. Sharing them without consent breaches UK data protection law. The harm to patients is indirect, but governance failure could undermine trust in the system and disrupt clinical services.
mitigation_new: The research export tool strips personal identifiers, including staff email addresses, before any data file leaves the system. The export tool runs automatically every time a clinician or researcher requests a data download (DI-58988BF2). A knowledge base monitoring dashboard lets the clinical safety team see what data has been exported and check that no personal identifiers appear in recent exports. The safety team reviews this dashboard on a scheduled basis (DI-E5609239). The clinical safety committee reviews both controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended. Additional controls are being identified.

title_old: LLM-generated AppropriatenessRule criteria may be incorrect or incomplete
title_new: AI-generated clinical rule criteria may be wrong or incomplete
hazard_old: The LLM consensus pipeline may generate AppropriatenessRule CriteriaGroup entries with incorrect SNOMED codes, missing exclusion criteria, or logically inverted PRESENT/ABSENT predicates. If such rules are approved and compiled into the active bitmap, patients may be inappropriately matched to (or excluded from) guideline recommendations.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads clinical guidelines can produce matching rules that contain wrong clinical codes, missing exclusion criteria, or conditions that are inverted so that present means absent and vice versa. If a rule like this is approved and activated, the system may wrongly match patients to a guideline recommendation, or fail to match patients who should be flagged.
hazardous_situation_old: The LLM consensus pipeline generates AppropriatenessRule CriteriaGroup entries with incorrect SNOMED codes or inverted predicates. An administrator approves the rule without detecting the error. The bitmap compiler includes the incorrect rule, and patient pathway evaluations produce false matches or missed flags.
hazardous_situation_new: The AI tool generates a clinical matching rule with a wrong clinical code or an inverted condition. An administrator reviews the rule but does not spot the error. The system activates the faulty rule. When a patient's record is checked against the rule, the system either flags the patient incorrectly or misses a flag that should have been raised. In a two-week-wait cancer pathway, a missed flag means a patient may not receive an urgent referral.
harm_old: Patients receive incorrect referral guidance -- either missing an urgent referral they should receive, or receiving an inappropriate referral. In a 2-week-wait cancer pathway context, a missed referral poses a direct patient safety risk.
harm_new: A patient on a two-week-wait cancer pathway either misses an urgent referral they need, or receives a referral that is not clinically appropriate. Missing an urgent cancer referral poses a direct risk to the patient's safety and could delay diagnosis of a serious condition.
mitigation_new: First, the AI tool records exactly which part of the source guideline it used and which version of its instructions it followed when creating each rule candidate. This gives reviewers a clear audit trail to check the AI's working (DI-147C8EF0). Second, every AI-generated rule candidate must pass through a mandatory review queue before it can be activated. A clinician or administrator must make an explicit decision to approve or reject each candidate, and the system keeps a two-way link between the original source and the approved rule so the decision can always be traced (DI-F94EB13F). Third, the AI tool is prevented from generating direct diagnostic or treatment recommendations on its own; it only produces structured rule candidates for human review, which limits the impact of any single error (DI-A3107424). Fourth, when a referral rule is being reviewed, the system shows the reviewer the eligibility criteria and comparable patient outcomes side by side, making it easier to spot a rule that does not match clinical intent (DI-6C5D77CA). Fifth, the system can run two independent AI models and compare their outputs before a candidate rule is put forward for review; differences between the two models highlight potential errors for the reviewer (DI-80DD8A47). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs from the review queue and checks that all controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: Bitmap may become stale after approved rules are added or changed in Neo4j
title_new: Updated clinical rules may not take effect after an administrator approves them
hazard_old: After an administrator approves new or edited AppropriatenessRules, the Redis bitmap is not automatically recompiled. If a new guideline is loaded and its rules are approved but the bitmap is not recompiled and activated, the inference pipeline continues to use the old ruleset and new rules have no clinical effect.
hazard_new: When an administrator approves new or updated clinical rules, a separate step is needed to make those rules active. If that step is missed, the system carries on using the old rules. The new rules have no effect on patients until the step is completed.
hazardous_situation_old: An administrator approves new AppropriatenessRules but does not recompile and activate the bitmap. The inference pipeline continues using the previous ruleset. Newly approved rules have no effect on patient pathway evaluations.
hazardous_situation_new: An administrator approves new clinical rules but does not complete the step needed to activate them. The system continues checking patients against the old rules only. The newly approved rules are silently ignored during patient pathway checks.
harm_old: Patients are not matched against newly approved guideline rules. This is a missed-guidance failure mode (false negatives in rule matching) that could delay appropriate referrals.
harm_new: Patients are checked against out-of-date clinical rules. The system may miss patients who should be referred or flagged under the new guidance. This could delay appropriate referrals for those patients.
mitigation_new: First, the system uses a verified deployment package to confirm that only approved, checked rule sets are loaded into the live system. This gives the team confidence that what is deployed matches what was approved (DI-EC27E4E7). The clinical safety team checks this at every deployment. Second, administrators can update and activate clinical rule sets directly, without needing a software release. This makes it quicker and simpler to complete the activation step and reduces the chance it is missed (DI-AA8014F9). Administrators follow this process whenever rules are approved. Third, the NICE catalogue tracks which clinical rules are active and flags any gaps in coverage against current pathways. This gives the clinical team a way to spot if newly approved rules have not taken effect (DI-9843D732). The clinical safety committee reviews the catalogue and activation logs every quarter to confirm controls are working.

title_old: NICE-sourced AuditDomain misclassification could propagate incorrect SNOMED concepts to audit pipelines
title_new: Wrong clinical codes from AI tool could spread errors across multiple care pathway checks
hazard_old: When NICE taxonomy sync creates AuditDomain nodes (source=nice) and an administrator subsequently promotes AppropriatenessRule SNOMED criteria to that domain, there is a risk that the rule's SNOMED coding is incorrect (e.g. wrong concept selected by the LLM) or that the guideline has been mapped to the wrong taxonomy subcategory. This misclassification then propagates into the domain's ValueSet, affecting all audit pipelines and pathway evaluations that consume that
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads clinical guidelines can pick the wrong clinical code when sorting a rule into a care category. An administrator can then approve and save that rule without noticing the error. Once saved, the wrong code spreads into the list of codes used to check patients across several care pathways at once.
hazardous_situation_old: NICE taxonomy sync creates AuditDomain nodes. An administrator promotes LLM-generated SNOMED criteria to the wrong domain or the criteria contain incorrect concepts. The corrupted ValueSet propagates to all audit pipelines consuming that domain, affecting patient matching across multiple pathways.
hazardous_situation_new: The AI tool assigns a wrong clinical code when processing a NICE guideline. An administrator approves the rule and saves it to the wrong care category. The incorrect code list then flows into every pathway check that uses that category, causing wrong patient matching across multiple pathways at the same time.
harm_old: Incorrect SNOMED concepts in an AuditDomain ValueSet could cause the audit pipeline to flag patients incorrectly as meeting or not meeting a clinical criterion, leading to inappropriate clinical alerts or missed flags. Because domains are reused across multiple pathways, a single misclassification c
harm_new: Patients may be wrongly flagged as meeting or not meeting a clinical criterion. This could trigger inappropriate clinical alerts or cause the system to miss patients who need follow-up. Because one code list feeds many pathways, a single error can affect a large number of patients before anyone notices.
mitigation_new: The AI tool is designed to preserve important clinical detail, such as whether a condition is confirmed or suspected, when it picks clinical codes. This reduces the chance of a wrong code being chosen in the first place (DI-6A0B55A4). The system keeps a structured record of how each NICE guideline maps to a care category and whether that mapping is active, partial, or not yet covered. This gives administrators a clear view to spot mismatches before approving a rule (DI-9843D732). The AI tool can handle overlapping clinical codes and classify them separately, reducing the risk of one code being confused with another (DI-DC61F5B6). When an authoritative source such as NICE publishes a change, the system detects it automatically and sends an alert to the responsible team so they can review affected rules promptly (DI-EF37BDF9). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and alert records every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Unauthorized access to per-tenant AI costs, margin configuration, and discount rates
title_new: Non-admin users accessing private pricing and discount information
hazard_old: The billing and pricing subsystem stores commercially sensitive data: the platform's target gross margin, per-tenant billable amounts, and negotiated discount rates. If any of this data were accessible to non-admin users (including tenant users who can see their own patient pipeline costs), it would expose Mizaic's commercial model and the preferential terms applied to individual tenants.
hazard_new: The billing part of the system stores sensitive commercial information. This includes the platform's target profit margin, how much each organisation is charged, and any special discount rates agreed with individual organisations. If a non-admin user could see this information, it would expose Mizaic's commercial model and the private terms agreed with other organisations.
hazardous_situation_old: A non-admin user or API consumer discovers pricing endpoint URLs and sends direct requests. Without server-side access control, they could read target gross margin, per-tenant discount rates, and billable amounts -- exposing Mizaic's commercial model.
hazardous_situation_new: A non-admin user or an organisation's own staff member finds the web addresses used by the billing part of the system. They send requests directly to those addresses. If the system does not check who is asking, they could read the target profit margin, other organisations' discount rates, and billing amounts.
harm_old: Disclosure of gross margin to a tenant user or competitor would reveal Mizaic's cost structure. Disclosure of another tenant's discount rate could lead to reputational harm or contractual disputes. This is a business/commercial risk with no direct patient safety impact.
harm_new: If the profit margin is seen by an organisation's staff or a competitor, it reveals how Mizaic prices its service. If one organisation sees another organisation's discount rate, this could cause reputational damage or contract disputes. This risk is commercial only. There is no direct risk to patient safety.
mitigation_new: The system keeps a permanent, unchangeable record of every pricing change, including who made it and when. This means any unauthorised change is visible immediately (DI-F407CC45). The system also records how much AI processing each organisation uses and applies the correct commercial rates automatically, reducing the chance of manual errors exposing sensitive figures (DI-19B08FFC). A named system administrator reviews access to billing settings as part of routine checks. The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter. Additional controls are being identified.

title_old: Undocumented NICE API schema changes could silently break taxonomy sync, leaving the taxonomy browser empty
title_new: A silent change to the NICE guidelines list could leave clinicians unable to browse guidelines by clinical area
hazard_old: The NICE Syndication API's taxonomy endpoint (newtaxonomy.json) uses an undocumented JSON schema that differs from the published API guide. The live response uses lowercase keys ("name", "categories", "paths") and a self-contained nested tree structure, whereas the guide describes a different shape. If NICE changes this schema without notice, the fetch_taxonomy() parser could return 0 subcategories with no user-visible error, causing the taxonomy browser to si
hazard_new: The system fetches the NICE list of guideline categories from an online source. NICE can change the format of that list at any time without warning. If the format changes, the AI tool that reads the list may find zero categories and show no error message. Clinicians and administrators would see an empty browse screen with no explanation.
hazardous_situation_old: NICE updates newtaxonomy.json schema. The parser fails to extract categories or guideline codes. The taxonomy browser triggers repeated catalogue syncs (auto-sync loop), or shows "No areas found" without explaining why, blocking administrators from discovering and loading guidelines by clinical area.
hazardous_situation_new: NICE changes the format of its guidelines list without notice. The system fails to read the new format. The browse screen shows 'No areas found'. The system may repeatedly try to refresh the list, adding unnecessary load. Administrators cannot browse guidelines by clinical area to load them into the system. Guidelines already loaded continue to work, and clinicians can still find guidelines by typing a NICE code directly or using text search.
harm_old: Taxonomy sync failure does not directly harm patients -- guidelines can still be loaded by typing a NICE code directly or via text search on the Redis catalogue. However, sustained failure degrades the discoverability UX, may cause unnecessary API load from repeated syncs, and reduces confidence in
harm_new: This failure does not directly harm patients. Guidelines already in the system keep working normally. However, if the failure goes unnoticed for a long time, new or updated guidelines may not be loaded. Clinicians could miss updated guidance. Confidence in the system may fall. The risk is minor because direct code entry and text search remain available as alternatives.
mitigation_new: The system monitors the NICE online source for any changes to its format or content and sends an alert to the responsible team when a change is detected (DI-EF37BDF9). This check runs automatically every time the system fetches the guidelines list. The system uses a scheduled automated process to pull guideline information from NICE into the knowledge store; if this process fails, the team is notified (DI-E19F72DB). This runs on a fixed schedule, typically daily. The system records a clear, readable error message whenever a fetch or format problem occurs, so the support team can identify and fix the problem quickly (DI-6654FB0E). The system also classifies guidelines by clinical area and tracks which areas have current coverage; gaps caused by a failed update are visible to administrators (DI-9843D732). All changes to the guidelines list and any detected problems are logged in an auditable record that the clinical safety team can review (DI-5E721A71). The clinical safety committee reviews these logs and any outstanding alerts every quarter to confirm the controls are working.

title_old: A systematic drop in NER coding accuracy goes undetected for multiple weeks, allowing incorrect patient records to accumulate.
title_new: A drop in coding accuracy goes unnoticed for several weeks, letting incorrect patient records build up.
hazard_old: The NER coding pipeline introduces a systematic error -- for example, after a model update, a surface form change, or a new encounter type -- that causes many encounters to be coded incorrectly. Because monitoring is automated and weekly, a regression that begins mid-week may not be detected until the next audit cycle. If the audit itself fails to run, no alert is raised at all.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes and assigns clinical codes can develop a systematic error. This may happen after a software update, a change in how notes are written, or a new type of consultation. The weekly check that spots these errors may miss a problem that starts mid-week. If the weekly check fails to run at all, no alert is raised and no one is told.
hazardous_situation_old: A regression in coding quality occurs. The weekly audit fails to run (infrastructure failure, timeout, or immutability guard blocking a retry) or the auditor LLM misses the regression (false negative). No SafetyNetAlert is raised. Clinical staff and operations team are unaware. Patients accumulate incorrect or missing SNOMED codes in their records for several weeks before the next manual clinical audit detects the problem.
hazardous_situation_new: Coding quality falls across many patient records. The weekly accuracy check either fails to run due to a technical fault or runs but does not spot the problem. No alert reaches clinical staff or the operations team. Patients accumulate incorrect or missing clinical codes in their records for several weeks until a manual clinical review finds the problem.
harm_old: Patients with incorrect or missing clinical codes may receive wrong clinical decisions, incorrect triage classifications, or be missed by QOF recall searches. Systematic under-coding of safety-critical conditions (cancer, safeguarding, mental health) may delay referrals.
harm_new: Patients with incorrect or missing clinical codes may receive the wrong clinical decision or be placed in the wrong triage group. They may be missed by recall searches for long-term condition reviews. If serious conditions such as cancer, safeguarding concerns, or mental health problems are not coded correctly, referrals or follow-up may be delayed.
mitigation_new: Six controls reduce this risk. First, the system continuously measures coding accuracy and raises an alert if it detects a drop; the AI workflow runs this check automatically and without interruption (DI-1126FFD1). Second, the system checks how often each type of clinical code is used and raises an alert if the pattern changes beyond a set threshold; the operations team can adjust that threshold; this check runs automatically each week (DI-37315D03). Third, when a drift alert is raised, the system records the reason and stores a full history of all alerts for two years in a way that cannot be altered; the operations team reviews this log (DI-B1E0EE52). Fourth, the system automatically checks that coded consultations follow clinical guidelines; this check runs on every coded encounter as it is processed (DI-2AFF691F). Fifth, a registry of guideline monitoring rules is kept under clinical change control; it holds the full context of every alert and sets out who must be told and when; the clinical safety team maintains this registry and reviews it when guidelines change (DI-ED3A89F5). Sixth, before any update goes live, the AI tool that assigns clinical codes must reach a minimum accuracy score on a set of encounters checked by an expert; if it does not reach that score, the update is blocked; the clinical safety team runs this check before every release (DI-12015DBC). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all six controls are working at least every quarter.

title_old: Repeated false-positive quality alerts cause the operations team to stop responding, allowing a genuine regression to be ignored indefinitely.
title_new: Too many false alerts cause staff to ignore them, so a real coding failure goes unnoticed.
hazard_old: If the auditor generates frequent false-positive alerts -- for example, because the statistical threshold is too sensitive or because normal week-to-week variation exceeds the trigger -- operations staff learn to dismiss alerts without investigation. When a genuine coding regression occurs, the alert is acknowledged without action or left unacknowledged until the auto-escalation fires at 14 days.
hazard_new: The AI tool that checks coding quality can fire alerts too often. This happens when its trigger threshold is set too low, or when normal week-to-week variation sets it off. Staff who see repeated false alerts learn to dismiss them without looking. When a real problem occurs, such as cancer codes being missed, the alert is dismissed in the same way. The problem then continues for up to 14 days before the system automatically pauses the AI workflow.
hazardous_situation_old: Auditor generates repeated false-positive SafetyNetAlerts. Operations staff develop alert fatigue and acknowledge alerts without reading them. A genuine coding regression (e.g. cancer codes being missed) generates an alert that is acknowledged reflexively within minutes with no investigation. The regression persists for up to 14 days until the auto-pause fires, or longer if the auto-pause is manually overridden.
hazardous_situation_new: The AI quality checker sends repeated alerts that turn out to be false alarms. Operations staff stop reading them properly and click to acknowledge without investigating. A genuine coding failure, for example cancer or safeguarding codes being missed, triggers an alert that staff dismiss within minutes. The coding failure continues for up to 14 days until the system automatically pauses. If staff manually override that pause, the failure continues even longer.
harm_old: Safety-critical coding gaps (cancer, safeguarding, mental health) persist undetected for weeks. Patients whose encounters are affected do not receive timely clinical follow-up triggered by the correct code.
harm_new: Serious coding gaps, covering cancer, safeguarding, and mental health, go unnoticed for weeks. Patients whose records are affected do not get the timely clinical follow-up that the correct code would have triggered.
mitigation_new: The AI workflow uses configurable thresholds to suppress alerts that fall within normal variation, reducing the number of false alarms that reach staff (DI-79509E39). The clinical safety team reviews and adjusts these thresholds regularly. The system continuously monitors coding quality and sends a regression alert whenever accuracy drops below an agreed level (DI-1126FFD1). The clinical safety team reviews these metrics at least monthly. If an alert is not acknowledged within the agreed time, the system automatically pauses the AI workflow and escalates to a senior responsible person (DI-5A802C83). This escalation runs without any manual step. Every alert acknowledgement is recorded with the clinician or operator identity and a timestamp, creating a permanent log that cannot be altered (DI-B46AD5CE). The clinical safety team audits this log quarterly. When a regression alert fires, staff must label the root cause before closing it. All alert history is kept for two years and cannot be deleted (DI-B1E0EE52). The clinical safety team uses this history to spot patterns of alert fatigue. Safety-critical entity types, including cancer and safeguarding codes, are counted and checked against a minimum quality gate before any update to the AI workflow goes live (DI-AE477327). The clinical safety team runs this check before every release. Any change to the coding rules used by the AI tool must pass through a staged review, be approved, and be version-controlled so it can be rolled back if a regression is detected (DI-9FD54AD6). The clinical safety committee reviews all of these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: An overcoded diagnosis remains in a patient record undetected, causing incorrect clinical decisions or inappropriate follow-up.
title_new: A false diagnosis code stays in a patient record and leads to wrong clinical decisions or unnecessary follow-up.
hazard_old: The NER pipeline or LLM extractor incorrectly codes a condition that the patient does not have (overcoding). If the audit identifies this but the remediation item is not reviewed promptly, the false code persists in the patient's record and may influence clinical decisions, triage classifications, or QOF register memberships.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes can wrongly add a diagnosis the patient does not have. This is called overcoding. If the audit spots the error but no one reviews it quickly, the false code stays in the record. Clinical staff may then act on it, affecting treatment decisions, waiting-list membership, or care pathways.
hazardous_situation_old: Audit Phase 3 identifies an overcoded diagnosis (e.g. cancer code on a record where the patient does not have cancer). A CodingReview node is created with priority='urgent'. The review item is mixed into the general queue and deprioritised, or the reviewer is on leave. After 48 hours, no SafetyNetAlert is raised because the alert logic does not check overcoded SLA. The false code persists for days or weeks. Clinical staff reviewing the record act on the false code. har
hazardous_situation_new: The audit finds an overcoded diagnosis — for example, a cancer code on a record where the patient does not have cancer. The system creates an urgent review task. That task gets lost in a general queue, or the reviewer is on leave. After 48 hours, no safety alert is raised because the alert rules do not check whether urgent overcoding tasks have been completed on time. The false code stays in the record for days or weeks. Clinicians reading the record see the false code and make decisions based on it.
harm_old: Patient receives unnecessary clinical follow-up, investigation, or anxiety from a false cancer or serious condition code. Alternatively, an incorrect condition code affects downstream QOF searches, pathway decisions, or referral routing.
harm_new: The patient may receive unnecessary tests, referrals, or treatment based on a condition they do not have. They may also suffer significant worry or distress from a false serious-illness code. The false code may also place the patient on the wrong care register or direct them down the wrong care pathway.
mitigation_new: First, the system holds all urgent overcoding review tasks in a dedicated queue with a strict time limit and automatic escalation if the task is not completed on time. The clinical informatics team monitors this queue daily (DI-5E1BA369). Second, a human-review gate stops any audit findings from being used or reported until a trained reviewer has checked and approved them. The clinical coding team runs this check before each audit report is released (DI-BD696225). Third, a separate accuracy check compares the results from the AI tool that reads notes against a second set of rules to catch disagreements before any code reaches the patient record. The clinical safety team reviews these comparison results weekly (DI-F298AE65). Fourth, a change-control gate requires review and approval before any update to the way the AI tool labels diagnoses can go live, with the ability to roll back if a problem is found. The clinical safety officer approves each change (DI-9FD54AD6). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all four controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: An incorrect reusable surface form mapping is approved by a single reviewer and systematically miscodes all future encounters with the same phrase.
title_new: A single reviewer approves a wrong clinical code for a common phrase, causing every future patient record with that phrase to be coded incorrectly.
hazard_old: A reviewer resolves a CodingReview with an incorrect concept (perhaps a plausible but wrong SNOMED code). If the system immediately creates a MAPS_TO relationship from this single decision, every future encounter containing the same phrase will be coded with the wrong concept, without any further human review.
hazard_new: When a reviewer links a phrase to a clinical code, the AI tool saves that link and uses it automatically for every future patient record containing the same phrase. If the reviewer picks the wrong code, no second check happens. Every record with that phrase is then coded incorrectly until someone notices.
hazardous_situation_old: Reviewer A resolves a CodingReview for phrase "chest tightness" with SNOMED code for "anxiety" instead of "angina". The system creates a MAPS_TO immediately. All subsequent encounters containing "chest tightness" are auto-coded as anxiety. Patients with cardiac symptoms are miscoded for weeks until the next audit detects the pattern.
hazardous_situation_new: A reviewer links the phrase 'chest tightness' to the clinical code for anxiety instead of angina. The AI tool immediately saves this link. All future patient records containing 'chest tightness' are automatically coded as anxiety. Patients with possible heart symptoms are miscoded for weeks until a routine audit spots the pattern.
harm_old: Systematic miscoding of a clinical phrase causes incorrect SNOMED codes in multiple patient records. Patients with the phrase may receive wrong clinical decisions, incorrect pathway routing, or be missed by QOF searches for the correct condition.
harm_new: Many patient records carry the wrong clinical code for the same phrase. Patients with that phrase may be sent down the wrong care pathway, receive the wrong clinical decisions, or be missed when the system searches for patients with a specific condition such as angina.
mitigation_new: First, the system holds any new phrase-to-code link in a staging area before it goes live. A second reviewer must approve the change, and the system keeps a full version history so any wrong link can be rolled back quickly (DI-9FD54AD6). The clinical safety team checks this gate is working every quarter. Second, when a reviewer is deciding on a code, the screen shows how many patient records use that phrase. This helps the reviewer understand the impact of their choice before approving it. The system also blocks duplicate links from being created (DI-30D95132). Third, every coded entry in a patient record keeps a clear link back to the original note and the source of the code. This makes it straightforward to trace and correct a wrong code if one is found (DI-740BE510). Fourth, the AI tool cannot publish any coded interpretation without a reviewer making an active decision. No code reaches a patient record without human sign-off (DI-604767B1). Fifth, the review screen shows whether a change has already been deployed to live records. Reviewers can see the potential reach of a decision before they approve it (DI-6EA84931). Sixth, the review screen shows which patient records and phrases depend on the link being changed. Reviewers can see the full impact before approving (DI-4221A226). Seventh, after codes are saved to patient records, an automated check runs to flag any coded entries that do not match accepted clinical guidelines. This catches patterns of miscoding early (DI-2AFF691F). The clinical safety committee reviews audit results from all these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Revoking an incorrect surface form mapping removes future use but leaves all previously coded encounters still carrying the wrong code.
title_new: Fixing a wrong clinical code link stops future errors but leaves past patient records with the wrong code.
hazard_old: A surface form mapping is identified as incorrect and revoked. The MAPS_TO relationship is deleted and future encounters will no longer use it. However, all encounters that were coded using this mapping after first_used_at still carry the incorrect SNOMED code, and there is no mechanism to trace or correct them.
hazard_new: Sometimes a link between a written term and a clinical code is found to be wrong. The AI tool that reads notes can be told to stop using that link. This prevents new errors. However, every patient record already coded using that wrong link keeps the incorrect code. There is no automatic way to find those records or correct them.
hazardous_situation_old: An incorrect MAPS_TO mapping has been in use for 3 weeks. 47 encounters have been coded with the wrong concept. A reviewer notices and revokes the mapping. The MAPS_TO is removed, but the 47 DOCUMENTS relationships still carry the incorrect source='provisional' code. No CodingReview nodes are created for them. Clinical staff reviewing those 47 records continue to see the incorrect code.
hazardous_situation_new: A wrong code link goes unnoticed for three weeks. During that time, 47 patient encounters are saved with the wrong clinical code. A reviewer spots the error and removes the link. Future encounters are now coded correctly. But those 47 records still show the wrong code. No alert or review task is created for them. Any clinician looking at those 47 records will see the wrong code and may act on it.
harm_old: Historical patient records carry incorrect SNOMED codes from a revoked mapping. Depending on the clinical domain, this may affect triage decisions, QOF register memberships, referral routing, or audit data quality. The scope of harm is proportional to use_count and the severity of the incorrect conc
harm_new: Past patient records carry wrong clinical codes. Depending on the clinical area, this could affect how urgent a referral appears, whether a patient is added to a disease register, which care pathway they follow, or the accuracy of audit data. The more records affected and the more serious the clinical area, the greater the potential harm to patients.
mitigation_new: Five controls reduce the chance of harm from past records carrying a wrong clinical code. First, the system shows clinicians a referral triage view with eligibility rules and comparable outcomes, helping them spot when a referral decision looks unusual; this runs automatically each time a referral is reviewed (DI-6C5D77CA). Second, the system automatically checks whether coded encounters follow current clinical guidelines; this check runs on every coded encounter and flags those that do not match expected patterns (DI-2AFF691F). Third, the coding correction review page shows how often a clinical code has been used over time; a reviewer can see a sudden spike in use that may signal a wrong code link has been active, and this display is available to any clinician or coder opening the review page (DI-22F4E3CE). Fourth, the coding correction review page also shows which written terms depend on a given code link; this helps reviewers understand how many records may be affected before and after a correction, and is available on demand to reviewers (DI-4221A226). Fifth, any change to a code link must pass through a staged review and approval process before it takes effect; changes are versioned and can be rolled back if needed, and this gate is applied every time a code link is created or changed (DI-9FD54AD6). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and flagged encounters every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Patient-identifiable information leaks into the NER training corpus via evidence_sentence storage or training export, creating a UK GDPR data breach.
title_new: Patient details leak into AI teaching files, causing a data breach.
hazard_old: The de-identification pipeline (deidentify_with_span) fails to remove all patient-identifiable information from an encounter sentence before it is stored as evidence_sentence on a DOCUMENTS relationship, or before it is written to a training export JSONL file. The resulting training artefact contains patient data that was processed under a different lawful basis (direct care) than the one documented in the DPIA for AI training.
hazard_new: The system is designed to remove patient details from clinical notes before storing or exporting them. If this removal step fails, real patient details — such as a name, NHS number, date of birth, or address — can end up saved inside the system or written into files used to teach the AI. Those files are then accessible to people who have no right to see patient records.
hazardous_situation_old: A patient's name, NHS number, date of birth, or address appears within an encounter sentence. The de-identification pipeline misses this token (failure mode: entity type not in the PII recogniser vocabulary, or sentence structure confuses the recogniser). The raw identifier is stored in evidence_sentence. During training export, detect_phi() also misses it (same failure mode). The identifier appears in the training JSONL file, which is accessible to NLP engineers and pote
hazardous_situation_new: A patient's name, NHS number, date of birth, or address appears in a clinical note. The tool that removes patient details misses it — for example, because it does not recognise that type of detail, or because the sentence is written in an unusual way. The raw detail is saved into the system. When teaching files are later created, a second check also misses it. The patient's detail ends up inside a teaching file that AI developers can read.
harm_old: Patient-identifiable information disclosed to NLP engineers without a valid lawful basis under UK GDPR Articles 6 and 9. Constitutes a notifiable data breach under Section 67 of the Data Protection Act 2018. Potential harm: patient privacy violated, ICO regulatory action, loss of patient and commiss
harm_new: A patient's private details are shared with AI developers without a lawful reason under UK data protection law. This is a reportable data breach under the Data Protection Act 2018. The patient's privacy is violated. The organisation may face investigation and enforcement action by the Information Commissioner's Office. Commissioners and patients may lose trust in the service.
mitigation_new: First, before any teaching file is created, an automatic check scans the file for patient details and stops the export if any are found, logging the problem for review by the clinical safety team (DI-452D4303). This check runs every time a teaching file is produced. Second, the system stores a protected set of teaching examples that are kept separate and cannot be changed, so there is always a clean reference set to compare against (DI-BB64E479). This separation is set up once and maintained permanently by the technical team. Third, the system records accuracy figures for each type of detail the removal tool is supposed to catch, and stores these results each time the AI is retrained (DI-CE0A08E5). The clinical safety team reviews these figures after every retraining run to spot any drop in performance. Fourth, if an export fails or a problem is logged, the system provides a list of affected records with the reason for failure, and allows the team to reprocess them with one action (DI-69CE20C1). The clinical safety team reviews this list at least weekly. Fifth, the system exports teaching examples in a format that preserves all detail labels without loss, so that any remaining patient details are not hidden during review (DI-6EFD68D0). The technical team checks this format is working correctly with each new software release. The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Holdout encounters leak into training data, inflating evaluation metrics and concealing true model performance on unseen encounters.
title_new: Test patient records used during AI training, making accuracy results misleading and hiding true performance.
hazard_old: Encounters designated as holdout (marked holdout=true on DOCUMENTS relationships) are included in a training export, either because the export query does not correctly filter on the holdout flag, or because a holdout encounter was added to the set after training data had already been collected from it. The trained NER model has effectively seen its own test data, making the evaluation metrics meaningless.
hazard_new: Some patient records are set aside as test records, so the AI tool that reads notes is never trained on them. This keeps the test fair. If those test records are accidentally included in training, the AI has already seen its own test. Its accuracy scores look good, but they no longer reflect how it will perform on real, unseen records.
hazardous_situation_old: The training export query omits the holdout filter (e.g. due to a code change that drops the WHERE clause). Holdout encounters are included in ner_training_gold.jsonl. The model trains on these examples. At evaluation, the model scores well on the holdout set because it has already seen the data. The NER team concludes the model is production-ready. In production, the model performs worse than the metrics indicated, including on safety-critical categories (cancer, safegua
hazardous_situation_new: A change to the system removes the filter that keeps test records separate. Test records are included when training data is collected. The AI tool that reads notes trains on these records. When the team checks accuracy using the same records, the scores are high because the AI has already seen them. The team concludes the AI is ready for use. In practice, the AI performs worse than the scores suggested. This includes detecting safety-critical conditions such as cancer, safeguarding concerns, and mental health problems.
harm_old: An NER model is deployed believing it meets quality thresholds, but the real-world performance is unknown and potentially worse. Safety- critical entity detection (cancer, safeguarding, mental health) may be below threshold, leading to missed codes in patient records with no warning.
harm_new: The AI tool is released believing it meets the required accuracy standard. Its true real-world accuracy is unknown and may be below that standard. It may miss clinical codes for cancer, safeguarding, or mental health in patient records. No warning is given to the clinician. A patient's condition may go unrecorded and unacted upon.
mitigation_new: Four controls are in place to reduce this risk. First, the training data is kept in a fixed, separate store with an immutable barrier between training records and test records. No training run can access test records. The AI development team maintains this separation at all times (DI-BB64E479). Second, before any training run is approved, an automated check counts how many safety-critical records, covering cancer, safeguarding, and mental health, are present in the training set. If the count does not meet the required threshold, training is blocked. The AI development team runs this check before every training cycle (DI-AE477327). Third, after the AI tool is deployed, an automated check runs against coded patient records to confirm the AI is still performing as expected. The AI development team runs this check on a scheduled basis (DI-2AFF691F). Fourth, the system monitors how often each type of clinical code appears over time. If the frequency drifts beyond a set limit, an alert is raised. The AI development team reviews these alerts on a scheduled basis (DI-37315D03). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all four controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Administrative appointment header lines are coded as clinical SNOMED findings
title_new: Admin appointment details are saved as clinical findings in the patient record
hazard_old: EMIS encounter exports include structured administrative header lines (e.g. timestamps, staff names, entry locations, appointment confirmations). If the NLP pipeline processes these lines as clinical text, the extractor may produce SNOMED codings such as "Seen in general practitioner surgery" or "Seen in primary care establishment" derived solely from administrative metadata rather than clinician-documented clinical content.
hazard_new: Patient records in EMIS include administrative lines such as timestamps, staff names, and appointment confirmations. The AI tool that reads notes may treat these lines as clinical content. If it does, it can attach clinical codes to them — for example, codes meaning 'seen in GP surgery' — even though no clinician wrote a clinical finding. These codes come from admin data, not from a doctor's assessment.
hazardous_situation_old: During encounter processing, the sentence splitter produces a chunk from an administrative header line. The NER or LLM extractor identifies a clinical context code and the pipeline writes a DOCUMENTS relationship with the header line as the evidence phrase. This coded record appears in the patient clinical graph as a clinical finding, potentially inflating encounter-level coding counts and distorting audit dashboards. Reviewers may accept the code without recognising it w
hazardous_situation_new: When the AI workflow processes an encounter, it may pick up an admin header line and treat it as a clinical statement. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible then assigns a clinical code to that line. The code is saved into the patient's clinical record as if it were a real finding. This can inflate the count of coded findings in the record. Audit dashboards may then show misleading results. A clinician reviewing the record may accept the code without realising it came from an admin line rather than a clinical note.
harm_old: Patient clinical records contain spurious SNOMED codes not supported by clinical documentation. Audit quality metrics are distorted. In a HITL context, a reviewer accepting a header-sourced code may create a misleading training label. In autonomous mode, the patient record is directly corrupted.
harm_new: The patient's clinical record contains clinical codes that are not supported by any clinical note. Audit quality reports become inaccurate. When a clinician reviews and approves a code that came from an admin line, that approval may also be used as an example to teach the AI — making the problem worse over time. If the system is running without clinician review, the patient record is changed directly on the basis of admin text, not clinical judgement.
mitigation_new: First, the AI workflow stores the exact words it used as evidence alongside every clinical code it assigns. This lets a reviewing clinician see at a glance whether the evidence is a clinical note or an admin line. The clinical safety team checks this is working every quarter (DI-23822663). Second, every clinical code is shown to the reviewer with a plain-English explanation of what the code means and where the evidence came from. This helps clinicians spot codes that do not match any real clinical finding. The clinical safety team audits a sample of reviewed codes monthly (DI-66F1B177). Third, the review screen shows the reviewer the exact evidence phrase and the AI's judgement — whether the finding was present, absent, or possible — for every code on the review card. This makes it easier to reject codes sourced from admin lines. The clinical safety team checks the review screen design every quarter (DI-375C7EB1). Fourth, the AI workflow runs two independent checks on every code: the AI tool that reads notes and a separate rules-based check. If the two checks disagree, the code is flagged for human review rather than saved automatically. The clinical safety team reviews disagreement rates monthly (DI-F298AE65). Fifth, the system tracks coding accuracy continuously and raises an alert if the rate of unexpected or low-quality codes rises above a set threshold. The clinical safety team reviews these alerts weekly (DI-1126FFD1). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls together every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Ambiguous GP abbreviation resolved to clinically incorrect SNOMED concept
title_new: A common GP abbreviation is matched to the wrong clinical code
hazard_old: A GP abbreviation with multiple valid clinical meanings (e.g. CA = carcinoma OR CA = calcium; NAD = no abnormality detected OR nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide; MSK = musculoskeletal specialty OR a clinical finding) is resolved to the wrong SNOMED concept by the NLP pipeline without sufficient disambiguating context.
hazard_new: GPs often use short abbreviations that can mean more than one thing. For example, CA can mean cancer or calcium. NAD can mean no abnormality detected or a body chemical. MSK can mean a musculoskeletal problem or a specialty. The AI tool that reads notes may pick the wrong meaning if the surrounding text does not make the intended meaning clear. The wrong clinical code is then saved to the patient record.
hazardous_situation_old: The LLM extractor or NER model extracts a short abbreviation from encounter text and passes it to the terminology resolver without the organ/site context required to disambiguate the intended meaning. The resolver returns a biochemistry concept, a generic concept, or a specialty tag concept instead of the clinically correct one. The incorrect code is written to the patient graph and displayed in the clinical review UI, potentially influencing coding decisions, QOF reporti
hazardous_situation_new: The AI tool that reads notes pulls a short abbreviation from a consultation entry. It passes the abbreviation to the part of the AI workflow that matches words to clinical codes. That part does not have enough surrounding detail, such as the body site or organ, to choose the correct code. It returns a biochemistry code, a vague general code, or a specialty label instead of the clinically correct one. The wrong code is saved into the patient record and shown on the clinical review screen. This could affect how the patient is coded, influence GP contract reporting, and shape future clinical decisions.
harm_old: Patient record contains an incorrect SNOMED code: either a false-positive cancer/biochemistry code (overcoding) or a missing cancer/chronic-disease code (undercoding, e.g. standalone CA not coded at all without site context). Overcoding poses the greater immediate risk as it may trigger unnecessary
harm_new: The patient record holds the wrong clinical code. If a cancer or serious disease code is added in error, the patient may be referred or investigated unnecessarily. If a genuine cancer or long-term condition code is missed entirely, the patient may not receive the follow-up, monitoring, or treatment they need. Adding a code in error carries the greater immediate risk because it can trigger urgent clinical actions based on incorrect information.
mitigation_new: First, the AI workflow checks that any clinical code it suggests is supported by the specific words found in the notes. This stops codes being suggested when the surrounding text is too vague to confirm the meaning. The clinical informatics team sets this up as part of the system build, and it runs automatically every time the AI processes a note (DI-C899D282). Second, the AI tool that reads notes and a separate checking step must both agree on whether a condition is present, absent, or possible before a code is suggested. If they disagree, the code is held back for a clinician to review. The clinical informatics team configures this check, and it runs automatically on every entry (DI-F298AE65). Third, the clinical review screen shows the clinician the exact words from the notes that led to each suggested code, together with a label saying whether the condition was recorded as present, absent, or possible. The clinician can see this information before accepting or rejecting any code. The development team builds this into the review screen, and it is visible at every coding review (DI-375C7EB1). Fourth, the review screen also shows which other words or phrases in the notes the suggested code depends on, so the clinician can judge whether the full context supports the code. The development team builds this into the review screen, and it is visible at every coding review (DI-4221A226). Fifth, a coding correction workflow lets clinicians flag and correct any wrong code. When a correction is made, the system checks that related codes in the record are still consistent. The clinical informatics team maintains this workflow, and it is available to clinicians at all times (DI-1B8AC856). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data on coding corrections and disagreements between the AI steps every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Automated audit remediation applies an incorrect SNOMED coding change to a patient record
title_new: The AI workflow applies a wrong clinical code change to a patient record
hazard_old: The remediation script misinterprets an audit finding or the LLM verification agrees with an incorrect proposed change, resulting in a DOCUMENTS relationship being deleted, added, or updated incorrectly.
hazard_new: The AI workflow misreads an audit finding. The AI tool that checks the proposed change then agrees with the wrong answer. This causes a clinical code link in the patient record to be wrongly deleted, added, or altered.
hazardous_situation_old: A patient encounter record has a SNOMED code incorrectly deleted (removing a genuine active diagnosis), incorrectly added (creating a false diagnosis), or has its assertion changed incorrectly (e.g., active condition marked as historical). A clinician subsequently views the record and makes a decision based on the incorrect coding.
hazardous_situation_new: A patient's record ends up with a wrong clinical code. A real active diagnosis may be removed. A false diagnosis may be added. Or a current condition may be wrongly marked as past history. A clinician then reads the record and makes a clinical decision based on that wrong information.
harm_old: Incorrect clinical coding may cause a patient to receive inappropriate treatment, miss preventive care, or be incorrectly triaged. In safety- critical categories (cancer, mental health, safeguarding), this could delay diagnosis or treatment.
harm_new: A wrong clinical code can lead to a patient receiving the wrong treatment. They may miss preventive care or be sent down the wrong care pathway. In high-risk areas such as cancer, mental health, or safeguarding, this could delay a diagnosis or delay the start of treatment.
mitigation_new: The system shows the reviewing clinician the original code, the proposed replacement code, the clinical concept, and the reason for the change in a structured display, so the clinician can spot errors before approving any change (DI-04105500). The review screen also shows how often each code has been used historically, helping the clinician judge whether a proposed change looks unusual (DI-22F4E3CE). Before any replacement code is accepted, the system checks that the code is current and valid in the clinical terminology, blocking out-of-date codes automatically (DI-26CBDB16). The review screen shows which words in the clinical notes the AI tool that reads notes used to identify the code, so the clinician can see whether the AI read the notes correctly (DI-4221A226). A dedicated review step brings together the code dependency information and the terminology validity check in one place, so the clinician has everything needed to make a safe decision (DI-1B8AC856). When a large number of coding changes are proposed at once, the system requires a second clinician to review and approve the batch before any changes are saved to patient records (DI-13F340B9). The AI tool that reads notes is designed to preserve clinical detail such as severity and certainty, reducing the risk that a specific diagnosis is replaced with a vague or wrong one (DI-6A0B55A4). The review screen shows the AI tool's decision about whether a condition is present, absent, or possible, alongside the supporting text from the notes, so the clinician can check the AI's reasoning (DI-375C7EB1). All patient record data coming into the system and all audit results leaving it pass through a validated system component, reducing the risk of data being corrupted in transit (DI-1795254D). A separate system component records a full history of every change, showing who proposed it and why, without exposing the full clinical record unnecessarily, so errors can be traced and investigated (DI-09E26C1D). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and any reported incidents every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: LLM coding agent produces incorrect SNOMED codes applied without human review
title_new: AI coding tool assigns a wrong clinical code without a clinician checking it first
hazard_old: The LangGraph coding agent selects an incorrect SNOMED concept, assigns a wrong assertion, or omits a safety-critical finding, and the write-back gate fails to block the incorrect change from reaching the patient graph.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes picks the wrong clinical code, gets the context wrong (for example, marking a finding as absent when it is present), or misses a safety-critical finding entirely. The check that should block incorrect codes from being saved into the patient record fails to catch the error.
hazardous_situation_old: An encounter note contains a cancer red-flag symptom or safeguarding indicator. The agent's search_snomed tool returns a plausible but incorrect concept (e.g. benign lesion instead of suspected malignancy). The agent submits with confidence >= 0.95. The post-processing tier classifier passes the entity at Tier 1. The write-back transaction applies the incorrect code to the patient graph. A downstream clinical dashboard shows the patient as lower-risk than they are, delayi
hazardous_situation_new: A consultation note contains a red-flag cancer symptom or a safeguarding concern. The AI tool that reads notes finds a plausible but wrong clinical code — for example, it codes a benign lesion instead of a suspected malignancy. The AI workflow rates its own confidence as high and passes the code through without triggering a human review. The wrong code is saved into the patient record. A clinical dashboard then shows the patient as lower risk than they truly are. The clinician does not escalate or refer the patient.
harm_old: Delayed referral for suspected cancer or missed safeguarding alert, causing patient harm through late diagnosis or failure to protect a vulnerable person.
harm_new: The patient's cancer referral is delayed or a safeguarding alert is missed. This can cause serious harm through late diagnosis or failure to protect a vulnerable person.
mitigation_new: Seven controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool rates its own confidence and flags the context for every finding it identifies — for example, whether a condition is present, absent, or possible — so reviewers can see the basis for each code (DI-48AD06E5). Second, a separate check compares the context label produced by the AI tool that reads notes against the context label produced by the AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible; any mismatch is flagged before the code is saved (DI-F298AE65). Third, the coding review card shown to the clinician displays the context label and the exact text from the note that the AI used as evidence, so the clinician can judge whether the code is correct (DI-375C7EB1). Fourth, a human-review gate blocks any action — including saving codes — on unreviewed safety alerts; no code linked to a guideline alert reaches the patient record until a clinician approves it (DI-7913344A). Fifth, the system component that supplies clinical codes is kept up to date, and any change in a clinical code version triggers a blocking review before the update is applied (DI-553F50A2 and DI-B193C816). Sixth, the examples used to teach the AI are checked to ensure enough safety-critical findings are included; a quality gate stops training if the count falls below a safe threshold (DI-AE477327). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of flagged mismatches, human-review gate activations, and coding accuracy every quarter to confirm all controls are working.

title_old: Episode of care created from negated or historical concept, causing false pathway tracking
title_new: A patient record shows an active care pathway when the condition is absent or historical
hazard_old: The episode detector creates an EpisodeOfCare node based on a SNOMED concept that was coded as absent, refuted, or historical rather than as an active or suspected clinical finding.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes can find mentions of conditions that are recorded as absent, ruled out, or historical. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible must filter these out before creating a care pathway record. If this filtering fails, the system creates an active pathway record based on a condition the patient does not currently have.
hazardous_situation_old: A clinician documents "no evidence of cancer" or "history of breast cancer (resolved)". The NER pipeline codes these as cancer-type concepts with assertion=absent or assertion=historical. Without assertion filtering, the anchor detector classifies these rows as diagnosis anchors and creates an EpisodeOfCare node. A downstream dashboard or report then incorrectly shows the patient as having an active cancer pathway episode, potentially leading to unnecessary follow-up acti
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician writes "no evidence of cancer" or "history of breast cancer (resolved)". The AI tool that reads notes correctly finds the cancer mention but the AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible does not filter it out. The system then creates an active cancer pathway record for that patient. A dashboard shows the patient as being on an active cancer pathway. A clinician may then arrange unnecessary follow-up or investigations for a condition the patient does not have.
harm_old: Clinicians may act on incorrect episode data, either triggering unnecessary interventions for patients without active pathways, or missing patients whose episodes were incorrectly suppressed due to misconfigured assertion filters.
harm_new: A clinician may act on an incorrect active pathway record and arrange unnecessary tests or treatment for a patient who does not have the condition. Equally, if the filtering is set too broadly, real active pathways may be hidden, and a patient who needs follow-up may be missed. Both errors could cause the patient direct harm.
mitigation_new: The system stores the exact words from the notes alongside every decision the AI tool makes about whether a condition is present, absent, or possible. This lets a clinician or reviewer check why a pathway record was created (DI-23822663). The coding review card shows the clinician the AI tool's decision and the supporting words from the notes, so errors can be spotted quickly during routine review (DI-375C7EB1). The AI workflow uses multi-type classification to handle overlapping clinical codes correctly, reducing the chance of a wrong pathway record being created in the first place (DI-DC61F5B6). Any pathway record that is flagged as potentially incorrect is blocked from appearing in reports until a clinician has reviewed and resolved the flag, preventing incorrect information from reaching clinical dashboards (DI-A0579B64). The system uses an up-to-date clinical coding reference so that code meanings are current and correctly interpreted (DI-553F50A2). A workflow is in place to manage changes to clinical coding releases and resolve any conflicts before they affect pathway records (DI-B193C816). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and flagged pathway records every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Spurious benign closure of active cancer episode due to unrelated 395100000 coding
title_new: Active cancer investigation wrongly closed because an unrelated test result is misread by the AI tool
hazard_old: SNOMED concept 395100000 (No evidence of cancer found) is used in multiple clinical contexts beyond cancer pathway discharge -- e.g. negative cervical smear results, routine health checks, or screening negatives. If the episode builder queries 395100000 globally across the patient record without a date window, an unrelated coding could close an active cancer investigation episode as 'closed_benign'.
hazard_new: A clinical code meaning 'no evidence of cancer found' is used in many different situations. It can appear after a cervical smear, a routine health check, or a cancer pathway discharge. The AI tool that reads notes may search for this code across the whole patient record without checking the date. If it finds the code from an unrelated test, it can wrongly decide that an open cancer investigation has been resolved.
hazardous_situation_old: A patient has an open 2WW breast cancer investigation (referral 2024-07). In 2026, a cervical smear result is coded as 395100000 (no malignancy detected). Without a date window constraint, the episode builder closes the breast investigation as 'closed_benign', removing it from the open episodes dashboard. The breast cancer investigation is now invisible to clinical reviewers.
hazardous_situation_new: A patient has an open urgent two-week-wait breast cancer investigation started in July 2024. In 2026, a cervical smear result is recorded using the same clinical code for 'no cancer found'. Because the AI tool does not check whether the code relates to the breast investigation, it closes the breast investigation and marks it as resolved.
