The breast investigation disappears from the open cases dashboard. Clinicians reviewing open cancer cases can no longer see it.
harm_old: An active cancer investigation is incorrectly marked as resolved, removing it from clinician review queues. Delayed follow-up increases risk of delayed cancer diagnosis.
harm_new: The active breast cancer investigation is wrongly marked as finished. It is removed from the clinician review list. The patient may not receive timely follow-up. This increases the risk of a delayed cancer diagnosis, which could cause serious harm.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool that decides if a finding is present, absent, or possible displays its reasoning and the supporting evidence on a coding review card, so a clinician can see why the investigation was closed (DI-375C7EB1). This check runs each time the AI tool processes a patient record. Second, the system shows a plain-English summary of what each coded finding means, so reviewers can quickly spot if a code has been applied in the wrong context (DI-66F1B177). This is shown to the reviewing clinician every time a coded finding is displayed. Third, any episode the AI tool has flagged as uncertain is blocked from being reported as closed until a clinician resolves the flag (DI-A0579B64). This quality gate runs automatically before any episode status is finalised. Fourth, when clinical guidelines that underpin the AI rules are updated or withdrawn, the system enforces a review of all episodes that relied on those rules, preventing outdated rules from silently closing investigations (DI-F1A768AE). This runs whenever a guideline change is recorded. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and flag resolution rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Historic specialist visits attributed to later same-site referrals, causing false stale episode status
title_new: An old specialist visit is wrongly linked to a new referral, making an active pathway look finished
hazard_old: The episode detection algorithm assigns specialist visit anchors to episode nodes using only a cancer-site keyword match, with no constraint that the visit date must fall after the episode referral date. A specialist visit from an earlier pathway is re-attributed to a later same-site episode.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes links specialist visits to a cancer pathway using only the cancer site (for example, breast). It does not check whether the visit happened before or after the referral was raised. This means a specialist visit from a completed old pathway can be wrongly attached to a new, still-open pathway for the same cancer site.
hazardous_situation_old: A patient completes a breast cancer 2WW pathway in 2024 (specialist seen, no cancer found). A new breast referral is raised in 2025. During episode rebuild, the 2024 specialist visit is attributed to the 2025 episode. The 2025 episode is flagged stale_post_specialist (>90 days since "specialist visit"). The actual open pathway -- where the patient still needs a specialist appointment -- is auto-closed with a HITL flag instead of remaining in_progress for active follow-up.
hazardous_situation_new: A patient finishes a breast cancer urgent referral pathway in 2024. A new breast referral is raised in 2025. When the AI workflow rebuilds the episode, it attaches the 2024 specialist visit to the 2025 pathway. The 2025 pathway then appears to have had a specialist visit over 90 days ago. The system marks it as stale and auto-closes it, adding it to the human review queue instead of keeping it open for active follow-up. The patient still needs a specialist appointment, but the pathway no longer shows as active.
harm_old: An active cancer investigation pathway is incorrectly closed as stale. The patient may not receive timely specialist review. Clinical audit metrics undercount open pathways and overcount completed ones. Quality managers reviewing the HITL queue may miss a genuinely at-risk patient.
harm_new: An active cancer investigation pathway is wrongly closed. The patient may not receive a timely specialist review. Audit reports undercount open pathways and overcount completed ones. Clinicians reviewing the human review queue may not spot that this patient is still waiting and at risk.
mitigation_new: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the AI workflow only uses milestone dates that a human reviewer has accepted before calculating pathway timings. This stops wrongly dated visits from triggering a stale status. The clinical informatics team configures this gate, and it runs on every pathway rebuild (DI-EE4E6477). Second, a risk-scored change queue holds any auto-closure that would affect an active pathway. No change reaches live records until a reviewer approves it. The deployment team manages this queue continuously (DI-7C5EC850). Third, the system checks coding quality metrics automatically and raises an alert if accuracy drops or a pattern of wrong episode links appears. The clinical safety team reviews these alerts at least weekly (DI-1126FFD1). Fourth, an automated audit checks the examples used to teach the AI for labelling errors. It flags suspect labels for human review and limits how many it can correct on its own. The clinical informatics team runs this audit before each model update (DI-CFA65509). Fifth, before any pathway status changes, the system checks for conflicts with clinical guidelines and preserves an under-review status so the pathway stays available to clinicians while the conflict is resolved. The clinical safety team oversees this check on every release (DI-48ACD153). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all five controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Post-specialist inference incorrectly classifies a cancer pathway as benign
title_new: AI tool wrongly marks a cancer pathway as benign after a specialist appointment
hazard_old: The outcome inference engine scans post-specialist encounters for textual signals and may produce an inferred_outcome of 'benign' when the true outcome is cancer, either because cancer-treatment signals did not appear in the 180-day window or because the outcome letter was private/redacted.
hazard_new: After a patient sees a specialist, the AI tool reads the clinical notes to decide whether the outcome was cancer or benign. It may wrongly decide the outcome was benign. This can happen if notes about cancer treatment did not appear within six months, or if the outcome letter was private or hidden from the system.
hazardous_situation_old: A patient with a confirmed or unconfirmed cancer diagnosis has their stale_post_specialist episode inferred as 'benign'. This propagates to the analytics KPIs, potentially masking the episode from the HITL review queue and giving the quality lead a false sense that the pathway was resolved.
hazardous_situation_new: A patient who has or may have cancer has their specialist episode wrongly labelled as benign. This label feeds into reporting dashboards. The episode may then be removed from the list of cases waiting for a human review. The quality lead sees the pathway as closed when it is not.
harm_old: Delayed detection of a cancer case that should have triggered follow-up, leading to possible patient harm if the pathway is not reviewed manually.
harm_new: A cancer case that needs follow-up is missed. If no one reviews the pathway manually, the patient may not receive timely care. This could lead to serious harm from delayed cancer treatment.
mitigation_new: The AI workflow uses a fixed, rule-based method to build each episode from linked clinical encounters, so no encounter is silently dropped (DI-FF9C74E2). The AI tool applies a clear status label to every episode, marking it as confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive rather than defaulting to benign when information is missing (DI-37DDAADE). The system shows the reviewing clinician guideline-recommended treatments alongside comparable patient outcomes, so gaps in the pathway are visible at a glance (DI-82D5359B). The system also flags recovery markers and compares the patient trajectory against similar cases, making it easier to spot when an expected cancer treatment pathway is absent (DI-49403C92). A structured multidisciplinary team summary template prompts the reviewer to work through a pathway checklist and compare the case against similar patients before closing it (DI-DBC2399F). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and dashboard accuracy every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Incorrect patient graph mutation via DQ remediation API
title_new: Patient record corrupted by an admin using the data-correction tool
hazard_old: A platform administrator uses the DQ remediation API endpoints to delete encounters, modify assertions, or write DOCUMENTS edges incorrectly, corrupting patient clinical data in the graph.
hazard_new: A platform administrator uses a data-correction tool to delete consultations, change clinical findings, or update patient records. If used with wrong settings, this can corrupt the patient's clinical data.
hazardous_situation_old: An admin runs a remediation operation (e.g. delete-patient, fix-assertions, writeback) with incorrect parameters or without reviewing the dry-run preview, causing valid clinical data to be deleted or incorrect clinical coding to be written to the patient graph, which downstream affects episode detection, safety-net alerts, or clinical coding outputs.
hazardous_situation_new: An administrator runs a data-correction action without checking the preview first, or enters the wrong settings. This can delete valid clinical information or write wrong clinical codes into the patient record. Downstream, this affects whether the system correctly identifies a cancer pathway, triggers safety-net alerts, or produces correct clinical codes for clinical users.
harm_old: Patient episode or coding data is corrupted, leading to incorrect cancer pathway status, missed safety-net alerts, or incorrect SNOMED codes being exported or displayed to clinical users.
harm_new: The patient's record holds wrong or missing information. This can mean the system shows the wrong cancer pathway status, misses a safety-net alert, or sends wrong clinical codes to clinicians. A patient could be harmed if their cancer care is delayed or a warning about their condition is not raised.
mitigation_new: The system requires the administrator to run a preview check before any data-correction action is applied. This shows exactly what will change before anything is saved. The administrator must review and approve the preview before the action runs (DI-ACB587DD). The system detects changes from authoritative sources and routes alerts to the responsible team so that unexpected changes are spotted quickly (DI-EF37BDF9). The system builds each patient episode from linked consultations in a fixed, rule-based way, so a single wrong entry is less likely to corrupt the whole episode (DI-FF9C74E2). Any alert from a clinical guideline check must be reviewed by a clinician before the system takes further action, acting as a human check on the process (DI-7913344A). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of all data-correction actions every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Incorrect episode stage assignment from explicit stage or TNM evidence
title_new: Wrong cancer stage recorded at diagnosis
hazard_old: Stage-at-diagnosis derivation may map explicit stage text or TNM components to the wrong stage group (early vs late) because of unsupported patterns, ambiguous evidence, or incorrect site-rule matching.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes may assign the wrong stage group to a cancer diagnosis. This can happen when the notes use unusual wording, when the evidence is unclear, or when the rules for a specific cancer site are not matched correctly. For example, a late-stage cancer could be recorded as early-stage, or the other way round.
hazardous_situation_old: A confirmed-diagnosis episode is assigned an incorrect stage group by the enrichment pass. Audit dashboards then misstate the early-stage diagnosis rate, leading quality teams to infer inaccurate pathway performance.
hazardous_situation_new: A patient's cancer episode is given the wrong stage group. Quality dashboards then show incorrect figures for early versus late diagnosis rates. Quality teams use these figures to judge how well the cancer pathway is performing, so they draw the wrong conclusions.
harm_old: Inaccurate quality improvement decisions and delayed corrective actions for late diagnosis patterns at programme level.
harm_new: Quality teams make improvement decisions based on wrong data. Problems with late diagnosis are not spotted or acted on quickly enough. This delays action that could improve outcomes for future patients on the cancer pathway.
mitigation_new: First, a data quality dashboard tracks how often the staging rules produce a valid result, broken down by cancer programme and rule type. The clinical safety team reviews this regularly to spot unusual patterns or drops in accuracy (DI-E6A32FF5). Second, the AI tool stores the exact text from the notes that it used to decide the stage. Clinicians reviewing a record can see this evidence and check whether the decision was correct (DI-23822663). Third, cancer programme leads can update the staging rule sets without needing a software release. This means errors in the rules can be corrected quickly when they are found (DI-AA8014F9). Fourth, population-level pathway dashboards show local staging rates alongside national benchmarks. Unexpected differences alert quality teams to possible data errors (DI-BA2C8F3E). Fifth, programme leads can set thresholds that control when staging results are shown or suppressed, reducing the risk that unreliable results reach dashboards (DI-0D7DCC52). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Auditor reviews and approves a cancer episode that contains incorrect AI-extracted data, leading to flawed clinical decisions
title_new: An auditor approves a cancer episode containing wrong AI-generated data, leading to flawed clinical decisions
hazard_old: The Mission Control interface displays AI-extracted cancer episode data (cancer type, stage, milestones, coded SNOMED concepts) to clinical auditors. If this data contains errors introduced by the NLP pipeline (wrong cancer type, missing milestone, incorrect assertion) and the auditor does not detect the error before marking the episode as reviewed, downstream clinical decisions may be made on flawed data.
hazard_new: The system shows auditors cancer episode information pulled from clinical notes by the AI tool that reads notes. This information includes cancer type, stage, key dates, and clinical codes. If the AI tool has made an error — for example, recording a benign finding as a cancer diagnosis — and the auditor does not spot the mistake before approving the episode, that wrong information enters the record as validated.
hazardous_situation_old: An auditor opens a patient episode in Mission Control where the NLP pipeline has incorrectly coded a benign finding as a cancer diagnosis (or vice versa). The auditor reviews the coded data tab but does not cross-check the raw encounter text tab. The auditor marks the episode as reviewed. The episode is subsequently used to calculate cancer prevalence statistics, which influence GP referral pathway prioritisation.
hazardous_situation_new: An auditor opens a patient episode where the AI tool that reads notes has wrongly coded a benign finding as a cancer diagnosis, or missed a cancer diagnosis entirely. The auditor checks the coded summary but does not look at the original clinical notes to confirm it. The auditor marks the episode as reviewed and approved. That episode is then used to calculate how common certain cancers are across the practice population. Those figures are used to decide which GP referral pathways to prioritise.
harm_old: Clinical decisions (referral pathway prioritisation, resource allocation, quality improvement plans) are made on the basis of incorrect cancer prevalence data that was incorrectly marked as validated. This could lead to delayed diagnosis for patients in under-prioritised pathways or misdirection of
harm_new: Clinicians make referral and resource decisions based on cancer prevalence figures that contain undetected errors. Pathways may be under-prioritised or over-prioritised as a result. Patients in under-prioritised pathways may experience delayed diagnosis or delayed access to treatment.
mitigation_new: The system blocks any approved episode from influencing pathway decisions until a human auditor has reviewed it. This human-review gate is built into the system and runs automatically for every episode (DI-7913344A). The AI tool that reads notes stores the exact text it used to reach each clinical decision, so auditors can check the original wording alongside the coded result. This is available on every episode at the point of review (DI-23822663). The system runs automatic quality checks on each episode, flagging unusual durations, missing key dates, and events recorded in the wrong order. These checks run automatically each time an episode is processed (DI-1206D9E8). A live performance dashboard shows auditors and the safety team how accurately the AI tool is performing across all episode types. It refreshes automatically and is available to the clinical team at all times (DI-067E471A). Any episode the system cannot process correctly appears in a failed episode list with a clear reason for failure. A member of the team can send it for reprocessing with one click, so no episode is silently lost (DI-69CE20C1). The accuracy of the AI tool is measured separately for each type of clinical information it extracts. These figures are recorded each time the AI is updated and are available for review at any time (DI-CE0A08E5). When the AI tool is retrained, only annotations checked by an expert are used, and any that do not align correctly with the original text are automatically excluded (DI-E7AFFDA5). The AI tool is retrained regularly using a structured improvement cycle that includes expert-checked examples and performance tracking over time (DI-37B3DC71). The clinical safety committee reviews audit completion rates, AI accuracy figures, and any flagged episodes every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Spinal vertebral level notation misclassified as cancer TNM staging observable entity
title_new: Spinal level labels mistaken for cancer staging codes
hazard_old: Alphanumeric vertebral level labels (e.g. C3, T4, L5) used in musculoskeletal, physiotherapy, or spinal medicine encounters share the same token pattern as TNM staging components (T0-T4, N0-N3, M0-M1). The LLM extraction pipeline and the SNOMED surface-form resolver may incorrectly map these spinal anatomical references to cancer staging SNOMED concepts (e.g. 78873005 T category).
hazard_new: Spinal anatomy uses letter-number labels such as C3, T4, and L5 to describe vertebrae. Cancer staging also uses labels like T4 and N2 to describe tumour spread. The AI tool that reads notes cannot always tell these apart. When it sees 'T4' in a physiotherapy or back-pain note, it may treat it as a cancer staging code and save it to the patient record.
hazardous_situation_old: A GP consultation note contains spinal physiotherapy or musculoskeletal text such as "C3-T4 facet areas" or "NAGs C3". The LLM extraction model, lacking an explicit disambiguation rule, labels the isolated token "T4" as an observable entity. The terminology resolver maps "T4" to SNOMED 78873005 (T category, observable entity) via an existing surface-form mapping. The resulting cancer-staging entity is persisted to the patient graph and surfaced in the cancer audit pipelin
hazardous_situation_new: A GP writes a note about a patient's back or neck, for example 'C3-T4 facet areas' or 'NAGs C3'. The AI tool that reads notes picks out 'T4' as a separate item. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible does not have a rule to check whether 'T4' is a spinal level or a cancer stage. It assigns a cancer staging clinical code and saves it to the patient record. The cancer audit system then picks up this code as if the patient has a confirmed cancer stage.
harm_old: Incorrect cancer staging observable entity on patient record. Audit dashboards misstate the stage distribution of the cancer pathway cohort. Clinical quality teams may make inaccurate quality-improvement decisions based on inflated or incorrect staging data.
harm_new: The patient record now shows a cancer staging code that does not belong there. Cancer audit dashboards show the wrong stage distribution across the cancer pathway. Clinical quality teams may make incorrect improvement decisions based on this inaccurate data. Individual patients could also be incorrectly flagged as having a cancer stage, causing unnecessary concern or follow-up.
mitigation_new: The AI workflow uses rules that constrain which clinical codes can be assigned based on the surrounding clinical context, reducing the chance that a spinal label is mapped to a cancer staging code (DI-3EA60D5A). This rule set is maintained by the clinical informatics team and reviewed whenever the AI workflow is updated. A separate gate checks and approves any change to the way staging surface forms are matched to clinical codes; changes must be reviewed, approved, and versioned before going live, and can be rolled back if a problem is found (DI-9FD54AD6). This gate is operated by the clinical safety team and runs for every proposed change. The AI tool that reads notes preserves the clinical context around each term, such as whether it appears in a musculoskeletal or oncology section, so that the correct clinical code can be chosen (DI-6A0B55A4). This is applied automatically during every note-reading process. The cohort builder applies rule-based checks across clinical codes, pathway stage, and patient details to catch records that do not fit expected patterns (DI-FE3FFE50). The clinical informatics team reviews cohort outputs at each audit cycle. The examples used to teach the AI are checked to ensure safety-critical entities such as cancer staging codes are represented accurately and in sufficient numbers, with a quality gate that blocks training if counts fall below a safe threshold (DI-AE477327). This check is run by the data science team before every training run. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs, cohort outputs, and gate reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Extraction quality check drops valid entities or adds unsupported entities
title_new: AI quality check removes correct clinical findings or adds ones not supported by the notes
hazard_old: The extraction quality LLM check may incorrectly remove clinically valid entities or add unsupported mentions due to prompt misinterpretation.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes includes a quality check step. This step may wrongly remove a real clinical finding from the notes. It may also add a finding that the notes do not actually support. This can happen when the AI misreads the instruction it is given.
hazardous_situation_old: A valid disorder or finding mention is dropped by extraction_check, or an unsupported mention is added. Relation linking may also attach the wrong body-site link. The modified entity set proceeds to terminology and persistence, resulting in under-coding or incorrect coded evidence in patient and training stores.
hazardous_situation_new: A genuine disorder or finding is removed by the quality check, or an unsupported finding is added. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible may also link a finding to the wrong part of the body. The altered set of findings then moves forward in the AI workflow. This results in clinical codes being missed or wrong codes being saved into the patient record and into the examples used to teach the AI.
harm_old: Clinical coding quality metrics are degraded and review queues may contain missing or spurious entities, delaying remediation and increasing residual coding error in downstream analytics.
harm_new: Clinical coding becomes less accurate. The review queue shown to clinicians may contain missing or incorrect findings. This delays correction and leaves errors in the data used for patient care and clinical reporting.
mitigation_new: The AI follows a fixed set of clinical rules when pulling information from notes, which limits the findings it can produce to recognised clinical concepts (DI-3EA60D5A). The AI preserves specific clinical detail, such as how a finding is described, so that the correct clinical code can be assigned (DI-6A0B55A4). All AI-suggested findings go into a single review queue where a trained reviewer checks and corrects them; corrections are saved as structured examples for future AI improvement (DI-890BE989). A reviewer must actively engage with the evidence in the notes before confirming any AI suggestion, and urgency criteria must be met before confirmation is allowed (DI-A23D11FA). If a reviewer corrects a suggestion, the confirmation is reset and the reviewer must re-engage before confirming again (DI-5ADEC3D1). Only authorised staff can review and finalise AI output, enforced by access controls (DI-RBAC enforcement for all AI output review and finalisation actions, DI-E83828A9). Coding corrections are checked against related findings and clinical terminology rules before they are saved (DI-1B8AC856). Quality checks run continuously on clinical coding accuracy, and the system raises an alert if accuracy drops (DI-1126FFD1). The AI model for linking findings to body sites must pass defined quality checks before it is used in live care (DI-80BD2F86). Reviewer engagement is logged and the clinical safety officer monitors this data to detect over-reliance on AI suggestions (DI-22D862B0). The clinical safety committee reviews these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Coding quality check removes valid coded entities or escalates excessively
title_new: AI quality check wrongly removes correct clinical codes or sends too many for manual review
hazard_old: The coding quality LLM check may drop valid coded entities or overuse force_review, reducing autonomous throughput and creating hidden under-coding.
hazard_new: The AI tool that checks coding quality may remove clinical codes that are actually correct. It may also flag far too many codes for a clinician to check manually. Both problems can mean that valid clinical codes are never saved to the patient record, or are saved much later than they should be.
hazardous_situation_old: After terminology resolution, coding_check marks a valid coded entity for drop or applies force_review too broadly. Persisted coding output is reduced or delayed, and operational queues increase. If tier override is ignored or routing is bypassed, flagged coding errors may still be written as auto-coded patient graph links.
hazardous_situation_new: After the AI workflow assigns clinical codes, a second AI quality check runs. This check may wrongly discard a correct code or send it for manual review when it does not need one. If this happens repeatedly, a backlog builds up. In some cases, a code that has been flagged as needing review may still be saved automatically to the patient record without a clinician checking it first.
harm_old: Valid clinically relevant coding may not be written to the patient graph or may be delayed for manual review, reducing timeliness and completeness of coding-driven audit outputs.
harm_new: Correct and clinically important codes may be missing from the patient record, or may arrive there too late. This can make audit reports and care pathway checks incomplete or misleading. A clinician relying on those reports may not get a full picture of the patient's conditions.
mitigation_new: First, the AI workflow automatically checks the examples used to teach the AI quality checker. It flags any that look wrong and limits how many it can fix on its own. A member of the clinical informatics team reviews the rest. This runs continuously and is reviewed at least monthly (DI-CFA65509). Second, when a code is queried by the quality check, a separate review step checks whether the code is correct and whether it links properly to other codes and clinical terms. A trained coder or clinician carries out this review before any change is saved to the patient record (DI-1B8AC856). Third, the audit programme is set up using real data patterns so that the quality check is calibrated to the actual volume and type of codes seen in practice. The clinical informatics team configures this before any new version is deployed (DI-CD931485). Fourth, every output shown to a clinician includes a clear indicator of how complete and reliable the coding data is. This means a clinician can see at a glance if something may be missing or unverified (DI-900CB621). Fifth, every clinical statement in the system carries a clear link back to the original consultation note and the source code, so a clinician or auditor can trace exactly where each code came from (DI-740BE510). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: ConText double-negation inverts assertion on pre-negated SNOMED situation concepts
title_new: AI tool misreads 'No suicidal thoughts' and records the opposite meaning
hazard_old: ConText assigns assertion=absent to a SNOMED situation concept whose preferred term already encodes a negative (e.g. "No suicidal thoughts", "No thoughts of deliberate self harm"), inverting the clinical meaning.
hazard_new: Some clinical codes already contain a negative in their name, for example 'No suicidal thoughts' or 'No thoughts of deliberate self-harm'. The AI tool that decides if something is present or absent sees the word 'No' and treats it as a second negation. This flips the meaning, so the record suggests the risk is present when the clinician documented that it is absent.
hazardous_situation_old: A clinician documents a negative mental health risk screen using a Read or SNOMED situation code whose preferred term begins with "No" (e.g. 134420004 "No suicidal thoughts", 401228008 "No thoughts of deliberate self harm"). The pipeline extracts the span, ConText detects the preceding "No" as a negation cue and sets assertion=absent. The SNOMED concept is then resolved. The persisted coded record now carries assertion=absent on a concept that already means absent -- sema
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician completes a mental health risk screen and records a negative finding using a clinical code whose name starts with 'No', such as 'No suicidal thoughts'. The AI workflow pulls this from the notes and the AI tool that decides if something is present or absent detects the word 'No' as a negation signal. It marks the finding as absent. Because the clinical code already means absent, the double negation inverts the intended meaning. The patient record is then saved with a coded entry that implies active suicidal or self-harm ideation, which is the opposite of what the clinician documented.
harm_old: Coded patient record incorrectly implies active suicidal ideation or active self-harm ideation where the clinician documented their absence. Could cause a downstream system or reviewer to over-escalate risk, or alternatively fail to record the documented negative screen, removing evidence of risk as
harm_new: The patient record incorrectly suggests the patient has active suicidal ideation or active thoughts of self-harm. A clinician or another system reviewing the record could wrongly escalate the patient's risk level. Alternatively, the documented evidence that the clinician checked and found no risk may be lost. Either outcome could lead to the patient receiving the wrong level of care.
mitigation_new: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the AI workflow uses a classification step that recognises overlapping and pre-negated clinical codes and handles them separately from ordinary negation cues. This runs automatically every time the AI workflow processes a note (DI-DC61F5B6). Second, the AI tool rates its own confidence for each finding it identifies and flags low-confidence results for human review. This runs automatically on every entry the AI produces (DI-48AD06E5). Third, the coding review card shown to the clinician displays the exact words from the note that led to the present-or-absent decision, so the clinician can spot errors before saving (DI-375C7EB1). Fourth, the text evidence behind each present-or-absent decision is stored alongside the coded entry in the patient record, giving reviewers a clear audit trail (DI-23822663). Fifth, the system component that supplies clinical codes is kept up to date so that pre-negated code names are correctly identified (DI-553F50A2). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and coding accuracy reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Coded entities with absent assertion included in CCI score or cohort selection
title_new: A condition recorded as absent is wrongly counted as present in a patient's risk score or care group
hazard_old: Analytics queries traverse :DOCUMENTS relationships without filtering by assertion status, causing explicitly negated conditions (assertion='absent') to be treated identically to confirmed conditions (assertion='present').
hazard_new: The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible labels some conditions as 'absent' in the notes. However, the system does not check this label when it calculates a patient's comorbidity score or assigns them to a care group. It treats 'absent' conditions the same as confirmed ones.
hazardous_situation_old: A patient has an encounter documented with "No diabetes mellitus" coded as a SNOMED finding with assertion='absent'. The CCI query returns this concept because it does not check the assertion field, scoring the patient as diabetic and inflating their comorbidity index. Similarly, cohort filters include the patient in a diabetic cohort they do not belong to.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician documents 'No diabetes' in a patient's notes. The AI tool correctly marks this as absent. But when the system calculates the patient's comorbidity score, it ignores the absent label and counts the diabetes as confirmed. The system gives the patient a higher risk score than they deserve and places them in a diabetes care group they do not belong to.
harm_old: Incorrect risk-stratification scores and inaccurate cohort membership lead to wrong clinical decisions: patients may receive inappropriate screening invitations, incorrect triage priority, or skewed audit outcomes that mask true population health patterns.
harm_new: The patient receives an incorrect risk score. This can lead to wrong clinical decisions. The patient may get screening invitations they do not need. They may be given the wrong triage priority. Audit reports may show a false picture of the population's health, hiding real problems.
mitigation_new: The system checks that the AI tool reading the notes and the AI tool deciding if a condition is present or absent agree on the status of every condition before saving it to the record. This check runs automatically every time notes are processed (DI-F298AE65). Each condition in the record is stored with a clear status: confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive. The system only counts confirmed conditions when calculating scores or assigning care groups. The clinical informatics team sets and maintains these status rules (DI-37DDAADE). The referral triage view applies eligibility rules that require a confirmed condition status before a patient is included in a care group or pathway. This stops patients with absent conditions from being wrongly routed. The clinical team reviews these rules when the system is updated (DI-6C5D77CA). The system suppresses alerts and actions automatically if a coded clinical response confirms a condition is not present. This acts as a safety net if an incorrect score has already been generated. The clinical safety team monitors this function continuously (DI-0E215ADE). Escalation thresholds for investigations are set against comparable groups of patients with confirmed conditions, so a wrongly scored patient would stand out as an outlier. The clinical safety team reviews these thresholds regularly (DI-49A8F570). The clinical safety committee reviews all these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Corrupt or non-present clinical entities in training data cause NER model to produce clinically incorrect outputs
title_new: Errors in the examples used to teach the AI cause it to suggest wrong clinical codes
hazard_old: NER training data may contain entities with stale span offsets (offset drift after text edit) or non-present assertions (negated, hypothetical, family_history, possible). If these reach DocBin creation uncorrected, the trained model learns incorrect span boundaries or learns to identify conditions the patient does not have.
hazard_new: The AI learns to recognise conditions in patient notes by studying checked examples. Two faults can corrupt these examples. First, if a clinician edits the source text after marking it up, the marked positions can shift and point to the wrong words. Second, if examples showing that a condition is absent or not confirmed are left in the teaching set by mistake, the AI learns to treat absent conditions as present. Both faults can reach the AI training process uncorrected.
hazardous_situation_old: A clinical informatician curates GoldLabel records and edits the source text, leaving entity start/end offsets pointing to wrong characters. Separately, entities with assertion=negated are left in the dataset. Both categories propagate to the next spaCy training run, producing a model that misidentifies entity boundaries and codes present conditions as absent or vice versa.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinical informatician reviews and edits patient notes used to teach the AI. After editing, the position markers for clinical terms can drift and point to the wrong characters. Separately, examples where a condition was recorded as absent, not confirmed, or belonging to a family member are not removed before training begins. Both types of faulty example are included in the next AI training run. The AI then learns incorrect boundaries for clinical terms and may treat conditions the patient does not have as if they are present, or miss conditions that are genuinely present.
harm_old: Downstream clinical coding suggestions surface incorrect SNOMED codes or miss genuinely present diagnoses. This may result in incorrect disease prevalence calculations, missed QOF coding, or inaccurate clinical summaries visible to clinical staff.
harm_new: The AI suggests wrong clinical codes to clinical staff. Conditions the patient does not have may appear as present diagnoses. Conditions the patient does have may be missed. This can lead to incorrect disease registers, missed Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF) coding, and inaccurate clinical summaries seen by doctors and nurses caring for the patient.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, every clinical term pulled from a patient note is stored with a permanent, unbreakable link back to the exact source text it came from, so any drift in position can be detected before training begins; the engineering team applies this automatically every time examples are prepared (DI-B2512CB3). Second, when a reviewer selects a clinical term to mark up, the tool highlights the exact words in the source note so the reviewer can immediately see if the position is wrong; reviewers use this check during every curation session (DI-E81545BE). Third, when the AI pulls a clinical term from a note it records a confidence score and full details of where the term came from; the clinical safety team inspects these records to spot patterns of error before any training run is approved (DI-31126C6C). Fourth, the process that converts checked examples into the training format preserves every label without loss, so faults are not introduced at the final export step; the engineering team validates this at each export (DI-6EFD68D0). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs from all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended. Additional controls are being identified.

title_old: NER model assigns spurious additional semantic label to a span, producing an incorrect SNOMED coding in the patient record
title_new: The AI tool incorrectly labels clinical information, adding a wrong clinical code to the patient record
hazard_old: A spancat NER model trained on multi-label gold data may learn to assign additional semantic labels to spans where only a single label is clinically correct. Unlike the single-label NER, the model can now emit multiple labels per span without an architectural constraint preventing it from doing so.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes can label the same piece of text with more than one clinical meaning. Sometimes it adds a second label that is clinically wrong. For example, it might label a medicine as both a drug and a procedure at the same time. There is no built-in check that stops this from happening.
hazardous_situation_old: A GP consultation note is processed by the spancat NER model. The model assigns two semantic labels to a span (e.g. "metformin 500mg" tagged as both substance and procedure). The second label is incorrect. Both labels flow through post-processing and SNOMED resolution, producing two DOCUMENTS relationships on the encounter node: one correct, one spurious. The spurious coding appears in QOF reports, disease prevalence dashboards, or care-pathway episode detection, potentia
hazardous_situation_new: A GP writes a consultation note. The AI tool reads the note and labels a piece of text, such as a medicine name, with two clinical meanings. One label is correct. The other is wrong. Both labels are saved into the patient record as clinical codes. The wrong code then appears in reports used for QOF (Quality and Outcomes Framework) scoring, disease registers, or care pathway alerts. A clinician reading these reports may not realise one code is wrong.
harm_old: Spurious SNOMED codings in patient records inflate disease prevalence counts, trigger incorrect QOF coding, or activate care-pathway rules for conditions the patient does not have. Clinical staff may act on erroneous coded summaries, risking incorrect treatment decisions.
harm_new: The wrong clinical code sits in the patient record. It may make it look as though the patient has a condition they do not have. Staff acting on this information could make incorrect treatment decisions. Disease registers and QOF reports may also show inaccurate figures, affecting care planning for wider patient groups.
mitigation_new: Five controls are in place to reduce this risk. First, the AI tool is taught using carefully prepared examples that correctly show when more than one label is appropriate; this helps it learn the right boundaries from the start (DI-6EFD68D0). The clinical informatics team maintains these teaching examples and reviews them whenever the AI model is retrained. Second, the AI tool is only allowed to choose labels from a fixed, approved list; it cannot invent new label types outside that list (DI-C899D282). The clinical safety team sets and reviews this approved list at each model release. Third, when the AI tool returns its results, the system checks that each result follows a strict format, one result per label per piece of text; results that do not match this format are rejected before they reach the patient record (DI-6E6C9336). This check runs automatically every time the system processes a note. Fourth, where a piece of text genuinely does carry more than one correct clinical meaning, the system is designed to handle this safely so that only valid combinations are accepted (DI-DC61F5B6). The clinical informatics team reviews these rules at each model update. Fifth, when results are saved into the patient record, the system preserves only the labels that have been correctly matched to a clinical code; unmatched or duplicate labels are flagged and not saved (DI-378F987A). This runs automatically on every record update. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of rejected and flagged labels every quarter to confirm all five controls are working as intended.

title_old: Invalid or missing entity relations cause incorrect clinical interpretation and coding suggestions
title_new: Missing or wrong links between clinical findings lead to incorrect coding suggestions
hazard_old: Clinical entities can be stored without explicit relation semantics, or with invalid source-target relation types. This can apply negation and context to the wrong concept and lead to unsafe coding interpretation.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes can attach negation or context to the wrong clinical finding. This happens when the link between two related findings is missing or uses an unsupported type. The result is that the AI misreads what the notes actually say.
hazardous_situation_old: A reviewer links a finding to an unsupported target type, or relation tuples are not persisted for a multi-site finding. Runtime inference then interprets disconnected entities as independent facts and suggests an incorrect SNOMED coding path.
hazardous_situation_new: A reviewer connects a finding to an unsupported target, or a link between related findings is not saved correctly. The AI workflow then treats those findings as separate, unrelated facts. It suggests an incorrect clinical code based on that misreading.
harm_old: Incorrect coded summaries can affect pathway classification, prevalence reporting, and reviewer decisions, potentially delaying the identification of significant clinical conditions.
harm_new: An incorrect clinical code can place a patient on the wrong care pathway. It can also distort disease reporting and mislead the reviewing clinician. This may delay recognition of a serious clinical condition.
mitigation_new: The AI follows a strict set of rules that only allows supported, valid links between clinical findings. This stops unsupported connections from being made in the first place (DI-3EA60D5A). The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible is limited to working only with structured, confirmed facts from the notes. It cannot draw on information outside those facts (DI-69C29EEF). Every clinical statement carries a record of where it came from and which clinical code it is linked to. This lets reviewers trace any suggestion back to its source (DI-740BE510). The system classifies overlapping clinical findings separately, so one finding does not incorrectly absorb the meaning of another (DI-DC61F5B6). When a reviewer selects a finding, the system highlights the exact words in the original notes that the AI used. The reviewer can then check the AI has read the context correctly (DI-E81545BE). The system compares results against reference ranges and assigns a severity band, flagging findings that may need urgent attention (DI-21E93377). Alerts are automatically suppressed once a clinician has confirmed a coded response, reducing noise for the reviewer (DI-0E215ADE). Every action a clinician takes is saved with their identity and a timestamp. This record cannot be altered (DI-B46AD5CE). Reviewers can filter their worklist by severity, how long a finding has been outstanding, and patient group. This helps them prioritise the most important cases (DI-520A8674). The system maintains a worklist of findings that have not yet been followed up, within a time window that can be adjusted for local needs (DI-4C73DC01). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and worklist data every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Graph algorithm results are misinterpreted and acted on clinically without understanding the data limitations hazard: description: > Graph algorithms run over incomplete or low-qua
title_new: Analysis of too few patients produces misleading results that a clinician acts on
hazard_old: Graph algorithms run over incomplete or low-quality patient data may produce outputs (e.g. community groupings, importance scores) that appear authoritative but are statistically unreliable, leading a clinician or service improvement lead to take a pathway or care decision based on misleading information.
hazard_new: The tool analyses patient data to find patterns and group patients into pathways. If the underlying data is incomplete or covers too few patients, the results can look reliable but are not. A clinician or service lead may then make a care or pathway decision based on figures that do not reflect reality.
hazardous_situation_old: A user runs a Pathway Explorer mission against a thin data set (e.g. fewer than 30 patients in a 3-month window). The algorithm returns a result with a headline in confident plain-English. No data coverage warning is displayed. The user makes a service redesign or patient triage decision based on this finding.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician or service lead runs a pathway analysis on a small group of patients, for example fewer than 30 patients over three months. The tool returns a clear, confident-sounding result. No warning appears to say the data is too thin to trust. The user redesigns a service or changes how patients are triaged based on this result.
harm_old: Incorrect service changes or patient routing decisions that could delay care, misallocate clinical resource, or cause patient harm through deprioritisation or sub-optimal pathway assignment.
harm_new: A service change or patient routing decision is made on unreliable evidence. This could delay care, send patients down the wrong pathway, or cause harm by deprioritising patients who need urgent attention.
mitigation_new: The tool shows a data coverage indicator in the research workspace whenever results are based on limited data. This warns the user before they act on the findings (DI-93162C3C). The AI workflow automatically detects gaps in the data and must display a clear warning on any clinician-facing result that is based on incomplete information. This runs every time a result is produced (DI-88F20177). Every clinician-facing output includes a prominent indicator showing how complete and reliable the underlying data is. The clinical team reviews this indicator as part of normal use (DI-900CB621). Each output also shows details about the patient group it is based on, including how many patients were included and over what time period. This helps the user judge whether the result can be trusted (DI-098D2C0D). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Algorithm terminology exposed in the UI causes users to misinterpret findings and take incorrect action hazard: description: > If technical algorithm names or scores (e.g. "between
title_new: Technical score labels shown in the system are misread by staff, leading to wrong service decisions
hazard_old: If technical algorithm names or scores (e.g. "betweenness centrality
hazard_new: The system displays technical score names and numbers that clinical and service staff do not recognise. Staff may not know what these scores mean or how to read them correctly.
hazardous_situation_old: A service improvement manager sees a column labelled "betweenness centrality" with a value of 0.73 and interprets this as a percentage (73%) criticality score. They escalate or deprioritise services based on this misreading.
hazardous_situation_new: A service improvement manager sees a column with a technical score label and a value such as 0.73. They assume this means 73% and treat it as a criticality rating. They then escalate or deprioritise services based on this misreading.
harm_old: Incorrect service prioritisation or de-prioritisation that misallocates clinical capacity or delays pathway improvement work.
harm_new: Services are prioritised or deprioritised incorrectly. Clinical capacity may be misallocated. Pathway improvement work may be delayed or misdirected, affecting patient care.
mitigation_new: The system shows plain-language explanations alongside any scored findings so that staff understand what each value means. The clinical informatics team maintains these explanations and reviews them whenever score labels change (DI-66F1B177). A coding correction review checks that all terms and labels shown to users are accurate and clearly described. The clinical safety lead runs this review after any update to the scoring outputs (DI-1B8AC856). The clinical safety committee checks both controls are working every quarter by reviewing a sample of score labels shown in the system and confirming plain-language explanations are present and correct.

title_old: Observable entity value field is left empty when the result is a string descriptor or appears before the entity span, causing downstream abnormal detection to treat the result as u
title_new: A test result given as a word rather than a number is not recognised by the AI tool, so abnormal findings are not flagged on the dashboard
hazard_old: The Layer 6 value-unit linker only processes numeric measurement spans. String results (positive, negative, borderline) and values that appear before the entity in the encounter text are not linked, leaving obs["value"] = None even when the encounter clearly records a result.
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes only links results to a test when the result is a number. Word results such as positive, negative, or borderline are ignored. Results that appear before the test name in the notes are also ignored. When this happens, the patient record shows no result value, even though the notes clearly record one.
hazardous_situation_old: A clinician records a microbiological or immunological result such as "Urine culture -- negative" or "positive -- COVID antigen rapid test". The NLP pipeline extracts the observable entity but leaves obs.value empty because the value-unit linker skips non-numeric candidates. The abnormal result detection layer treats the result as missing and does not flag the finding. A clinician reviewing the audit dashboard sees no alert for a positive result that should have been acti
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician records a word-based result, for example a urine culture reported as negative or a COVID antigen test reported as positive. The AI tool that reads notes finds the test name but leaves the result blank because it only handles numbers. The part of the AI workflow that checks for abnormal results sees a blank and does not raise an alert. A clinician checking the audit dashboard sees no alert for a positive result that needs action.
harm_old: Clinically significant positive or abnormal test results are not surfaced in the audit dashboard. Pathway coordinators miss findings that require follow-up, increasing the risk of delayed treatment or missed safety netting for the patient.
harm_new: A clinically important positive or abnormal test result does not appear as an alert on the audit dashboard. The care coordinator does not see it and does not arrange follow-up. The patient may not receive timely treatment or safety netting, which could lead to serious harm.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the system keeps an open worklist of findings that have been flagged but not yet acted on, with a configurable time window for follow-up. This gives care coordinators a safety net to catch outstanding results. The clinical team reviews this worklist daily (DI-4C73DC01). Second, every action a clinician takes on a flagged finding is recorded permanently with the clinician's name and the date and time. This creates an auditable trail so nothing can be silently lost. The clinical safety team reviews these records at each audit cycle (DI-B46AD5CE). Third, once a clinician records a confirmed coded clinical response to a finding, the system automatically suppresses duplicate alerts for that finding. This keeps the worklist focused on genuinely unactioned results and reduces the chance that a real gap is hidden by noise (DI-0E215ADE). Fourth, any changes to how the AI workflow is configured can only be made through the user interface, and a separate approval step is required before a failed test mode can be promoted to live use. This stops untested configuration changes from silently worsening the problem (DI-F2C18D2E). The clinical safety committee reviews all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Users with low vision, colour-blindness, age-related sight loss, or vestibular sensitivity cannot read or safely perceive clinical information rendered in LEO because the UI uses l
title_new: Clinicians or patients with visual or vestibular conditions cannot safely read clinical information shown by the system
hazard_old: The LEO UI uses a hardcoded 14px body font, chips at 0.65rem (approximately 10px), and historically banned low-contrast greys. Motion is always on. As a result, users with visual or vestibular impairment, including older clinicians and patients exposed to patient-reachable screens, cannot reliably read safety-netting advice, coding assertions, or status signals; or they experience motion-induced discomfort that causes them to look away during a critical
hazard_new: The system displays some text very small — around 10 pixels — and uses light grey text on a white background. The contrast between the text and background is too low to meet accessibility standards. Moving images on screen cannot be turned off. This means clinicians with age-related sight loss, colour-blindness, or low vision may not be able to read important clinical information clearly. Patients who are sensitive to screen movement may look away before reading safety advice fully.
hazardous_situation_old: A clinician with age-related macular degeneration reviews a list of coded encounters with small grey chips indicating assertion (e.g. "refuted", "not present"). The chip text is at 10px with a contrast ratio below 3:1. The clinician misses an "absent" marker on a significant-finding code and approves the record, causing a false-positive to propagate. Or: a patient with a vestibular disorder reads safety-netting advice on a page with an animated banner that cannot be d
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician with age-related macular degeneration reviews a list of coded patient encounters. Small grey labels show whether a finding is confirmed, absent, or possible. The text is tiny and the contrast is poor. The clinician misses a label showing a finding is absent and approves the record as if the finding is present. This incorrect entry then carries forward into the patient record. Separately, a patient with a vestibular condition — one that causes dizziness or nausea from movement — tries to read safety advice on screen. An animated banner is running and cannot be stopped. The patient looks away and does not take in the advice.
harm_old: Clinical decisions are made on misread or missed information. Safety-netting advice is not absorbed by the patient. For children, older patients, and patients with disability, the product is de-facto unusable, constituting discrimination under the Equality Act 2010 and posing a direct patient-safety
harm_new: A clinician makes a clinical decision based on information they misread or missed entirely. A patient does not absorb safety advice because they could not read it comfortably. For older patients, children, and patients with a disability, the system may be effectively unusable. This creates a direct patient safety risk and may also breach the Equality Act 2010.
mitigation_new: The following controls are in place to reduce this risk. The system automatically suppresses alerts when a confirmed clinical response has already been coded, reducing the number of small status labels a clinician must read at once (DI-0E215ADE). This control is built into the system and runs automatically every time the system processes a coded encounter. The system flags outputs where confidence is low or the patient group is small, so clinicians are prompted to look more carefully before acting (DI-CB3DF3E1). This control runs automatically as part of the AI workflow each time results are generated. The system produces a structured written summary drawn from coded encounters, the patient's pathway stage, and any safety alerts, giving clinicians a clear plain-text overview that does not rely on small labels alone (DI-30D9CC61). This summary is generated automatically each time a relevant encounter is reviewed. The system shows how often a clinical code has been used historically on the coding review page, helping clinicians spot unusual or unexpected entries that may reflect a misread label (DI-22F4E3CE). This is displayed automatically during coding correction review. The system builds episode records from related encounters in a consistent, rule-based way, reducing the chance that a misread label leads to a structurally incorrect record (DI-FF9C74E2). This runs automatically each time a new episode is constructed. The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working effectively every quarter. Additional controls specifically addressing font size, contrast ratios, and motion settings are being identified and will be added to this risk record once confirmed.

title_old: A patient or carer on a touch device mis-taps a safety-netting or portal control because targets are smaller than 44x44 CSS pixels, or an older clinician with mild tremor triggers
title_new: A patient or clinician on a touch screen taps the wrong button because touch targets are too small
hazard_old: The current UI has a single compact density with no user control. Buttons, chips, and list rows can be under 36 CSS pixels tall. On a touch device or for a user with dexterity impairment, the wrong control is easy to hit. On patient-reachable screens this is high risk because the user may be a child, an older patient, or a carer under stress.
hazard_new: The system shows buttons and list rows that can be too small to tap accurately. On a phone or tablet, a patient, carer, or clinician with mild hand tremor can easily tap the wrong control. This risk is higher when the user is a child, an older person, or a carer under stress.
hazardous_situation_old: A patient opens their safety-netting advice on a phone, tries to tap the "I understand" confirmation, and instead taps the "I am worried - contact NHS 111" button below it. The incorrect action is taken; either a false-positive 111 call is made, or, worse, the confirm is mis-tapped and the patient never reads the red-flag list. Or: an older coder reviewing a long list of candidate codes accidentally approves the code immediately below the one they intended because row
hazardous_situation_new: A patient opens their safety-netting advice on a phone and tries to tap the confirmation button. Instead they tap the NHS 111 contact button just below it. This sends a false alert, or the patient never reads the red-flag warning list. Separately, a clinician reviewing a list of clinical codes accidentally approves the wrong code because the rows are too close together.
harm_old: Patient misroutes into the wrong care pathway; or clinical codes are approved in error, propagating incorrect clinical data into the patient record and downstream reports. Both are clinical-safety harms with potential delayed diagnosis or inappropriate onward action.
harm_new: The patient is sent down the wrong care pathway. Or an incorrect clinical code is saved into the patient record and passed on to other systems. Both errors could delay the right diagnosis or trigger the wrong clinical action.
mitigation_new: Every safety-netting action is recorded automatically with the clinician's identity and the exact time it happened. This means any mis-tap can be identified and reviewed. The clinical safety team checks these records regularly (DI-B46AD5CE). When a patient-facing step fails or is completed incorrectly, the system adds that encounter to a failed list. A clinician can review it and re-run the step with one click, correcting any error before it affects care (DI-69CE20C1). The system also records a clear, machine-readable reason for every error. This helps the safety team spot patterns of mis-taps quickly and act on them (DI-6654FB0E). A plain-language explanation of what each action means is always available to the patient or clinician in one tap, reducing the chance they act without understanding (DI-B95A73E9). Any change to safety-netting guidance is managed through a controlled registry. The safety team is alerted when guidance changes, so they can check whether touch-target risks need to be reassessed (DI-ED3A89F5). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and error reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Users of screen readers, keyboard-only navigation, or colour-blindness aids lose track of which page they are on, cannot activate the LEO logo from the keyboard, or cannot tell sta
title_new: Clinicians using assistive technology cannot tell where they are in the system or read status alerts correctly
hazard_old: The AppShell does not set aria-current in rail mode, renders the LEO logo as an with onClick, and the OrgSelect has no associated label. StatusDot conveys status in colour only. ConfirmDialog has no aria-describedby. Collectively, users relying on assistive technology lose the ability to orient themselves and to distinguish critical status information during clinical tasks and safety-netting.
hazard_new: The system does not tell screen readers which page is currently open. The logo cannot be activated using a keyboard alone. The organisation selector has no label that a screen reader can announce. Status dots use colour only to show whether something is healthy or has an error. Confirmation dialogs do not describe what the clinician is agreeing to. Together, these gaps mean clinicians who rely on assistive technology cannot safely orient themselves or spot critical alerts during clinical tasks.
hazardous_situation_old: A blind clinician using NVDA opens the encounter review page, wants to navigate to 'Audit', but the rail drawer does not announce which item is the current page. They choose 'Patients' instead, operate on the wrong cohort, and approve records that belong to the wrong context. Or: a colour-blind coder cannot tell apart healthy-green from error-red status dots on a pathway dashboard and misses an alert.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician using a screen reader opens the encounter review page and wants to go to the Audit section. Because the system does not announce which page is currently open, they navigate to the wrong section and work on the wrong group of patients. They approve records that do not belong to the correct context. Separately, a clinician with colour blindness cannot tell a healthy status dot from an error status dot on a pathway dashboard and misses a clinical alert.
harm_old: Clinical decisions made against the wrong cohort; alerts missed by users with visual impairment; safety-netting confirmations submitted without the user understanding the dialog content. All constitute clinical-safety harm with potential for delayed or incorrect care.
harm_new: Clinical decisions may be made against the wrong group of patients. Alerts may be missed by clinicians with visual impairment. Safety-netting confirmations may be submitted without the clinician understanding what they are agreeing to. Each of these outcomes could lead to delayed or incorrect care for patients.
mitigation_new: A deployment status panel shows the current state of approved changes and is visible from the review interface. This helps clinicians confirm they are working in the correct context before acting (DI-6EA84931). The clinical safety team checks this panel is present and correct as part of each approved change review. Safety-netting actions are recorded permanently with the clinician's identity and the time they were taken. This creates an auditable trail so any action taken in the wrong context can be identified and corrected (DI-B46AD5CE). The clinical safety team reviews these records regularly to spot patterns of error. Automatic alert suppression activates only after a confirmed coded clinical response has been recorded. This reduces the risk that an alert is silently missed because a status dot was misread (DI-0E215ADE). The clinical safety team checks suppression events each quarter to confirm they are triggered correctly. The AI-generated structured summary brings together coded encounters, pathway stage, and safety-netting alerts in one place. This gives clinicians a text-based overview that does not rely on colour alone (DI-30D9CC61). The clinical safety committee reviews whether this summary is being used and whether it is reducing missed alerts, every quarter. Reference ranges and review status are shown in the content currency dashboard. This provides an additional text-based check that does not depend on colour coding (DI-E7609DD8). The clinical safety committee reviews this dashboard quarterly to confirm it remains current and accessible. Additional controls to address the underlying accessibility gaps in the interface are being identified.

title_old: A patient, carer, or junior staff member acts on a LEO screen they do not fully understand because no inline 'what-is-this' or 'why-am-I-here' affordance exists, leading to a wrong
title_new: A patient, carer, or junior staff member acts on a screen they do not fully understand because no plain-English explanation is shown, leading to a wrong or missed action
hazard_old: LEO surfaces use clinical terminology (e.g. 'microalbuminuria', 'refuted assertion', 'HbA1c', 'scope guard') without in-product definitions. Patients, carers, and new staff either guess the meaning or proceed anyway. No PageIntro explains why the screen exists or what action the user should take.
hazard_new: The system shows clinical terms such as 'microalbuminuria' (protein in the urine) and 'HbA1c' (a blood sugar test) without explaining what they mean. There are no plain-English labels telling the user why they are on a screen or what they should do next. Patients, carers, and new staff may guess the meaning or ignore the information entirely.
hazardous_situation_old: A carer reads a safety-netting paragraph that says "persistent haematuria should be reviewed". They do not know what haematuria means. The carer assumes it is not relevant and closes the page. The patient goes without the intended follow-up. Or: a junior coder approves a record marked 'refuted' without realising that 'refuted' means the initial diagnosis was overturned, not that the record itself is being rejected.
hazardous_situation_new: A carer reads a safety-netting message saying 'persistent haematuria (blood in the urine) should be reviewed'. The carer does not recognise the word and assumes it does not apply. They close the screen. The patient does not get the follow-up the clinical team intended. Separately, a junior coder sees a record marked in a way they do not understand and approves it without realising the original diagnosis was overturned. Incorrect clinical information then moves forward through the system.
harm_old: Patients miss safety-netting prompts; coders propagate incorrect clinical data into the audit pipeline. Both cause clinical-safety harm by delay or wrong onward routing.
harm_new: A patient misses an important safety-netting prompt and does not receive timely follow-up care. Incorrect clinical information is passed on, causing the patient to be directed to the wrong care pathway. Both situations can lead to delayed diagnosis or inappropriate treatment.
mitigation_new: The system records every safety-netting action, including who took it and when, so that nothing can be silently missed or altered. This log is maintained automatically by the system at all times (DI-B46AD5CE). The system keeps a worklist of all safety-netting items that have not yet been acted on. The clinical team reviews this worklist regularly to spot any outstanding items (DI-4C73DC01). When a clinician records a confirmed clinical response, the system automatically removes the related alert from the worklist. This stops the same item being acted on twice or left open in error. The system does this without any manual step (DI-0E215ADE). The worklist can be filtered by how serious an item is, how many days it has been outstanding, and which group of patients it relates to. This helps the clinical team prioritise the most urgent items quickly (DI-520A8674). Patient information and clinical reference information are held in separate parts of the system. This reduces the risk that a display error in one area affects the other (DI-84F44836). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter. Additional controls to address plain-English labelling and in-screen guidance are being identified.

title_old: A junior trainee or older clinician misreads the Operations workspace and either skips a quality alert or triggers a training run they did not intend. hazard: description: > The Op
title_new: A clinician or trainee misreads the operations screen and either misses a quality alert or starts a live deployment too early.
hazard_old: The Operations workspace orchestrates model training, deployment, and quality review. Without clear in-product explanation, a new operator may not understand that the page is the entry point for all four steps, may dismiss the context banner by accident, or may fail to spot a status dot because it is encoded only by colour.
hazard_new: The operations screen controls four key steps: training the AI, checking its quality, approving it, and making it live. Without clear labels and explanations, a less experienced user may not understand what each step does. They may accidentally close an important notice. They may also miss a status indicator if it relies on colour alone.
hazardous_situation_old: An operator with low experience, low vision, or atypical colour perception opens /admin/operations, sees four unlabelled accordion rows, and either (a) ignores an unacknowledged quality alert, or (b) opens 'Make it live' before the model has finished training, causing a premature promotion.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician or trainee with limited experience, reduced vision, or difficulty telling colours apart opens the operations screen. They see four unlabelled sections. They either ignore an unacknowledged quality alert, or they press 'Make it live' before the AI has finished training. This causes an unvalidated version of the AI to go live too soon.
harm_old: A coding error introduced by a not-yet-validated model propagates into patient records before a reviewer catches it. A missed quality alert delays remediation of a systematic coding drift.
harm_new: An AI that has not been properly checked starts adding clinical codes to patient records. Coding errors spread through records before anyone catches them. A missed quality alert means a pattern of incorrect coding continues for longer than it should.
mitigation_new: First, the deployment status panel shows the current state of any approved change directly on the review screen. This stops a clinician from promoting an AI model before all steps are complete. The clinical safety team checks this panel is working at each deployment review (DI-6EA84931). Second, quality gates are set for each type of clinical relationship the AI learns. The AI cannot be made live unless it meets these quality thresholds. The clinical safety team reviews the gate settings at each model release (DI-80BD2F86). Third, if a quality alert is not acknowledged within the set time, the AI workflow pauses automatically. No further changes can be made until the alert is reviewed. The clinical safety committee checks that this automatic pause is triggering correctly every quarter (DI-5A802C83). Fourth, historical coding frequency data is shown on the coding review screen. This helps a reviewer spot unusual patterns quickly, even if they are less experienced. The clinical safety team audits this display during quarterly case record reviews (DI-22F4E3CE). Fifth, the data quality engine applies configurable rules to each patient episode and records whether each rule passed or failed, along with a suggested fix. This gives reviewers a clear, plain-language summary of any problems. The clinical safety committee reviews rule performance and remediation rates every quarter (DI-FC80B65A). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls together every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: A junior trainee misinterprets a coding-review case because clinical terms like 'assertion', 'semantic tag', or 'suppress' are not explained in product, and either accepts an incor
title_new: A junior trainee misunderstands unclear review screen labels and suppresses a real clinical finding
hazard_old: The coding-review queue asks the operator to accept LEO's suggestion, override it with a different SNOMED term, or suppress the finding from future pipeline runs. Each decision writes to the patient record. Without plain-language explanations of the terms shown on the card, a junior or non-clinical operator may not know what they are agreeing to.
hazard_new: The coding-review screen asks the reviewer to accept the AI tool's suggestion, choose a different clinical code, or suppress the finding so it never appears again. Each choice saves a change to the patient record. The screen uses terms that a junior or non-clinical reviewer may not understand. Without plain-language explanations, the reviewer may not know what they are agreeing to.
hazardous_situation_old: A trainee opens the coding-review cases modal, sees a case with assertion 'declined' and a suggested semantic tag mismatch. Unsure of what either term means, they click 'Suppress' to make the case go away. The finding was in fact a real clinical event that should have been coded, and it is now filtered from future runs.
hazardous_situation_new: A trainee opens the coding-review screen. They see a case where the AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible has marked the finding as 'declined', and the suggested clinical code does not match the expected category. The trainee does not understand either term. To clear the case from their queue, they click 'Suppress'. The finding was a real clinical event that should have been coded. It is now hidden from all future AI workflow runs.
harm_old: A real clinical finding is systematically suppressed from the patient record, leading to missed follow-up or a coding gap in the patient's care audit.
harm_new: A real clinical finding is permanently hidden from the patient record. The patient may miss follow-up care. The finding will also be absent from care audit records, creating a gap that could affect the patient's ongoing treatment.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk.
