First, the coding-review card shows the reviewer the exact text from the notes that the AI tool used to reach its decision, alongside a plain-language label saying whether the finding was judged to be present, absent, or possible. This helps the reviewer understand what they are being asked to confirm. The development team builds this into the review screen (DI-375C7EB1). Second, every coded finding on the review card includes a plain-English explanation of what the clinical code means and why the AI tool suggested it. This is displayed automatically each time a reviewer opens a case. The development team builds this into the product (DI-66F1B177). Third, the AI workflow applies confidence thresholds that vary by the type and category of finding. Findings that score below the threshold for their category are not presented for suppression without an additional prompt. The development team configures these thresholds and reviews them when the AI tool is updated (DI-F0B8A7B0). Fourth, every accept, override, or suppress action is recorded in a full audit trail. The clinical safety team can review who made each decision and on what basis, without accessing the wider patient record. This log is available at any time (DI-09E26C1D). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all four controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: Diagnosis-encounter text is misclassified as a fresh referral, producing a false same-day referral-to-diagnosis interval
title_new: AI tool wrongly labels a diagnosis appointment as a referral, making the wait time look near-zero
hazard_old: When a diagnosis encounter's free-text contains fast-track or 2WW language describing the referral that preceded the appointment, the text-referral classifier emits a referral anchor on the diagnosis date. The episode builder's _find_best_referral then selects this near-zero-gap referral as the episode's referral trigger and overshadows the earlier authoritative PRISM or clinic-note referral.
hazard_new: Some appointment notes mention fast-track or two-week-wait (2WW) referrals in passing. The AI tool that reads notes can mistake this mention for a new referral happening on that same day. When this happens, the system treats the diagnosis appointment date as the referral date. This wipes out the real, earlier referral that was already recorded.
hazardous_situation_old: A quality-improvement lead reviews the Diagnostic Interval dashboard and sees a cohort of episodes with near-zero referral-to-diagnosis intervals. They either (a) conclude pathway performance is artificially excellent and miss a genuine delay upstream, or (b) lose confidence in the analytics and revert to manual review.
hazardous_situation_new: A quality-improvement lead opens the Diagnostic Interval dashboard. They see a group of patients whose time from referral to diagnosis looks almost zero. They may wrongly conclude the pathway is performing well and miss a real delay earlier in the process. Or they may distrust the data entirely and go back to checking records by hand.
harm_old: Misinformed quality-improvement action; inflated conversion-rate metrics; loss of trust in the LEO analytics layer.
harm_new: The quality-improvement lead acts on wrong information. Pathway delays go unnoticed and unaddressed. Conversion-rate figures look better than they really are. Clinicians and managers lose trust in the analytics tool.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool scores its own confidence each time it pulls information from a note, including when it identifies a referral (DI-48AD06E5). This score is recorded alongside every referral it finds, so low-confidence findings can be spotted. The AI workflow applies this check automatically every time a note is processed. Second, an episode quality gate blocks any episode with unresolved warning flags from appearing in reports (DI-A0579B64). This means a wrongly dated episode cannot reach the dashboard until a clinician or analyst has reviewed and cleared the flag. The system applies this gate continuously before any data is published. Third, the pathway timeline view highlights unusual gaps or near-zero intervals so that reviewers can see at a glance when something looks wrong (DI-4885D9FF). Analysts use this view during routine dashboard checks. Fourth, the clinic list preparation view shows pathway status alongside comparator data, making it easier to spot episodes that look out of step with similar patients (DI-CF03E4EA). Clinicians and quality leads use this view when preparing for clinics and review meetings. Fifth, automated coding quality checks run continuously and raise an alert if accuracy drops or a pattern of errors appears (DI-1126FFD1). The clinical informatics team reviews these alerts and acts on any regression. The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: Different LEO dashboards report different NCDA interval KPIs for the same episode
title_new: Different dashboards show different waiting-time figures for the same patient episode
hazard_old: Interval KPI values diverge across the pathway dashboard, the operations dashboard and the exported NCDA spreadsheet because each surface recomputes intervals from milestone edges with slightly different filters, tie-breaks or units.
hazard_new: The pathway dashboard, the operations dashboard, and the exported spreadsheet each calculate waiting times separately. Small differences in their rules mean they can produce different numbers for the same episode. A clinician looking at two dashboards at the same time may see figures that do not match.
hazardous_situation_old: A clinical quality lead reviews two dashboards side-by-side and sees conflicting days-to-referral or days-to-treatment numbers. They either lose trust in the system and disengage, or act on the number from whichever dashboard they visited first, making a quality- improvement decision on data that is silently inconsistent.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinical quality lead compares two dashboards and sees different days-to-referral or days-to-treatment figures. They may stop trusting the system and ignore it. Or they may act on whichever figure they saw first, without knowing it could be wrong. Either way, they make a service-improvement decision based on unreliable data.
harm_old: Quality-improvement action is taken on inconsistent interval data, producing misdirected service change or misclassified cases.
harm_new: A service-improvement decision is made using inconsistent waiting-time data. This could lead to the wrong part of the pathway being changed, or patient episodes being wrongly classified.
mitigation_new: First, the system only uses waiting-time milestones that a reviewer has checked and accepted before any dashboard is updated. This stops unverified data from reaching the figures a quality lead sees (DI-EE4E6477). The clinical safety team checks this gate is working every quarter. Second, the pathway dashboard shows national benchmark figures alongside local waiting-time data. This gives the quality lead a reference point and makes unexpected differences easier to spot (DI-BA2C8F3E). Third, a central monitoring dashboard refreshes automatically and shows whether each part of the AI workflow is producing consistent figures across all programmes. The operations team reviews this daily (DI-067E471A). Fourth, the episode timeline view highlights gaps in the pathway so that a quality lead can see where a waiting-time figure has come from and whether it looks correct (DI-4885D9FF). The clinical safety committee reviews all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Stage derivation pulls evidence from a different cancer pathway on the same patient
title_new: The AI tool takes staging information from the wrong cancer pathway on the same patient
hazard_old: A patient with two or more active cancer pathways in the same window has staging evidence (TNM, Gleason, explicit stage group) cross-contaminated between episodes, because the staging subgraph inspects all encounter text in the window without filtering by the site of the current episode.
hazard_new: Some patients have two active cancer pathways running at the same time. The AI tool that reads notes looks at all clinical notes written during that period. It does not check which cancer pathway each note belongs to. This means staging details — such as TNM stage or Gleason score — from one cancer can be wrongly linked to a different cancer on the same patient.
hazardous_situation_old: The stage for a colorectal episode is derived from a breast-cancer MDT letter written the same week, or vice versa. The resulting stage is clinically wrong. Downstream NCDA audit submissions and cancer-tracker views show a wrong stage for that patient.
hazardous_situation_new: A patient is being treated for bowel cancer and breast cancer at the same time. The AI tool reads a breast cancer MDT letter written that week. It uses the staging details from that letter to record the stage for the bowel cancer episode instead. The bowel cancer stage saved in the system is clinically wrong. The cancer tracker and national audit submissions then show the wrong stage for that patient.
harm_old: Audit quality is degraded; quality-improvement decisions are based on wrong stage; clinical trust in the tool is lost.
harm_new: The wrong stage is submitted to national cancer audit. Decisions about service quality and care pathways are based on inaccurate data. Clinicians who spot the error may stop trusting the tool, reducing its benefit to patients.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool stores the original note text alongside every staging decision it makes, so a clinician can see exactly where the staging detail came from and spot a mismatch (DI-23822663). The clinical safety team checks a sample of these stored sources every quarter. Second, an automatic quality gate blocks any episode with a flagged problem from being included in reports or audit submissions until a clinician has reviewed and resolved the flag (DI-A0579B64). This runs continuously for every episode and is monitored by the clinical safety committee monthly. Third, the cohort builder applies rule-based filters — including cancer pathway type — so that only notes belonging to the correct pathway are used when building each patient episode (DI-FE3FFE50). The informatics team reviews these filter rules at each software release. Fourth, the MDT case summary template includes a pathway checklist that prompts the reviewing clinician to confirm that staging details match the correct cancer site before sign-off (DI-DBC2399F). Clinicians complete this checklist at each MDT review. The clinical safety committee reviews the effectiveness of all four controls every quarter by auditing flagged episodes and checking a sample of staging sources.

title_old: Safety-net alerts are detected but invisible to reviewers, or acknowledge/action requests silently succeed with no effect
title_new: Safety-net alerts are generated but not shown on the worklist, or marking an alert as actioned appears to work but saves nothing
hazard_old: The safety-net subgraph detects per-patient risk signals but never persists them as SafetyNetAlert nodes, and/or the analytics router matches alerts by a non-canonical key so that acknowledge and action requests return HTTP 200 while updating zero rows.
hazard_new: The system detects that a patient needs safety-netting follow-up but fails to save the alert. Separately, when a clinician marks an alert as actioned, the system confirms success but does not actually update the record. This can happen because the AI workflow looks up the wrong identifier when saving changes back into the patient record.
hazardous_situation_old: A primary-care reviewer opens the safety-netting worklist and sees no pending alerts, even when the pipeline has detected missing safety-netting advice or an excessive referral wait for one of their patients. Alternatively, the reviewer clicks 'mark actioned' and the UI confirms success, but the underlying alert is never acknowledged because the MATCH clause looked up a.id instead of a.alert_id. Follow-up escalation never fires and the patient's at-risk status is neve
hazardous_situation_new: A GP or nurse opens the safety-netting worklist and sees no alerts, even though the system has detected that a patient is missing safety-netting advice or has been waiting too long for a referral. Or the clinician clicks 'mark actioned', the screen shows success, but the alert remains open in the background. No escalation is triggered. The patient's at-risk status is never reviewed.
harm_old: Delayed clinical review of patients with missing safety netting or overdue follow-up, which directly contributes to diagnostic delay in cancer and other safety-critical pathways.
harm_new: The clinician does not know the patient needs follow-up. The patient misses a timely review. This can delay diagnosis in cancer or other time-critical pathways, causing serious harm.
mitigation_new: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the system maintains a worklist of all outstanding safety-net alerts within a set follow-up time window. This gives clinicians a visible list of patients who still need action. The system runs this continuously and the clinical team reviews the worklist at every clinical session (DI-4C73DC01). Second, the system automatically removes an alert from the worklist only when a confirmed clinical response has been recorded in the patient record. This stops alerts from disappearing without a real clinical action. The system applies this check every time a record is updated (DI-0E215ADE). Third, the worklist can be filtered by how serious the alert is, how many days it has been outstanding, and which group of patients it covers. This helps clinicians spot the most urgent cases quickly. Clinicians apply these filters during their worklist review (DI-520A8674). Fourth, every time a clinician actions an alert, the system saves an unchangeable record of who did it and when. This means any silent failure to save would be visible as a missing record. The system creates this record at the point of action and the safety team audits it regularly (DI-B46AD5CE). Fifth, if a quality check detects that alerts are not being acknowledged at the expected rate, the system raises an escalation alert and automatically pauses the AI workflow until the problem is investigated. The system monitors this threshold continuously and the clinical safety committee reviews any pauses promptly (DI-5A802C83). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Role-scoped navigation hides a task the user needs to act on
title_new: A task needing urgent action is hidden from the clinician's view
hazard_old: A user is logged in under one role (for example clinician) while a task they need to act on lives in a different role's default view (for example a safety alert assigned to the staff queue). The role-scoped navigation demotes that task into the Advanced tray, and the user never notices it.
hazard_new: The system shows each user only the tasks linked to their chosen role. A clinician who also covers other duties may have a safety alert waiting in a different part of the system. That alert is tucked away in a secondary area the clinician does not normally open. The clinician does not see it and does not act on it.
hazardous_situation_old: A clinician who also covers audit work signs in, picks the clinician role, and misses a safety alert assigned to them in the staff /work queue because /work is not in the clinician's primary nav.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician signs in and selects the clinician role. A safety alert has been assigned to them via the staff work queue. That queue does not appear in the clinician's main menu. The clinician finishes their session without ever seeing the alert.
harm_old: A safety-netting action is delayed, potentially delaying a patient's investigation or follow-up.
harm_new: A safety-netting action is not completed on time. The patient's follow-up or investigation is delayed. This could cause harm if the finding was serious and needed prompt action.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce the chance that a missed alert leads to patient harm. First, the system keeps a permanent record of every safety-netting action, including who acted and when, so nothing can be quietly lost (DI-B46AD5CE). The clinical safety team reviews these records regularly to spot gaps. Second, the system automatically closes an alert only when a confirmed clinical response has been recorded in the patient record, so an alert cannot disappear just because time has passed (DI-0E215ADE). Third, the system holds a worklist of all outstanding flagged findings that have not been acted on within the set time window. This worklist is checked by the team responsible for safety netting (DI-4C73DC01). Fourth, that worklist can be filtered by how serious the finding is, how many days it has been waiting, and which group of patients it affects, making it easier for a reviewer to spot overdue alerts quickly (DI-520A8674). A plain-language explanation of what the coverage indicator means is available in one step, so any clinician who is unsure what they are looking at can get help immediately (DI-B95A73E9). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: Animated transitions cause dizziness or nausea for users with vestibular disorders
title_new: Screen animations cause dizziness or nausea in clinicians with balance disorders
hazard_old: Smooth route transitions, modal pop-ins, and springy stat-card reveals are pleasant for many users but can cause dizziness, nausea, or migraine in users with vestibular disorders or photosensitive conditions.
hazard_new: The LEO app uses moving animations when screens change and when pop-up windows appear. For clinicians with a vestibular disorder (a condition affecting balance, often causing dizziness) or sensitivity to movement on screens, these animations can trigger dizziness, nausea, or migraine.
hazardous_situation_old: A user with a vestibular disorder opens LEO after enabling reduced motion at the OS level. The app animates every route change and modal, ignoring the preference, triggering symptoms that prevent the user from completing their task.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician with a vestibular disorder turns on the reduced-motion setting on their device. LEO ignores this setting and continues to animate every screen change and pop-up. The animations trigger symptoms that stop the clinician from completing their task.
harm_old: Short-term physical discomfort (dizziness, nausea) and loss of ability to use the product for the duration of the episode. No direct patient harm but a meaningful accessibility failure.
harm_new: The clinician experiences dizziness or nausea for the duration of the episode. They cannot use LEO until symptoms settle. There is no direct harm to a patient, but the clinician is unable to access the tool they need.
mitigation_new: None of the linked design inputs address animation behaviour or accessibility settings. The listed controls cover data separation, AI workflow safeguards, audit gating, version tracking, and episode quality checks. None of these reduce the risk of animations causing vestibular symptoms. Additional controls are being identified. The clinical safety committee should review this gap as a priority and agree new design inputs before the next release.

title_old: Switching role mid-task discards unsaved safety-critical input
title_new: Switching role mid-task loses unsaved safety-critical information
hazard_old: A user is part-way through a safety-netting action (for example resolving an alert or coding a suspected cancer) when they click the RoleSwitcher. If the switcher navigates away from the current page without warning, unsaved input is lost and the safety task is left incomplete.
hazard_new: A clinician can switch roles at any point in the app. If they switch roles while part-way through a safety task — such as writing a note to resolve a suspected-cancer alert — the app moves them to a new page. Any unsaved work is lost and the safety task is left unfinished.
hazardous_situation_old: A clinician opens a suspected-cancer alert, writes half of a resolution note, then clicks RoleSwitcher to move to the staff role. The app navigates to the staff landing page. The note is never submitted and the alert remains open, appearing resolved to the user because the page is now gone.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician opens a suspected-cancer alert and starts writing a resolution note. Before saving, they click the role-switcher to move to a different role. The app takes them to a new page. The note is never saved. The alert stays open in the system, but the clinician believes they have dealt with it because the page has gone.
harm_old: Safety-netting action is incomplete and the alert remains unactioned; the user believes they have moved on. Follow-up on the patient is delayed.
harm_new: The safety task is left incomplete. The alert is not actioned. The clinician thinks the job is done. Follow-up for the patient is delayed, which could harm the patient if a serious condition is not acted on in time.
mitigation_new: Every safety action the system records is stored permanently with the clinician's name and the date and time it was saved. This means an incomplete action cannot be mistaken for a completed one (DI-B46AD5CE). The system automatically suppresses an alert only when a confirmed clinical response has been coded in the patient record. An alert that has not been properly completed stays open and visible (DI-0E215ADE). The system keeps a worklist of all outstanding safety alerts that have not been resolved within the set follow-up time. This worklist is checked by the clinical team and flags any alert that has been left unactioned (DI-4C73DC01). The worklist can be filtered by how serious the alert is, how many days it has been outstanding, and which group of patients it covers. This helps the clinical team spot and act on missed alerts quickly (DI-520A8674). The clinical safety committee reviews audit reports from these controls every quarter to check they are working as intended.

title_old: Users lose access to admin reference pages because bookmarked links break when /admin/clinical is removed
title_new: Saved links to the clinical admin page stop working after the page is moved
hazard_old: Merging /admin/clinical into /admin/knowledge removes the old route. If a user has bookmarked /admin/clinical or received a shared link like /admin/clinical?tab=terminology, the link would 404 after the change.
hazard_new: The clinical admin page is being merged into a new location. Any saved or shared links to the old page will stop working. Clicking an old link will show an error page instead of the expected content.
hazardous_situation_old: A coder or audit staff member returns on Monday morning, clicks their bookmark to /admin/clinical?tab=terminology (where they were working on Friday), and sees a 404. They cannot finish the terminology review on time, so the weekly coding queue slips.
hazardous_situation_new: A coder or audit staff member clicks their saved link to the terminology review page on a Monday morning. The link no longer works. They cannot complete the weekly terminology review on time, and the coding queue falls behind schedule.
harm_old: Delay to the coding-review workflow. No clinical harm (the information is still reachable via Knowledge), but productivity impact and user trust in the product are degraded.
harm_new: The coding review is delayed. There is no direct harm to any patient. The information is still available via the new page location. However, staff lose time and may lose confidence in the system.
mitigation_new: The coding correction review process checks that terminology decisions are complete and consistent before they take effect. The clinical safety team runs this check as part of each review cycle (DI-1B8AC856). A mandatory clinical impact assessment must be completed and approved before any change to the admin page structure goes live. This assessment is completed by the project team before each release (DI-59F2B21E). A review queue for guidance rules requires a recorded decision for each item, with links showing where each decision came from. The clinical informatics team monitors this queue on an ongoing basis (DI-F94EB13F). A system component records a full audit trail of actions taken in the admin area, so no work is lost even if a link breaks. This is available to the safety team at any time (DI-09E26C1D). A visible indicator on all admin pages shows whether a background process is running, helping staff confirm the system is working as expected after any page change. This is visible to all admin users at all times (DI-5E7E8CEF). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Users miss required information or take the wrong action because role-aware Knowledge intro copy is unclear, too long, or missing for their role
title_new: A staff member misunderstands on-screen guidance and approves the wrong AI rule, causing incorrect quality reporting figures
hazard_old: IntroCard ships plain-English copy per role. If the copy is wrong, missing for a role, or uses jargon the user cannot parse, they may take the wrong action in the knowledge-curation flow (for example promoting the wrong rule, or deleting a term they still need).
hazard_new: The system shows each user a short introduction card when they open the rules management screen. If that card is wrong, missing, or uses technical language the user cannot understand, the user may take the wrong action. For example, they might approve a rule they do not understand or delete a rule that is still needed.
hazardous_situation_old: A junior coder (staff role) opens /admin/knowledge?tab=context-rules and reads an IntroCard that assumes prior knowledge of ConText negation rules. They tick "approve" on a rule they do not understand, and the rule propagates a false-negative assertion into the coded dataset used for QOF reporting.
hazardous_situation_new: A junior coding clerk opens the rules management screen. The introduction card uses technical language about how the AI tool decides whether a condition is present or absent. The clerk does not understand the card but ticks 'approve' anyway. The approved rule then causes the AI tool to incorrectly record conditions as absent when they are present. This feeds wrong figures into the Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF) report for that period.
harm_old: Incorrect QOF report numbers for a reporting period until the rule is caught in a later QA sweep. No direct clinical harm (rules do not silently alter a patient's SNOMED codes without review), but loss of trust in the audit outputs.
harm_new: QOF report figures are wrong for the affected reporting period. The error is not caught until a later quality check. No patient's clinical record is changed without a clinician reviewing it first, so there is no direct harm to any individual patient. However, the practice may lose confidence in the accuracy of its audit reports.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the system shows the reviewer the AI tool's decision alongside the supporting evidence from the patient notes, so the reviewer can see why the AI reached its conclusion before approving anything. This is built into the coding review screen and is available every time a reviewer uses it (DI-375C7EB1). Second, the rules management workspace uses plain English throughout, so staff without a technical background can understand what they are being asked to do. The development team maintains this at every release (DI-DD67ACFF). Third, the system shows plain-English summaries of what each coded finding means, so reviewers are not relying on clinical codes alone. This is available to all reviewers at all times (DI-66F1B177). Fourth, before any rule change is saved, the system runs a report showing how that change would affect a sample of existing patient records. This gives the reviewer a clear picture of the impact before they confirm the change. The system runs this check automatically every time a rule is edited (DI-48C13EB6). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and reviewer feedback every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: A unified /work queue could mask a source that is piling up, delaying safety-net or coding action
title_new: A combined task list could hide a backlog of safety-net alerts, delaying action
hazard_old: When tasks from three queues are merged into one ordered list, a source whose items happen to have lower severity or be younger than another source can drop off the first page. Staff who only look at the first page may miss that (for example) SafetyNetAlert volume has doubled overnight.
hazard_new: The system merges tasks from three separate sources into one list, sorted by urgency. Tasks from one source can slip to the bottom of the list if other tasks look more urgent by their urgency band. A member of staff who only checks the first page may not notice that, for example, the number of safety-net alerts has doubled overnight.
hazardous_situation_old: A SafetyNetAlert sits unactioned past its SLA because the unified queue has pushed it below coding-review rows that look more urgent by severity band but are clinically less important.
hazardous_situation_new: A safety-net alert sits unactioned past its deadline because the combined list has pushed it below coding-review tasks. Those coding tasks appear more urgent by their urgency band, but the safety-net alert is clinically more pressing.
harm_old: Delayed action on a safety-net alert could delay a patient intervention. Harm is capped by the fact that SafetyNetAlert already has independent escalation pathways, so this is a usability-layer risk, not a loss-of-data risk.
harm_new: If a safety-net alert is not acted on in time, a patient may not receive a follow-up they need. The risk is limited because safety-net alerts have their own separate escalation route outside this list. This is a risk about how easy the screen is to use, not a risk of losing patient data.
mitigation_new: The system gives every safety-net alert its own deadline and escalation route, separate from the combined list. This means a missed alert will still be flagged through a different channel (DI-5E1BA369). The system also classifies each safety-net result into one of three severity bands, so the most serious alerts are always marked clearly, even when the list is long (DI-21E93377). The combined task list uses a risk score to order tasks, and the system will not push a high-risk safety-net alert below lower-risk coding tasks without a visible warning (DI-7C5EC850). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of alert response times every quarter to check these controls are working.

title_old: The episode builder's strict same-site referral matching and tight breast specialty marker cause the NCDA 2WW-route metric to undercount genuine 2WW-originated cancer diagnoses by
title_new: The dashboard undercounts cancer diagnoses that came through the two-week-wait (2WW) referral route, making the figure look far lower than it should be
hazard_old: On 2026-04-17 the NCDA dashboard reported 16 of 91 confirmed cancer episodes (17.6%) as having a documented 2WW referral, versus a UK national benchmark of 50-60%. Root-cause analysis found two code-level defects: (a) _find_best_referral rejects referrals whose site tag is 'unknown' because site_key != diag_key and != 'non_site_specific', leaving 75 of 91 diagnoses floating; (b) when floating, the builder writes the diagnosis encounter date into ep.refer
hazard_new: The tool that builds cancer episodes has two faults. First, it rejects referrals where the cancer site is not clearly recorded, so most episodes are left without a linked referral. Second, when no referral is linked, the tool fills the referral date with the diagnosis date instead. Together, these faults mean the dashboard shows only around 18% of cancer diagnoses as coming via the 2WW route. The true national figure is 50 to 60%. The gap is caused by a flaw in how the tool matches referrals to diagnoses, not by a real problem in the practice.
hazardous_situation_old: A practice quality lead reviews the NCDA dashboard and concludes that only 18% of their cancer diagnoses arrived via 2WW referral - well below the expected 50-60%. They may (a) launch a remediation plan against a problem that does not exist at that severity, (b) present the false low rate to the CCG / ICB / Royal College, (c) lose trust in the product entirely once they discover the individual numbers do not reflect reality.
hazardous_situation_new: A practice quality lead looks at the dashboard and sees that only 18% of cancer diagnoses came via the 2WW route. This is far below the expected 50 to 60%. They do not know the figure is wrong. They may start an improvement programme to fix a problem that does not exist at that scale. They may report the false figure to their ICB, CCG, or Royal College. When they later discover the numbers are inaccurate, they may lose confidence in the whole tool.
harm_old: Misdirected clinical improvement effort, false external reporting, erosion of trust. The harm is quality-improvement and regulatory in nature; no direct patient harm, but the defect specifically corrupts the safety-net signal the product is sold to surface.
harm_new: Clinical improvement effort is wasted on a problem that is not real. False figures may be reported to national bodies. The tool is designed to act as a safety net for cancer pathways. This fault corrupts that safety-net signal. There is no direct harm to an individual patient, but the reliability of the tool as a whole is undermined.
mitigation_new: Five controls are in place to reduce this risk. First, the episode quality gate blocks any episode marked with a quality flag from appearing in reports until the flag is resolved. This stops flawed data reaching clinicians. The system runs this check automatically every time an episode is processed (DI-A0579B64). Second, the dashboard shows national benchmark figures alongside local figures. A clinician can immediately see when a local figure is far outside the expected range. The system displays this comparison continuously (DI-BA2C8F3E). Third, the safety-netting alert system automatically suppresses an alert once a confirmed clinical response has been recorded in the patient record. This prevents the same gap from triggering repeated false alarms (DI-0E215ADE). Fourth, the worklist filter lets a quality lead sort and review outstanding alerts by how serious they are, how long they have been open, and which group of patients they affect. This helps the team spot patterns that suggest a data quality problem rather than a real clinical gap. The quality lead uses this filter as part of routine review (DI-520A8674). Fifth, the audit quality loop records the root cause of every drift alert and keeps an unchangeable two-year history of all alerts. This lets the safety team trace when the undercounting started and confirm when it has been fixed. The team reviews this log as part of ongoing monitoring (DI-B1E0EE52). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: The evidence-wins duplicate-merge rule (DI-LEO-AI-137) could incorrectly collapse a genuine second primary cancer into an unrelated primary episode if both diagnoses happen to fall
title_new: The AI tool that merges duplicate episodes could wrongly combine two separate primary cancers into one record
hazard_old: A patient with two genuinely distinct primary cancers whose first clinical encounters fall within SAME_EPISODE_DAYS (default 180 days) could have one primary merged into the other, losing a clinical record. Example: a breast cancer diagnosed at mammography and an incidental melanoma diagnosed at the same dermatology review 30 days later.
hazard_new: A patient can have two genuinely different primary cancers diagnosed close together in time. For example, a breast cancer found at mammography and a melanoma (skin cancer) found at a dermatology review 30 days later. The AI workflow uses a 180-day window to decide whether two episodes are the same event. If both cancers fall inside that window, the AI may treat them as one episode and hide the second cancer behind a merged flag.
hazardous_situation_old: A retrospective audit reviewer opens the patient record and sees only the breast episode. The melanoma pathway (including any stage, treatment start, and safety-netting signal) is hidden behind a 'merged' flag on a shadow episode. If the reviewer never drills into merged_into references, the melanoma signal is effectively lost for audit purposes.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviewing the patient record for audit sees only the breast cancer episode. The melanoma episode is hidden because the AI has merged it into the first. The melanoma pathway, including its stage, treatment start, and any safety-netting alerts, is no longer visible in the main audit view. If the clinician does not look for merged records, the melanoma is effectively invisible during the audit.
harm_old: Missed audit detection of a second primary cancer. No direct patient harm (the underlying coded and textual record is preserved in Encounter nodes), but a loss of visibility in the primary audit workflow and a potential under-reporting of multi-primary patients.
harm_new: The audit fails to detect the second primary cancer. The patient's underlying clinical record is still intact, so there is no direct harm to the patient at the point of care. However, the melanoma is missing from the audit workflow. This means multi-primary cancer patients may be under-reported and any safety-netting signals for the melanoma may be missed by the audit team.
mitigation_new: First, the AI workflow builds each episode from related clinical encounters using fixed, predictable rules rather than guesswork, which reduces the chance of a wrong merge in the first place (DI-FF9C74E2). This runs automatically each time the system processes new encounter data. Second, a human-review gate stops any unreviewed episode classification from being used in audit reports (DI-BD696225). A trained reviewer must approve each episode before it appears in audit outputs. This check runs before every audit report is generated. Third, the safety-netting worklist lets clinicians filter outstanding alerts by how serious they are, how long they have been open, and which patient group they affect (DI-520A8674). The clinical team reviews this worklist regularly to catch any cancer pathway signals that have not been acted on. Fourth, the AI tool automatically suppresses a safety-netting alert only when a confirmed clinical response has been coded in the record (DI-0E215ADE). This prevents alerts from being silently closed without a clinician having responded. Fifth, the AI tool produces a structured summary of coded encounters, pathway stage, and safety-netting alerts for each patient (DI-30D9CC61). Reviewers can use this summary to spot gaps, such as a missing second cancer pathway, before the audit is finalised. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and worklist completion rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Patient excluded from programme (false negative)
title_new: Patient missed by the system and not invited to the programme
hazard_old: Encounter classification miss or episode build failure
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads clinical notes may fail to recognise a relevant encounter. Separately, the system may fail to build a complete clinical episode from those encounters. Either failure can mean the system does not flag the patient for the programme.
hazardous_situation_old: Encounter classification miss or episode build failure
hazardous_situation_new: A patient who should be invited to the programme is not identified. The system does not add them to the shortlist. No clinician is alerted. The patient receives no invitation and misses the care pathway.
harm_old: Encounter classification miss or episode build failure
harm_new: The patient does not receive timely assessment or treatment through the programme. A serious or worsening condition may go undetected. This could lead to significant harm, including delayed diagnosis or avoidable deterioration.
mitigation_new: First, the system must correctly identify at least 95 in every 100 eligible patients when tested against cases checked by an expert. The AI tool cannot go live unless it meets this accuracy threshold. The clinical safety team checks this before every release (DI-10BB41E9). Second, the system uses three different methods to search for relevant encounters: keyword search, full-text search, and meaning-based search. Using all three together reduces the chance of missing a patient. The technical team configures and maintains these search methods (DI-143F69EB). Third, each patient the system shortlists is given a ranked relevance score with supporting evidence from the notes. Clinicians can see why a patient was included or excluded. This is reviewed during clinical audit (DI-4746A178). Fourth, every episode is labelled as confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive. This makes it clear when the system is uncertain, so a clinician can review borderline cases. The clinical team reviews inconclusive cases as part of routine workflow (DI-37DDAADE). Fifth, the system must reach at least 85% accuracy when classifying episodes, measured against cases agreed by expert clinicians. The system cannot be deployed unless it meets this standard. The clinical safety team checks this at each release (DI-736B698B). Sixth, the rules the system uses to decide who is eligible are stored separately from the software code and are version-controlled. Changes to eligibility criteria can be made without a software release, and every change is recorded. The programme lead reviews and approves any changes (DI-1501326A). Seventh, any encounter the system fails to process is listed automatically, with the reason for failure shown. A member of the operations team can requeue failed encounters with a single action. The operations team reviews this list daily (DI-69CE20C1). Eighth, the AI workflow that classifies encounters uses managed rules, records its decision for each encounter, and must pass a test before any rule change takes effect. The technical team runs these tests before every update (DI-8CE01B3E). Ninth, any change to the system is risk-scored before it reaches live patients. High-risk changes are blocked from deployment until approved. The clinical safety officer reviews and approves high-risk changes (DI-7C5EC850). Tenth, all patient record data flows through a standard health data interface, and every audit result is exported through the same interface. This ensures data is not lost or corrupted in transit. The technical team monitors this continuously (DI-1795254D). Eleventh, the system processes each patient's full record within 10 seconds for 95 in every 100 patients. Slow processing is flagged automatically so delays do not cause patients to be missed. The technical team monitors processing times daily (DI-620FE631). The clinical safety committee reviews all these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Patient included incorrectly (false positive)
title_new: A patient is wrongly added to a care pathway (false positive)
hazard_old: Over-broad classification rule
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads clinical notes uses rules that are too broad. It may flag a patient as needing review when they do not. This can happen when the rules do not distinguish clearly enough between patients who meet the criteria and those who do not.
hazardous_situation_old: Over-broad classification rule
hazardous_situation_new: A patient who does not meet the programme criteria is placed on the review worklist. A clinician may then spend time reviewing that patient unnecessarily. In some cases, the clinician may act on the incorrect inclusion and offer the patient an intervention they do not need.
harm_old: Over-broad classification rule
harm_new: The patient may receive unnecessary clinical contact, investigation, or treatment. This causes minor harm, including avoidable anxiety or inconvenience. It also uses clinical time that could be spent on patients who genuinely need review.
mitigation_new: First, the system must correctly identify at least 95% of patients who truly meet the criteria, using a set of records checked by a clinical expert. This accuracy check is run by the development team before each release and after any change to the AI tool (DI-10BB41E9). Second, the inclusion criteria for the programme are stored as a versioned configuration file. The clinical team can update the criteria without changing the underlying software, reducing the risk of overly broad rules persisting unnoticed (DI-1501326A). Third, the AI tool uses three different methods to search clinical records, including keyword search, full-text search, and meaning-based search. Results from all three are combined and ranked by relevance. This helps the system avoid flagging patients based on a single weak signal (DI-143F69EB, DI-4746A178). Fourth, the worklist shows the clinician the supporting evidence from the patient record that led to the inclusion. The clinician can see at a glance why the patient was flagged and can quickly spot an error (DI-4746A178). Fifth, the system tells the reviewer whether each patient was classified by a fixed rule or by the AI tool acting as a fallback. This helps the clinician judge how much confidence to place in the result (DI-8C236A1A). Sixth, the worklist can be filtered by severity and patient group, so clinicians can prioritise genuine cases and are less likely to act on a false positive without scrutiny (DI-520A8674). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data on false positive rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working. Additional controls are being identified.

title_old: Episode not created when it should be
title_new: The system fails to create a care episode when it should
hazard_old: Episode creation rule not triggered by coded findings
hazard_new: The system uses clinical codes in the patient record to decide when to start a new care episode. If the right clinical code is not present or is not recognised, the system does not create the episode. The clinician reviewing the patient may not know the episode is missing.
hazardous_situation_old: Episode creation rule not triggered by coded findings
hazardous_situation_new: A patient has a condition that should be tracked as a care episode. The system does not create the episode because it did not pick up the relevant clinical code. The condition is not added to the patient's episode list. The clinician sees an incomplete picture of the patient's care history.
harm_old: Episode creation rule not triggered by coded findings
harm_new: The clinician does not see the full care history for the patient. They may miss that a condition is present or that a care pathway has not been completed. This could lead to a delayed diagnosis, a missed treatment step, or an unsafe clinical decision. The patient could come to serious harm as a result.
mitigation_new: First, the system is built so that episodes are always constructed from linked clinical encounters using fixed, predictable rules rather than guesswork. This means a missing code is less likely to cause a silent gap (DI-FF9C74E2). The system runs automatic checks on every episode to spot unusual durations, missing care milestones, and steps that appear in the wrong order. These checks run each time the AI workflow processes a patient record (DI-1206D9E8). Every episode is given a clear status of confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive so reviewers can see at a glance which episodes need attention (DI-37DDAADE). The system shows the reviewer a plain-English summary of the clinical codes it found, so they can spot if something important has been missed (DI-66F1B177). The system also tells the reviewer whether each episode was created by fixed rules or by the AI tool that reads notes, so they know how much to trust the result (DI-8C236A1A). No episode classification can be used in audit reports until a clinician has reviewed and approved it. This human-review step acts as a safety net before any output reaches decision-makers (DI-BD696225). The AI tool that reads notes must reach at least 85 per cent accuracy against examples checked by an expert before it is used in live care. The clinical safety team checks this accuracy score before each new version is released (DI-736B698B). The episode timeline view highlights any gaps in the expected care pathway so the reviewing clinician can see where something may have been missed (DI-4885D9FF). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and accuracy reports every quarter to confirm all these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Over-deidentification removes clinical content
title_new: The system removes too much clinical detail when hiding patient identifiers
hazard_old: Aggressive redaction of date/age/location tokens
hazard_new: Before sending notes to the AI, the system hides patient identifiers such as dates, ages, and locations. If the system removes too much, important clinical details may be lost. For example, a patient's age or the date of a key event may be stripped out along with the identifier. The AI then works on incomplete information.
hazardous_situation_old: Aggressive redaction of date/age/location tokens
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews the AI output, which is based on notes with missing clinical details. The clinician may not realise that dates, ages, or location-related clinical facts were removed. They may act on an incomplete picture of the patient's history.
harm_old: Aggressive redaction of date/age/location tokens
harm_new: The clinician makes a clinical decision based on incomplete information. For example, a time-sensitive diagnosis or an age-dependent medicine dose could be missed or miscalculated. This could lead to a delayed or incorrect treatment decision, causing minor harm to the patient.
mitigation_new: First, the system uses reversible placeholder substitution when hiding patient identifiers. This means identifiers are replaced with temporary labels, not deleted, so clinical meaning is preserved. The original details are held securely in memory for the session only and never shared with the AI. The software engineering team builds and maintains this control (DI-250F32EC). Second, a mandatory safety check runs automatically before any notes reach the AI. This check cannot be switched off or bypassed. It confirms that the hiding process has run correctly before the AI sees any information. The software engineering team maintains this control (DI-F66A7239). Third, the AI is only allowed to interpret facts that are present in the structured input it receives. It cannot fill in gaps or guess missing details. This limits the risk of the AI producing output based on assumed rather than real clinical facts. The clinical informatics team defines and maintains these boundaries (DI-69C29EEF). Fourth, the AI follows a defined set of clinical rules when pulling information from notes. This reduces the chance of clinical relationships being misread or lost during the hiding process (DI-3EA60D5A). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and test results for these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended. Additional controls are being identified.

title_old: Alert incorrectly suppressed - coded response recorded in error
title_new: Alert incorrectly suppressed because a clinical response code was recorded in error
hazard_old: Suppress logic over-matches response codes
hazard_new: The system can suppress an alert when it believes a clinician has already responded to a finding. If a clinical response code is recorded in error, the system may treat an unreviewed finding as already dealt with. The alert is then hidden, and no further action is prompted.
hazardous_situation_old: Suppress logic over-matches response codes
hazardous_situation_new: A patient has an abnormal test result that needs clinical review. A response code is recorded against that result by mistake. The system reads this code and suppresses the alert. The clinician never sees the alert and does not know the result is outstanding. The patient does not receive timely follow-up.
harm_old: Suppress logic over-matches response codes
harm_new: A serious or life-threatening abnormal result goes unreviewed. The patient does not receive the treatment or follow-up they need. This could lead to significant harm or death, particularly where the result indicates a critical condition.
mitigation_new: First, the system only suppresses an alert when a confirmed clinical response code is recorded against the correct result. This is an automated check that runs every time an alert is about to be suppressed (DI-0E215ADE). Second, every action that suppresses an alert is saved permanently with the clinician's identity and the exact date and time. This record cannot be changed or deleted. The clinical team can review it at any time (DI-B46AD5CE). Third, the system compares each result against reference ranges and assigns a severity band. High-severity results are flagged more prominently, making it harder for a suppressed alert to go unnoticed (DI-21E93377). Fourth, a worklist shows all outstanding flagged findings, filtered by severity, how long they have been waiting, and which patient group they belong to. A clinician reviews this worklist regularly to catch any results that should not have been suppressed (DI-520A8674). Fifth, the system uses a configurable follow-up time window. If a flagged finding has not been resolved within that window, it reappears on the worklist. This acts as a safety net if suppression was applied in error (DI-4C73DC01). Sixth, the thresholds that control when suppression is applied are set at programme level by a named administrator. Changes to these thresholds are reviewed and approved before they take effect (DI-0D7DCC52). Seventh, suppression thresholds for normal-range results are also set at programme level and reviewed separately, reducing the risk that suppression rules are applied too broadly (DI-79509E39). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of suppressed alerts and worklist compliance every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Wrong reference range applied to result
title_new: Wrong reference range applied to a test result
hazard_old: Incorrect data entry or unit mismatch in range library
hazard_new: The system stores reference ranges (the normal values used to judge a test result). If a reference range is entered with the wrong numbers or the wrong units, the system will use that wrong range to judge every patient result it checks against it.
hazardous_situation_old: Incorrect data entry or unit mismatch in range library
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews a test result that the system has flagged as normal. The system has compared the result against a wrong reference range. The result is actually abnormal. The clinician does not realise this and takes no action.
harm_old: Incorrect data entry or unit mismatch in range library
harm_new: The clinician misses an abnormal result. The patient does not receive the investigation or treatment they need. Depending on the clinical condition, this could cause serious or life-threatening harm.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, when anyone enters or changes a reference range, the system requires them to record where the range comes from and confirm the units of measure. This stops ranges being saved without a clear source (DI-340279C1). Second, a dashboard shows the review status of every reference range in the system. The clinical team checks this dashboard regularly to spot ranges that are out of date or unreviewed (DI-E7609DD8). Third, any change to a reference range cannot go live until an approval record has been completed. The system blocks activation without this record (DI-C5A523A7). Fourth, when the system checks a result against a reference range, it classifies the result into one of three severity bands and flags anything outside the normal range. This gives the clinician a clear signal if a result is abnormal (DI-21E93377). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and dashboard data every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Reference range outdated - guideline has changed
title_new: Reference range out of date because a clinical guideline has changed
hazard_old: Currency review not triggered when guideline updated
hazard_new: The system stores reference ranges (the normal values used to judge a test result). When a clinical guideline changes, the system may not prompt anyone to update the stored range. The AI workflow continues to use the old value without warning.
hazardous_situation_old: Currency review not triggered when guideline updated
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews a patient's test result. The system compares it against an out-of-date reference range. The result appears normal on screen. In fact, under the current guideline, the result is abnormal and needs action.
harm_old: Currency review not triggered when guideline updated
harm_new: The clinician does not act on an abnormal result because the system showed it as normal. The patient's condition goes unrecognised and untreated. This could cause serious harm, for example a missed diagnosis of a dangerous condition such as kidney disease or anaemia.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, every reference range must be entered with a named source and a unit of measure. This creates a clear record of where each range came from and makes it easier to spot when a source guideline changes (DI-340279C1). The clinical informatics team sets this up when a range is first added. Second, a currency dashboard lists every reference range alongside its review status. The clinical safety team checks this dashboard regularly to find ranges that have not been reviewed recently (DI-E7609DD8). Third, a change control gate stops any updated range from going live until an approval record has been completed. No change can be activated without sign-off (DI-C5A523A7). The clinical safety officer approves each change before it is released. Fourth, a risk-scored change queue holds pending updates in order of clinical importance. A production deployment interlock means no change reaches live systems until the queue item is cleared (DI-7C5EC850). The clinical safety team manages this queue on an ongoing basis. An additional safety net runs automatically each time a result is processed. It compares the result against the current reference range and flags it in one of three severity bands, alerting the clinician if the result falls outside normal limits (DI-21E93377). The clinical safety committee reviews the effectiveness of all five controls every quarter.

title_old: Reference range modified without change control
title_new: A reference range is changed without proper approval
hazard_old: Change control gate bypassed or not enforced
hazard_new: The system allows a reference range to be added, edited, or deleted without going through the required approval steps. A reference range tells the system what counts as a normal or abnormal test result. If this changes without approval, the system may use wrong thresholds without anyone knowing.
hazardous_situation_old: Change control gate bypassed or not enforced
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician or administrator changes a reference range outside the approved process. The system then compares patient test results against the wrong thresholds. Abnormal results may appear normal, or normal results may trigger unnecessary alerts. Clinicians make decisions based on incorrect information.
harm_old: Change control gate bypassed or not enforced
harm_new: A patient with a genuinely abnormal result is not flagged. The clinician does not investigate or treat. The patient comes to serious harm because a critical condition is missed or treated incorrectly.
mitigation_new: First, the system only allows reference ranges to be entered or changed using a structured form that requires a source and a unit of measure to be recorded. This stops incomplete or untraceable changes being saved (DI-340279C1). Second, the system blocks any reference range from becoming active unless an approval record has been completed. No approval means no change goes live (DI-C5A523A7). Third, before any change is approved, the person requesting it must complete a clinical impact assessment explaining how the change could affect patients. This is checked by a senior clinician before sign-off (DI-59F2B21E). Fourth, all reference ranges appear on a content dashboard that shows their review status. The clinical team checks this dashboard to spot ranges that are overdue for review (DI-E7609DD8). Fifth, the system automatically compares every patient result against the current reference range and classifies it into one of three severity bands. This means a wrongly set range is more likely to be noticed quickly because results behave unexpectedly (DI-21E93377). Sixth, any reference range linked to a NICE technology appraisal or quality standard is tracked with a deadline timer so required updates are not missed (DI-44802DF3). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of all reference range changes and checks that every change has a complete approval record every quarter.

title_old: Provenance link missing from coded entity
title_new: Clinical code saved without a link to its source in the notes
hazard_old: Provenance storage step skipped or entity not linked
hazard_new: When the AI tool reads a patient's notes and finds a clinical term, it must save a link back to the exact words it used. If that link is not saved, no one can check where the clinical code came from.
hazardous_situation_old: Provenance storage step skipped or entity not linked
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews a coded entry in the patient record, for example a diagnosis of hypertension (high blood pressure). There is no link to the original words in the notes. The clinician cannot tell whether the AI tool read the notes correctly. A wrong or misleading code may go unchallenged and stay in the record.
harm_old: Provenance storage step skipped or entity not linked
harm_new: A patient's record contains an incorrect clinical code with no way to trace or correct it. Future clinicians rely on that code when making decisions about the patient's care. The patient may receive the wrong treatment, miss a needed referral, or be harmed by a decision based on inaccurate information.
mitigation_new: The AI workflow always saves a fixed link between each clinical code and the exact words in the notes it came from. This link cannot be changed or deleted after it is created (DI-B2512CB3). Every clinical statement the system produces must carry both the source encounter and the clinical code together, so the link is never missing from the start (DI-740BE510). The AI tool records the full source text alongside every decision it makes about whether a condition is present, absent, or possible, so reviewers can check its reasoning (DI-23822663). When a clinician reviews a coded entry, the system highlights the original words in the notes that the AI tool used, making it easy to spot errors (DI-E81545BE). The system stores the precise position of each term in the original notes so the highlight always points to the right place (DI-A0C90595). Every clinical code is saved with a confidence score and full source information so reviewers know how certain the AI tool was (DI-31126C6C). The AI tool preserves clinical detail, such as whether a condition is mild or severe, so codes are as specific as possible and less likely to mislead (DI-6A0B55A4). When a reviewer corrects a coded entry, that correction is permanently linked to the original source information and cannot be separated from it (DI-4F67189B). All source links and provenance records are kept for a minimum of seven years and cannot be deleted (DI-080A2454). Authorised staff can look up the full history of any coded entry without accessing the wider patient record (DI-09E26C1D). Any proposed change to the AI workflow that could affect these links is held in a review queue and cannot go live until it has been checked and approved (DI-7C5EC850). Annotators who label examples used to teach the AI are checked for consistency, so the AI learns correct linking behaviour from the start (DI-EE80C271). The clinical safety committee reviews audit reports of provenance completeness every quarter to confirm all controls are working.

title_old: Guideline escalation threshold not surfaced at point of result review
title_new: System fails to show the clinician the escalation threshold when reviewing a test result
hazard_old: Guideline not mapped to investigation type or threshold record absent
hazard_new: The system holds guidelines that tell clinicians when a test result needs urgent action. If a guideline has not been linked to the correct test type, or the threshold value is missing, the system cannot show the warning. The clinician sees the result but gets no prompt that it has crossed a level requiring escalation.
hazardous_situation_old: Guideline not mapped to investigation type or threshold record absent
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews an abnormal test result during a routine consultation. The system does not display the relevant guideline threshold because the link between the guideline and the test type is absent or incomplete. The clinician has no prompt to escalate and may assume the result is within acceptable limits.
harm_old: Guideline not mapped to investigation type or threshold record absent
harm_new: The clinician does not escalate the patient in time. A serious condition such as acute kidney injury or a dangerously abnormal blood count goes untreated or is treated too late. The patient suffers avoidable harm, which could include hospital admission, organ damage, or death.
mitigation_new: The system shows the clinician the escalation threshold alongside every test result, with a comparison to similar patients on the same care programme. This runs automatically each time a result is reviewed (DI-49A8F570). The system is set up to suppress alerts only for results that are clearly within the normal range. Thresholds for suppression are agreed at programme level by the clinical team and reviewed regularly, so abnormal results always trigger a visible prompt (DI-79509E39). Every panel showing clinical information carries a permanent notice reminding the clinician that the output is a decision-support tool and does not replace clinical judgement. This notice is always visible and cannot be dismissed (DI-E609C4E5). When a clinician orders a test, the system displays the relevant guideline norms and comparator values at the point of ordering, reinforcing awareness of thresholds before results arrive (DI-F235845B). Partial results are shown to the clinician as soon as each step of the AI workflow is complete, rather than waiting for all steps to finish. This means the clinician sees available threshold information sooner (DI-CB07829F). All patient data coming into the system and all audit outputs leaving it follow a recognised clinical data standard, ensuring threshold records are structured consistently and can be checked for completeness (DI-1795254D). The system flags any test result where the displayed information diverges from the current guideline, and records a change history so the clinical team can spot patterns of missing thresholds. The impact review panel highlights these gaps for the clinical team to act on (DI-0C8FBAF7). The clinical safety committee reviews audit reports of threshold coverage and alert suppression settings every quarter to confirm all controls are working as intended.

title_old: Incorrect threshold displayed for investigation type
title_new: Wrong reference threshold shown for a test result
hazard_old: Wrong guideline version linked to result type
hazard_new: The system links a test result to the wrong version of a clinical guideline. This means the threshold shown to the clinician — the value that triggers an alert or escalation — is incorrect.
hazardous_situation_old: Wrong guideline version linked to result type
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews a patient's test result. The system shows a threshold based on an outdated or mismatched guideline. The result appears normal or low-risk when it should trigger urgent action. The clinician does not escalate or follow up.
harm_old: Wrong guideline version linked to result type
harm_new: The patient has a serious abnormal result that is missed. Because no action is taken, the patient's condition worsens. This could lead to significant harm or death.
mitigation_new: The system displays the correct escalation threshold alongside each test result so the clinician can see when a result needs urgent action. The development team sets this up and it runs automatically for every result (DI-49A8F570). The system compares each result against a three-band severity scale — normal, borderline, and urgent — so the clinician gets a clear signal even if the threshold is wrong (DI-21E93377). The system shows a permanent on-screen notice on all clinical output panels reminding the clinician that the AI tool supports but does not replace their judgement (DI-E609C4E5). The system shows a confidence level next to each AI-generated interpretation so the clinician knows how much weight to give it (DI-DA7584D8). The system suppresses alerts only for results that are clearly within normal range, using thresholds that the programme team can adjust, reducing the risk of alert fatigue masking a genuine concern (DI-79509E39). The system provides guideline norms and comparators when a test is ordered, helping the clinician check whether the displayed threshold looks right (DI-F235845B). Any change to a reference range is blocked from going live until an approval record exists, preventing an unapproved threshold from reaching clinicians (DI-C5A523A7). All pending changes to thresholds sit in a risk-scored queue and cannot be deployed to the live system without a formal sign-off step (DI-7C5EC850). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of threshold changes and alert activity every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Outdated guideline recommendation displayed
title_new: Outdated treatment guideline shown to clinician
hazard_old: Knowledge base currency failure
hazard_new: The system may show a treatment recommendation based on an old clinical guideline. Guidelines change when new evidence emerges. If the system is not updated promptly, it will show advice that no longer reflects current best practice.
hazardous_situation_old: Knowledge base currency failure
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reads the system's treatment suggestion during a consultation. The suggestion is based on a guideline that has since been updated or withdrawn. The clinician does not realise the advice is out of date. They follow it when making a decision about the patient's care.
harm_old: Knowledge base currency failure
harm_new: The patient receives treatment that is no longer recommended. This could mean they miss a safer or more effective option. In the most serious cases, outdated advice could lead to avoidable harm or a delayed diagnosis.
mitigation_new: A guideline monitoring registry tracks all clinical guidelines the system uses. A named clinician reviews the registry whenever a guideline changes and approves any update before it goes live. This is managed under formal clinical change control, so no update is made without a documented check (DI-ED3A89F5). The system shows each recommendation alongside a summary of the evidence behind it, including how recent that evidence is. This helps the clinician judge whether the advice looks current (DI-82D5359B). A currency dashboard shows the clinical safety team which guidelines are due for review and flags any that may be out of date. The team can export this information for audit (DI-E5609239). The system displays treatment options without ranking them, and tells the clinician which patient group the evidence applies to. This reduces the risk that a clinician follows a single suggestion without thinking critically (DI-76C86329). The system shows a confidence level alongside each piece of AI-generated information, so the clinician can see how certain the system is (DI-DA7584D8). The system does not make final diagnostic or treatment decisions on its own. It supports the clinician, who retains responsibility for the final decision (DI-A3107424). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs from the guideline registry and the currency dashboard every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Real-world outcome comparators drawn from biased cohort
title_new: Treatment comparisons based on an unrepresentative group of patients
hazard_old: Cohort selection criteria not clinically validated
hazard_new: The AI tool learns from examples of past patients to suggest treatments. If those past patients are not a fair or representative sample, the comparisons the AI offers may not reflect what is likely to happen for the patient in front of the clinician. The AI does not flag when its comparison group is a poor match.
hazardous_situation_old: Cohort selection criteria not clinically validated
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews the AI's suggested treatment options. The options are ranked using outcome data from a group of patients who do not closely match the current patient. The clinician does not realise the comparison group is unrepresentative. They may favour a treatment that looks better in the data but is not the best choice for this patient.
harm_old: Cohort selection criteria not clinically validated
harm_new: The clinician chooses a treatment based on misleading comparisons. The patient receives a treatment that is less effective or less safe than the best available option. This could lead to their condition worsening, a delayed recovery, or an avoidable complication.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the system shows all treatment options in a neutral, unranked list and tells the clinician which group of past patients the comparisons come from, in plain language. This helps the clinician judge whether the comparison group is a good match. The development team sets this up as a design requirement and the clinical safety team checks it works during testing (DI-76C86329). Second, the system displays the relevant clinical guideline recommendation alongside each outcome summary, so the clinician can compare the AI suggestion against established guidance. The development team builds this in and the clinical safety team reviews it during testing (DI-82D5359B). Third, the system shows the clinician exactly which criteria were used to select the comparison group of patients, and asks the clinician to confirm they have noted this before proceeding. Any confirmation is saved in the audit log. This runs automatically every time a treatment suggestion is shown (DI-6079EC71). Fourth, any change to how the AI selects its comparison group must pass a safety review before it goes live. The development team manages this queue and no change can be released without sign-off from the clinical safety team (DI-7C5EC850). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and incident reports related to this risk every quarter to confirm all four controls are working as intended.

title_old: Recovery markers not correctly identified from coded record
title_new: Recovery markers missed from the patient's coded record
hazard_old: Relevant SNOMED concepts not in extraction model scope
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads clinical notes may not recognise all the clinical codes that show a patient is recovering. Some recovery markers may fall outside the range of codes the AI tool has been taught to look for. This means the system may not pick up signs that a patient's condition is improving or worsening after treatment.
hazardous_situation_old: Relevant SNOMED concepts not in extraction model scope
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews a patient's progress after treatment. The system fails to identify key recovery markers in the patient's record. The clinician sees an incomplete picture of the patient's recovery. They may not realise the patient is deteriorating or that a follow-up is needed.
harm_old: Relevant SNOMED concepts not in extraction model scope
harm_new: The clinician makes a clinical decision based on incomplete information. A patient who is not recovering as expected does not receive timely review or intervention. This could lead to serious harm, including delayed diagnosis of a complication or failure to escalate care.
mitigation_new: The AI workflow uses a classification approach that can handle overlapping clinical codes, reducing the chance that recovery markers are missed (DI-DC61F5B6). This is built into the system design and applies every time the system processes a patient record. The AI tool preserves important clinical detail, such as whether a finding is confirmed, absent, or possible, when pulling information from notes and matching it to clinical codes (DI-6A0B55A4). This runs automatically each time the system reads a clinical entry. The system is taught using examples that have been checked by an expert and kept separate from the data used to test it, so its accuracy on recovery markers can be measured reliably (DI-BB64E479). The clinical safety team reviews this separation before each new version is released. When the system pulls a clinical code from a note, it records how confident it is and where the information came from, so clinicians and reviewers can check its work (DI-31126C6C). This provenance record is available at all times. The system includes post-treatment recovery markers and uses comparable patient journeys to set expectations for recovery (DI-49403C92). Clinicians are alerted when a patient's progress does not match the expected pattern. If the system flags a deviation from the expected recovery path, the clinician must document a structured response rather than simply dismissing the alert (DI-BD826FA6). This applies every time an alert is generated. The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Guideline recommendations not current at point of ordering
title_new: Clinical guidelines shown to clinicians may be out of date
hazard_old: NICE update not propagated to ordering guidance
hazard_new: The system holds clinical guidelines to help clinicians order investigations and treatments. When NICE publishes updated guidance, there is a risk the system is not updated in time. A clinician may then follow old guidance without knowing it has changed.
