hazardous_situation_old: NICE update not propagated to ordering guidance
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician uses the system to decide which investigations or treatments to order. The guidance shown is based on an older NICE recommendation. The clinician follows this guidance in good faith. They do not know the current NICE recommendation is different.
harm_old: NICE update not propagated to ordering guidance
harm_new: The patient receives investigations or treatment based on out-of-date guidance. This could mean a needed test is missed, an outdated medicine is prescribed, or a more effective treatment is not offered. For a patient with a serious condition, this delay or wrong choice could cause significant harm.
mitigation_new: The system shows clinicians guideline-based prompts when they order investigations. These prompts highlight when an order differs from current norms, so the clinician can reconsider (DI-F235845B). If a clinician chooses to order something that differs from the guideline, the system asks them to confirm and records their reason. This means every deviation is logged and visible (DI-6079EC71). The system also shows guideline-based treatment recommendations alongside outcome summaries for similar patients, giving the clinician a fuller picture before they decide (DI-82D5359B). To keep content current, each piece of guidance must be linked to a recent verification check. If that check is overdue, the system automatically flags the guidance as unverified. The interval between checks is set by the type of guidance (DI-2F157317). When a guideline update is ready to go live, it must pass through a risk-scored review queue before it can be deployed. No update reaches clinicians without this check being completed (DI-7C5EC850). The system tracks all NICE technology appraisals and quality standards that affect its content. It sets deadline timers so the team knows when an update must be reviewed and applied (DI-44802DF3). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs, overdue flags, and deviation records every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Wrong pathway stage displayed for patient
title_new: The system shows the wrong stage of a patient's care pathway
hazard_old: Stage calculation error or stale episode data
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads notes may calculate the wrong stage of a patient's care pathway. This can happen if the calculation contains an error or if the patient's record has not been updated recently. The system may then show a stage that does not match where the patient actually is in their care.
hazardous_situation_old: Stage calculation error or stale episode data
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician sees an incorrect pathway stage on screen before or during a consultation. They do not realise the information is wrong. They make a clinical decision based on the incorrect stage, such as skipping a step that is still needed or repeating one that is already done.
harm_old: Stage calculation error or stale episode data
harm_new: The patient receives the wrong care at the wrong time. For example, a needed test or treatment is delayed or missed entirely. This could cause the patient's condition to worsen, lead to a missed diagnosis, or result in a breach of waiting time targets with direct harm to the patient.
mitigation_new: The system shows the clinician a confidence level alongside every AI-generated pathway stage. This tells the clinician how certain the AI is, so they can treat low-confidence information with extra care (DI-DA7584D8). The system generates a structured summary for each patient that includes the pathway stage and any safety alerts. The clinician reviews this before acting on pathway information (DI-30D9CC61). The system provides a clinic list view that shows pathway status and comparison information. The clinician can use this to spot stages that look out of place before the consultation begins (DI-CF03E4EA). The system generates a timeline of the patient's episodes and highlights any gaps in the pathway. This helps the clinician see if a stage appears to have been skipped or recorded incorrectly (DI-4885D9FF). The system calculates pathway intervals and automatically flags any breach of waiting time targets. This prompts the clinician to check the pathway stage is correct (DI-F3FD2B63). The system keeps patient data and clinical coding data in separate databases. This reduces the risk of a coding error corrupting the pathway stage calculation (DI-84F44836). The system provides AI-generated labels on pre-read summaries with direct links to the relevant guideline. The clinician can check the expected pathway stage against the guideline before acting (DI-6D2B03E0). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and reported incidents related to pathway stage accuracy every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Incorrect pathway eligibility criteria displayed
title_new: Wrong pathway eligibility rules shown to the clinician
hazard_old: Wrong guideline version linked to pathway type
hazard_new: The system may show eligibility rules from an out-of-date or incorrect guideline. This can happen when the wrong guideline version is linked to a care pathway.
hazardous_situation_old: Wrong guideline version linked to pathway type
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reads the eligibility rules on screen and uses them to decide whether a patient qualifies for a pathway. If the rules shown are wrong, the clinician may refer a patient who should not be on that pathway, or turn away a patient who should be.
harm_old: Wrong guideline version linked to pathway type
harm_new: A patient is placed on the wrong care pathway, or is wrongly excluded from the right one. This could mean the patient receives the wrong treatment or misses treatment they need. For a pathway with critical clinical decisions, this could cause serious harm or delay in care.
mitigation_new: First, the system displays eligibility rules and comparable outcomes together in a dedicated referral triage view, so the clinician can check the criteria in context before making a decision (DI-6C5D77CA). The clinical team reviews this view during testing and after any guideline update. Second, the triage view uses clearly labelled, visually distinct panels and lets the clinician filter by age, symptom, and referral source, reducing the chance of reading the wrong set of rules (DI-37B52693). The design team checks this layout at each release. Third, the system shows a confidence level next to each piece of information the AI tool has produced, so the clinician knows how much weight to give it (DI-DA7584D8). Clinicians are trained to treat low-confidence items with extra caution. Fourth, every response from the AI includes a version identifier for the AI component that produced it, so the team can trace exactly which version of the rules was active if an error is reported (DI-0D26BE1B). The technical team logs and audits these identifiers continuously. Fifth, when a clinician corrects an AI-generated interpretation, that correction is permanently linked to the original source information, creating an audit trail (DI-4F67189B). The clinical safety committee reviews correction logs every quarter to spot patterns that may indicate a guideline version problem. The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Incomplete or incorrect MDT summary presented
title_new: AI tool produces an incomplete or wrong summary for a multidisciplinary team meeting
hazard_old: AI summary generation omits relevant coded findings
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads clinical notes may miss important findings when building a patient summary. It may leave out diagnoses, test results, or medicines that the multidisciplinary team (MDT) needs to make safe decisions.
hazardous_situation_old: AI summary generation omits relevant coded findings
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician presents the AI-generated summary at an MDT meeting without noticing that key findings are missing. The team makes decisions based on an incomplete picture of the patient's condition.
harm_old: AI summary generation omits relevant coded findings
harm_new: The MDT agrees a care plan that does not account for all the patient's problems. The patient receives the wrong treatment or misses a step in their care pathway. This could cause serious harm, for example a delayed cancer diagnosis or an unsafe medicine choice.
mitigation_new: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the AI uses a structured MDT summary template with a pathway checklist. This prompts the clinician to check that all expected information is present before the meeting (DI-DBC2399F). The clinical team reviews this template at every MDT. Second, the AI labels all content it has generated so the clinician can see exactly what the AI produced. The clinician can edit the summary before it is submitted, and the system saves a record of any changes alongside the original AI version (DI-45F83183). This happens every time a summary is prepared. Third, the AI translates clinical codes into plain-language descriptions so the reviewing clinician can quickly spot anything that looks wrong or out of place (DI-66F1B177). This runs automatically each time a summary is generated. Fourth, the system produces a timeline of the patient's care episodes and highlights any gaps against the expected pathway (DI-4885D9FF). The clinician checks this timeline before the MDT meeting. Fifth, the AI generates a structured summary using the SBAR format, drawing on coded encounters, the patient's pathway stage, and any safety-netting alerts (DI-30D9CC61). This gives the MDT a consistent, structured view of the patient at every meeting. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of edited summaries and pathway gap alerts every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: SBAR used in handover without human review step
title_new: AI-generated handover summary used without a clinician checking it first
hazard_old: Review gate not enforced - SBAR marked final automatically
hazard_new: The AI tool creates a structured handover summary (called an SBAR). If the system marks this summary as final without a clinician reviewing it first, errors in the summary may not be caught. The AI tool could misread notes, miss important information, or include details that are out of date.
hazardous_situation_old: Review gate not enforced - SBAR marked final automatically
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician receiving the handover reads an AI-generated summary that no one has checked. The summary may contain wrong diagnoses, missing medicines, or incorrect safety alerts. The receiving clinician acts on this unchecked information during a care handover.
harm_old: Review gate not enforced - SBAR marked final automatically
harm_new: The receiving clinician makes a clinical decision based on wrong or incomplete handover information. This could lead to the wrong treatment, a missed diagnosis, or a delayed response to a serious safety concern. For a patient with a critical condition, this could cause serious harm or death.
mitigation_new: A mandatory review step stops the system from marking any AI-generated handover summary as final until a named clinician has approved it. The system records what the AI originally wrote and what the clinician changed, so there is a clear audit trail. This review gate is built into the system design and runs every time a summary is created (DI-8804DA01). Every clinical statement in the summary is linked back to the original patient record entry and clinical code it came from. This lets the reviewing clinician check where each piece of information came from (DI-740BE510). The AI tool builds the summary from coded clinical encounters, the patient's stage on their care pathway, and any active safety alerts. This gives the reviewing clinician a structured starting point rather than a blank document (DI-30D9CC61). A separate review gate requires a clinician to make an individual decision on each clinical code the AI proposes before it is saved to the final record. This prevents unchecked codes from entering the audit data (DI-4247C7E5). If the system detects gaps in the patient's data or areas where information is missing, the clinician must actively acknowledge each warning before the summary can proceed. This stops incomplete summaries from being passed on silently (DI-00E16F9E). Any guideline alerts generated by the AI are blocked from triggering further actions in the system until a clinician has reviewed them. This prevents automated escalation based on unchecked alerts (DI-7913344A). The AI-generated summary cannot be published or shared with another team until a clinician has made an explicit decision to approve it. The system will not allow the summary to move forward without this step (DI-604767B1). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of these review gates every quarter to confirm that no summaries are being finalised without a clinician decision.

title_old: SBAR misses safety netting alerts
title_new: SBAR summary misses safety netting alerts
hazard_old: Safety netting alerts not included in SBAR generation
hazard_new: The AI tool that creates the SBAR summary may leave out safety netting alerts. Safety netting alerts remind clinicians to follow up if a patient's condition does not improve as expected. If the AI misses these alerts, the summary handed to the next clinician will not show them.
hazardous_situation_old: Safety netting alerts not included in SBAR generation
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reads the SBAR summary and sees no safety netting alerts. They do not know a follow-up check was needed. They may not arrange that follow-up, or they may not tell the patient what warning signs to watch for.
harm_old: Safety netting alerts not included in SBAR generation
harm_new: The patient does not receive the follow-up or safety advice they need. A serious or worsening condition may go undetected. This could lead to significant harm or, in the worst case, death.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the AI workflow is designed to pull safety netting alerts directly into every SBAR summary it creates, alongside coded clinical information and pathway stage details. A clinician can therefore see at a glance whether any alerts are present (DI-30D9CC61). Second, every clinical statement in the SBAR links back to the original encounter and clinical code it came from. This lets the reviewing clinician check that the source information, including any alerts, has been carried across correctly (DI-740BE510). Third, the episode timeline highlights gaps in the expected care pathway. This acts as a second prompt to the reviewing clinician if a safety netting step appears to be missing (DI-4885D9FF). Fourth, no SBAR summary can be sent to another clinician until a human clinician has reviewed and approved it. The system records what the AI produced and what the clinician changed before sign-off (DI-8804DA01). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of SBAR reviews and any reported missed alerts every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: AI interpretation inaccurate or misleading
title_new: AI tool gives an inaccurate or misleading interpretation of a clinical finding
hazard_old: LLM hallucinates or misrepresents coded finding
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads and summarises clinical codes can produce an interpretation that is factually wrong or misleading. This can happen when the AI generates plausible-sounding text that does not match the actual coded finding in the patient record.
hazardous_situation_old: LLM hallucinates or misrepresents coded finding
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews the AI-generated summary of a patient's coded findings. The summary contains an inaccurate or misleading statement. The clinician, under time pressure, accepts the summary without checking the underlying record. They base a clinical decision on the incorrect information.
harm_old: LLM hallucinates or misrepresents coded finding
harm_new: The clinician makes a wrong or delayed clinical decision because the AI summary misrepresented the patient's condition. This could lead to the wrong treatment being given, a needed treatment being missed, or a serious condition being overlooked. The patient could suffer serious harm as a result.
mitigation_new: First, the AI tool is designed to summarise only the structured facts already recorded in the patient record. It cannot add diagnoses or treatment recommendations of its own. This keeps the summary anchored to what is actually documented (DI-69C29EEF). The AI tool team sets and maintains this boundary. Second, the AI tool does not include diagnostic or treatment recommendations in any interpretation it produces. This reduces the risk that a clinician acts on AI-generated clinical advice rather than their own judgement (DI-A3107424). The AI tool team enforces this at the design level. Third, every AI-generated interpretation is written in plain language so the reviewing clinician can quickly check it against the original coded finding (DI-66F1B177). The AI tool produces this plain-language version automatically for every summary. Fourth, the AI tool displays a confidence level alongside every interpretation it generates. A lower confidence level prompts the clinician to check the source record before acting (DI-DA7584D8). This is shown automatically each time a summary is presented. Fifth, no AI-generated interpretation is published to the patient record or shared with a clinician until a human reviewer has made an explicit decision to approve it. The system blocks publication until this step is completed (DI-604767B1). The reviewing clinician carries out this check every time. Sixth, an automated check runs on each coded encounter to assess whether the AI interpretation follows accepted clinical guidelines. Any interpretation that does not conform is flagged before the reviewer sees it (DI-2AFF691F). This check runs automatically as part of the AI workflow. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and reviewer decisions every quarter to confirm all controls are working as intended.

title_old: Completeness indicator not surfaced on clinician-facing output
title_new: The AI tool does not show the clinician how complete the patient data is
hazard_old: Completeness check not run or not displayed
hazard_new: The AI tool reads patient notes and produces a clinical summary. It may not always have access to all relevant records. If the tool does not clearly show the clinician that some data is missing or unreliable, the clinician cannot tell how much to trust the output.
hazardous_situation_old: Completeness check not run or not displayed
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reads an AI-generated summary and sees no warning about missing or incomplete data. They assume the summary is based on a full picture of the patient's history. They make a clinical decision based on an incomplete summary without realising it.
harm_old: Completeness check not run or not displayed
harm_new: The clinician makes a diagnosis or treatment decision based on incomplete information. Important conditions, medicines, or test results may have been missed by the AI tool. The patient could receive the wrong treatment, a delayed diagnosis, or miss a referral they need. This could cause serious or lasting harm.
mitigation_new: The AI tool always shows a clear data completeness indicator on every clinical output, so the clinician can see at a glance how complete the underlying data is (DI-900CB621). The tool displays information about which patient group the summary is based on, including how many records were used, directly on the clinician-facing screen (DI-098D2C0D). When data from a small group of patients or low-confidence results are involved, the tool either hides the output or shows a clear low-confidence warning before the clinician sees it (DI-CB3DF3E1). The programme team sets the thresholds that decide when a warning is shown or an output is hidden, and reviews these settings regularly (DI-0D7DCC52). Before a clinician can act on a summary that has data gaps or coverage warnings, the tool requires them to actively confirm they have seen and understood the warning (DI-00E16F9E). The tool automatically detects when data is missing and always tells the clinician before they see any output that is based on incomplete records (DI-88F20177). A plain-English explanation of what the completeness indicator means is always available to the clinician in one click or tap (DI-B95A73E9). A short, clear disclaimer appears on every clinical intelligence panel at all times, reminding the clinician that the output is for information only (DI-E609C4E5). The confidence level the AI tool has in each interpretation it produces is shown alongside that interpretation on screen (DI-DA7584D8). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and user feedback every quarter to check that warnings are being displayed correctly and that clinicians are engaging with them.

title_old: Override miscategorised
title_new: Override reason recorded in the wrong category
hazard_old: Manual categorisation error not detected
hazard_new: When a clinician corrects the AI tool, they must select a reason for the correction. If they pick the wrong reason category, the system records why the correction was made incorrectly. This means the team cannot see the true pattern of AI errors.
hazardous_situation_old: Manual categorisation error not detected
hazardous_situation_new: Incorrect reason categories build up over time. The clinical safety team reviews the wrong data. They may miss a pattern showing the AI tool is making the same mistake repeatedly. The AI tool continues to make that mistake without anyone noticing.
harm_old: Manual categorisation error not detected
harm_new: If a repeated AI error goes undetected, clinicians may act on wrong information in patient records. This could lead to a missed or delayed diagnosis, or an incorrect medicine being prescribed, causing minor harm to a patient.
mitigation_new: The system uses a fixed, versioned list of correction reason categories. This list is set up by the clinical informatics team and updated in a controlled way, so clinicians always see clear, consistent options to choose from (DI-770FD74A). Every time a clinician corrects the AI tool, the system requires them to select a reason from this structured list before saving the correction. This makes it harder to skip or guess the category (DI-425CA252). A dashboard shows the clinical safety team how correction reasons are distributed across clinicians and over time. The safety team reviews this dashboard regularly to spot unusual patterns or a sudden rise in one category, which may signal miscategorisation (DI-FFCD4F96). Additional controls are being identified. The clinical safety committee reviews the dashboard findings and checks these controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Encounter classified to wrong audit programme
title_new: A patient visit is assigned to the wrong audit programme
hazard_old: Classifier confidence threshold not set correctly for programme overlap
hazard_new: The AI tool that sorts patient visits into audit programmes may place a visit in the wrong programme. This can happen when two programmes overlap and the AI is not sure which one applies.
hazardous_situation_old: Classifier confidence threshold not set correctly for programme overlap
hazardous_situation_new: A patient visit is filed under the wrong audit programme. The clinician reviewing that programme does not see the visit. The correct programme misses the visit entirely. The patient's care need goes unreviewed.
harm_old: Classifier confidence threshold not set correctly for programme overlap
harm_new: The patient does not receive the review or follow-up linked to the correct audit programme. A clinical need, such as a long-term condition check or a medicines review, may be missed. This could lead to delayed diagnosis or a gap in ongoing care.
mitigation_new: Six controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool that sorts visits uses a fixed set of managed rules and must pass a test before any decision is saved to the patient record. This test runs automatically every time a visit is classified (DI-8CE01B3E). Second, when a clinician spots a wrong classification, they can label it as incorrect. The AI tool learns from these corrections and the updated model is recorded in a central register. The clinical informatics team reviews labelled errors on an ongoing basis (DI-0ADE6A8E). Third, the rules that define each audit programme can be adjusted by a clinical lead without needing a software release. This means errors in programme boundaries can be fixed quickly (DI-AA8014F9). Fourth, the settings for each audit programme can be updated from data alone, again without a software release, so the team can respond rapidly to any drift in how visits are being sorted (DI-CD931485). Fifth, the AI workflow monitors how often clinical codes appear for each type of patient entry. If the pattern drifts beyond a set limit, an alert is raised for the clinical safety team to investigate. This check runs continuously (DI-37315D03). Sixth, the AI tool shows its confidence level next to every classification it produces. A clinician can see at a glance when the AI is uncertain and apply their own judgement before accepting the result (DI-DA7584D8). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs, labelled errors, and drift alerts every quarter to confirm all six controls are working as intended.

title_old: Encounter not classified - excluded from all programmes
title_new: A patient visit is not classified and is left out of all care programmes
hazard_old: Below-threshold confidence with no fallback rule
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads clinical notes gives a low-confidence result when deciding how to classify a patient visit. No backup rule exists to handle this situation. The visit is therefore left unclassified.
hazardous_situation_old: Below-threshold confidence with no fallback rule
hazardous_situation_new: When a visit is left unclassified, the system does not place the patient into any care programme. The clinician reviewing the record may not notice this has happened. The patient misses checks, reviews, or treatments they should receive.
harm_old: Below-threshold confidence with no fallback rule
harm_new: A patient who should be on a care programme is not enrolled. Their condition may go unmonitored. This could lead to delayed diagnosis or missed treatment, causing serious harm.
mitigation_new: First, the system uses a set of managed rules to classify every patient visit and saves that decision within the record. A test must pass before any classification is accepted (DI-8CE01B3E). This runs automatically each time a visit is processed. Second, when the AI tool cannot classify a visit with enough confidence, a defined backup method is used instead, and the confidence threshold is set to a safe level (DI-88C8BBCD). This runs automatically during the AI workflow. Third, the system records whether each visit was classified by the rules or by the backup method, and shows this clearly to the clinician reviewing the record (DI-8C236A1A). The clinician can see this at the point of review. Fourth, every visit is given a clear status: confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive (DI-37DDAADE). This prevents visits from being silently ignored. Fifth, the AI tool displays its confidence level alongside every result it produces (DI-DA7584D8). The reviewing clinician sees this each time they open the record. Sixth, when a visit is wrongly classified, the clinician can flag this as an error. These flags feed back into the AI tool to improve future accuracy (DI-0ADE6A8E). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data on unclassified visits and flags every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Canary not halted on F1 regression
title_new: New AI model version not stopped when accuracy drops
hazard_old: Halt threshold not configured or evaluation not running
hazard_new: When a new version of the AI tool is being tested on live patients, the system should automatically stop using it if its accuracy falls below a safe level. If the automatic stop is not set up correctly, or the accuracy checks are not running, the new version keeps working even when it is performing poorly.
hazardous_situation_old: Halt threshold not configured or evaluation not running
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician receives suggestions from an AI tool that is performing poorly. The clinician does not know the AI tool's accuracy has dropped. They may act on incorrect or missing clinical information without realising it is unreliable.
harm_old: Halt threshold not configured or evaluation not running
harm_new: A patient's condition may be missed, wrongly recorded, or managed on incorrect information. For a critical severity risk, this could lead to serious harm, such as a missed diagnosis or wrong treatment decision.
mitigation_new: The system automatically stops the new AI version and switches back to the previous version if accuracy falls below a set level during live testing. This runs continuously without human input (DI-7D710C52). The live testing uses a set proportion of real patient traffic, and every test run is logged so it can be reviewed later. The clinical safety team can adjust the proportion at any time (DI-A557AE91). The AI workflow checks whether clinical coding on patient encounters follows current guidelines. This check runs automatically on every relevant encounter (DI-2AFF691F). If an accuracy warning is not acknowledged within a set time, the AI workflow pauses automatically. An alert is sent to the responsible team so they can investigate (DI-5A802C83). The accuracy checks are designed to complete within five seconds for each patient at busy periods, so delays do not hold up clinical care (DI-5E25E872). Coding quality is monitored continuously. If quality drops, an alert is raised straight away so the team can act before patients are affected (DI-1126FFD1). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all these controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: Canary halted incorrectly - valid model rejected
title_new: Safety check wrongly stops a good AI model update
hazard_old: Threshold set too aggressively for entity type variation
hazard_new: The AI tool checks its own accuracy before a new version goes live. If the accuracy threshold is set too strictly, the check may reject a new version that is actually safe and working well. This can happen when different types of clinical information vary naturally in how often they appear in notes.
hazardous_situation_old: Threshold set too aggressively for entity type variation
hazardous_situation_new: A safe, accurate new version of the AI tool is blocked from going live. The older version stays in use. Clinicians continue to rely on results from a version that may be less accurate than the rejected update. Over time, this could mean the AI tool misses or misreads clinical information in patient notes.
harm_old: Threshold set too aggressively for entity type variation
harm_new: Clinicians may receive slightly less accurate information pulled from patient notes. This could lead to a missed or delayed clinical decision for a small number of patients. The harm is likely to be minor because clinicians review AI results before acting on them.
mitigation_new: The AI workflow includes an automatic accuracy check before any new version goes live. If accuracy drops below a set level, the system stops the update and keeps the previous version running. The safety team can adjust how strict this check is for each type of clinical information. This is reviewed whenever a new model is submitted for approval (DI-7D710C52). The system records which version of the AI tool handled each set of notes, so the team can trace any problems back to a specific update. All test runs are tagged and stored in an audit trail (DI-A557AE91). The system also monitors how often each type of clinical code appears in notes over time. If the pattern changes unexpectedly, the team is alerted. Thresholds for this check can be adjusted by the safety team (DI-37315D03). Accuracy figures for each type of clinical information are stored every time the AI tool is trained. The team can look these up in the model registry to compare versions (DI-CE0A08E5). Separate accuracy checks apply to the way the AI tool links pieces of clinical information together, such as linking a medicine to a diagnosis. These checks must be passed before any update is approved (DI-80BD2F86). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these checks are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: Unapproved change activates on pipeline
title_new: An unapproved change goes live in the AI workflow
hazard_old: Queue gate not enforced architecturally
hazard_new: The AI workflow can process patient data using a change that has not been reviewed or approved. There is no technical lock that stops an unapproved change from becoming active. This means a change could alter how the AI reads notes, scores risks, or updates patient records without any clinician or safety review.
hazardous_situation_old: Queue gate not enforced architecturally
hazardous_situation_new: An unapproved change becomes active in the AI workflow. The AI tool that reads notes or updates patient records then behaves differently from what was tested and approved. Clinicians receive results based on untested logic. They may not know anything has changed.
harm_old: Queue gate not enforced architecturally
harm_new: A clinician acts on results produced by an untested or faulty change. A patient could receive the wrong diagnosis, miss a needed treatment, or be given the wrong medicine. Because the change was never reviewed, no one has checked whether it is safe. The harm could affect many patients before anyone notices.
mitigation_new: Six controls work together to stop an unapproved change from going live. First, a risk-scored change queue blocks any change from reaching live systems until an approval record exists. The system enforces this automatically every time a change is submitted (DI-7C5EC850). Second, a separate gate specifically blocks any change to reference ranges from becoming active without a recorded approval. This runs automatically at the point of activation (DI-C5A523A7). Third, a gate for changes to the way the AI reads clinical terms holds each change in a staging area, requires a reviewer to approve it, records a version, and allows rollback if needed. This runs automatically for every such change (DI-9FD54AD6). Fourth, the change queue shows reviewers the full context of each change, lets them sort and filter items, sends notifications to reviewers, and escalates items that have been waiting too long. The system manages this continuously (DI-636D331A). Fifth, a technical control checks that each part of the system only processes data it is authorised to handle, preventing an unapproved or misdirected change from affecting the wrong patients. This is enforced automatically at the point of every query (DI-87CCCB18). Sixth, a safety gate in the AI client wrapper ensures that patient-identifiable information is always removed before it reaches the AI language tool, and this gate cannot be bypassed. This runs automatically on every request (DI-F66A7239). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and queue reports every quarter to confirm all six controls are working as intended.

title_old: Incorrect guideline implementation approved
title_new: A wrongly written clinical guideline is approved and used in patient care
hazard_old: Reviewer lacks clinical authority or is misled by impact summary
hazard_new: The system can suggest updates to clinical guidelines. A reviewer may approve a guideline that contains errors. This can happen if the reviewer does not have the right clinical knowledge, or if the summary shown to them does not clearly show what has changed or what the risks are.
hazardous_situation_old: Reviewer lacks clinical authority or is misled by impact summary
hazardous_situation_new: A flawed guideline is approved and becomes active. Clinicians follow it without knowing it is wrong. Patients are then assessed or treated using incorrect clinical rules.
harm_old: Reviewer lacks clinical authority or is misled by impact summary
harm_new: Patients may receive the wrong treatment or miss a treatment they need. Because the error is hidden inside a guideline, it could affect many patients before anyone notices. This could cause serious or lasting harm.
mitigation_new: The system shows the reviewer a side-by-side comparison of the old and new guideline versions. It lists every clinical rule that has changed. This makes it easier to spot errors before approval (DI-1E8D8678). A second, independent clinician checks that the updated guideline matches its source and is safe to use. This check happens for every guideline update (DI-F3EFEA88). Before any guideline can be approved, the reviewer must complete a clinical impact assessment. This step cannot be skipped (DI-59F2B21E). The system tracks updates to NICE technology appraisals and quality standards. It flags when a guideline update is overdue and sets time limits for review (DI-44802DF3). When a guideline is deployed, the system checks that what goes live exactly matches what was approved. Any difference blocks the deployment (DI-EC27E4E7). The AI tool that reads clinical notes follows a fixed set of rules when pulling clinical relationships from text. This reduces the chance of errors being introduced during automated steps (DI-3EA60D5A). The review panel shows the reviewer a history of past changes and highlights any place where the guideline differs from standard clinical guidance. This helps the reviewer spot patterns that may indicate an error (DI-0C8FBAF7). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all these controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: Conflict of interest not detected
title_new: A clinician reviews or approves their own work without this being detected
hazard_old: Self-review detection not implemented
hazard_new: The system may allow a clinician to review or approve clinical content that they themselves created or submitted. This is a conflict of interest. No check is in place to catch this automatically.
hazardous_situation_old: Self-review detection not implemented
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician approves their own guideline or clinical record entry. The system does not flag this. The approved content enters the clinical pathway without independent review. Errors or bias in the original content go unchallenged.
harm_old: Self-review detection not implemented
harm_new: A patient receives care based on clinical guidance that was never independently checked. Errors in that guidance may go unnoticed. This could lead to the wrong diagnosis, the wrong medicine, or a missed safety step, causing serious harm to the patient.
mitigation_new: The system blocks any clinician from approving content they created themselves. This is enforced automatically every time an approval action is attempted (DI-5EECDA58). Only administrators can manage user credentials and approval permissions. All approval actions are recorded in a full audit log, which the clinical safety team can review at any time (DI-5EECDA58). Before any approval action is completed, the system checks whether the approving clinician has a conflict of interest with the content being approved. This check runs automatically on every approval request (DI-DB62EF12). Before any guideline is moved into the active clinical pathway, the system checks for conflicts with existing guidance. Content under review stays available to clinicians in its current approved form until the check is passed (DI-48ACD153). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and conflict-check reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Impact summary incomplete - downstream effects not shown
title_new: The tool does not show all the knock-on effects of a change to a clinical pathway
hazard_old: Impact analysis query incomplete
hazard_new: When a clinician reviews a proposed change to a clinical pathway, the tool may not show every downstream effect. For example, it may miss how the change affects related medicines, diagnoses, or referral steps. The clinician sees only part of the picture.
hazardous_situation_old: Impact analysis query incomplete
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician approves a pathway change without realising it will affect other parts of patient care. They do not know the full impact because the tool has not shown it. They act on incomplete information.
harm_old: Impact analysis query incomplete
harm_new: Patients may receive the wrong treatment, miss a referral, or be given a medicine that no longer fits their pathway. Because the clinician did not see the full impact, the error may not be caught until the patient is harmed. The harm could be serious.
mitigation_new: The tool shows a clear side-by-side view of what the pathway looked like before and after every proposed change. This helps the clinician spot differences quickly (DI-BC39B803). The tool also flags when a change does not match current NICE guidance, and highlights any history of similar changes that caused problems before (DI-0C8FBAF7). Before a clinician can approve any change, the tool requires them to complete a clinical impact assessment section. This step cannot be skipped (DI-59F2B21E). The tool checks whether the change affects any ICD-10 diagnosis codes or OPCS procedure codes and will not activate the change until this check is complete (DI-337D44DE). The tool tracks whether the change affects any NICE technology appraisals or quality standards, and sets time limits to make sure these are reviewed promptly (DI-44802DF3). If the data used to assess the impact is incomplete, the tool tells the clinician clearly before they make a decision (DI-88F20177). Every response from the AI includes a version identifier so the safety team can trace exactly which version of the AI produced the assessment (DI-0D26BE1B). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and near-miss reports every quarter to check that all these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Post-approval modification deployed
title_new: A changed version of the AI tool is used without proper approval
hazard_old: Deployment process does not validate artefact hash
hazard_new: When the AI tool is updated and sent out to clinical systems, the system does not check that the version being installed matches the version that was approved. A different or altered version could be installed without anyone noticing.
hazardous_situation_old: Deployment process does not validate artefact hash
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician uses the AI tool believing it is the approved, tested version. In fact, a different version is running. That version may give different results, miss diagnoses, or suggest incorrect information. The clinician acts on those results without knowing they are unreliable.
harm_old: Deployment process does not validate artefact hash
harm_new: A patient receives incorrect or delayed care because the clinician acted on results from an unapproved version of the AI tool. For example, a serious condition could be missed or an incorrect medicine could be suggested. This could cause serious harm or death.
mitigation_new: First, every deployment package is checked to confirm it exactly matches the approved version before it is installed. This check is automatic and runs every time a new version is deployed (DI-EC27E4E7). Second, a deployment status panel shows whether the installed version matches the approved change record. Any reviewer can see this at any time (DI-6EA84931). Third, a list of approval conditions must be confirmed one by one before deployment is allowed to proceed. The system blocks deployment if any condition is unconfirmed (DI-8FDE6740). Fourth, before any version is approved, a clinical impact assessment must be completed. This ensures a clinician has reviewed what the change could mean for patients (DI-59F2B21E). Fifth, an audit programme checks deployment activity on an ongoing basis. This does not require a new deployment to run and can be updated without changing the live system (DI-CD931485). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all five controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Decision submitted without mandatory rationale
title_new: Clinical decision submitted without a recorded reason
hazard_old: Rationale field not enforced at submit
hazard_new: The system allows a clinician to submit a clinical decision without typing a reason. There is no check that stops the submission if the reason field is empty.
hazardous_situation_old: Rationale field not enforced at submit
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician approves or rejects a clinical recommendation without recording why. The decision is saved to the patient record with no explanation. Another clinician reading the record later cannot tell why the decision was made. This could lead to the wrong care being continued or repeated.
harm_old: Rationale field not enforced at submit
harm_new: A patient receives incorrect or inappropriate care because a previous clinical decision had no recorded reason. The next clinician cannot challenge or review the decision safely. This could cause delayed treatment, wrong treatment, or patient harm.
mitigation_new: The system blocks submission if the reason field is empty. A clinician cannot approve or reject a recommendation without first typing a reason. This is enforced automatically every time a decision is submitted (DI-6B085C04). The system also tracks each approval step separately and will not allow the next stage to proceed until all required fields, including the reason, are completed. This check runs automatically at every approval stage (DI-8FDE6740). When a decision is rejected and sent back for changes, the clinician resubmitting it must confirm they have addressed the recorded reasons before the system accepts the resubmission. This is enforced automatically on every resubmission (DI-C2F1FF32). Every decision, including the recorded reason, is saved in a secure log that cannot be altered. This log is created automatically each time a decision is submitted (DI-D49BCE55). The log can be exported for review at any time by the clinical safety team (DI-0A5CC384). Each candidate recommendation must have a recorded decision with a clear link to its source before it can be used in care. This is checked automatically before any recommendation is promoted (DI-F94EB13F). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and system enforcement checks every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Audit trail tampered after creation
title_new: Audit trail records altered or deleted after they are created
hazard_old: Immutability not enforced at storage layer
hazard_new: The system does not reliably prevent someone from changing or deleting audit trail records once they have been saved. An audit trail is the permanent log of who did what, and when, in the system. If these records can be altered, the log can no longer be trusted.
hazardous_situation_old: Immutability not enforced at storage layer
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician, manager, or investigator reviews the audit trail to check a clinical decision or investigate a patient safety concern. Unknown to them, one or more records have been changed or removed. They base their review on incomplete or false information.
harm_old: Immutability not enforced at storage layer
harm_new: A patient safety investigation reaches the wrong conclusion because the audit trail has been tampered with. A harmful clinical decision may go undetected. A clinician may be wrongly blamed or wrongly cleared. Future patients may be harmed because the true cause of an earlier error is never found.
mitigation_new: The system creates a tamper-evident ledger of every review decision. This ledger is designed so that any change to a record is immediately detectable. The technical team maintains this ledger continuously (DI-0A5CC384). All audit trail records are kept for ten years and cannot be deleted. The system also records which version of the software was running at the time of each entry. A summary report can be produced for any date range. The technical team enforces this retention automatically (DI-B88F2A76). A dedicated system component allows authorised staff to access the full history of any decision without exposing the wider patient record. This keeps the audit trail accessible for review while protecting patient confidentiality. The technical team maintains this component continuously (DI-09E26C1D). When a guideline is withdrawn or retired, all users who previously relied on it are notified. The audit trail entry for that guideline is kept permanently, even after the guideline is no longer active. The technical team manages this process at the point of each withdrawal (DI-FC4CA3C1). The clinical safety committee reviews audit trail integrity reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Audit trail entry missing for key decision
title_new: A clinical decision is made but no record of it is saved
hazard_old: Event not emitted on all state change paths
hazard_new: The system does not always save a record when a clinician makes or changes a decision. Some actions in the AI workflow do not trigger a log entry. This means certain decisions leave no trace in the audit trail.
hazardous_situation_old: Event not emitted on all state change paths
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews a patient record and makes a decision. The system fails to log that decision. If the decision is later questioned, there is no record to show what was decided, by whom, or when. A different clinician may then repeat or contradict the decision without knowing it was already made.
harm_old: Event not emitted on all state change paths
harm_new: Without a complete audit trail, errors in a patient's care may go undetected. A patient could receive the wrong treatment, a missed diagnosis could go unchallenged, or a harmful decision could be repeated. Investigations into patient safety incidents would be hampered because the evidence needed to understand what happened is missing.
mitigation_new: The system keeps a tamper-evident record of every review decision. This log can be exported and checked at any time. The safety team can verify that no entries have been altered (DI-0A5CC384). All audit records are kept for ten years. The system records which version of the software was running at the time of each entry. The safety team can run summary reports covering any date range to check for gaps (DI-B88F2A76). When a clinician corrects a decision, the system saves that correction in a fixed format that is permanently linked to the original record. This means every change can be traced back to its source (DI-4F67189B). If a clinician corrects a decision, the system resets the confirmation status. The clinician must actively re-confirm before the decision is accepted again. This prevents unchecked changes from passing through silently (DI-5ADEC3D1). The system records which version of the AI model handled each case, including any test runs using a smaller share of traffic. This allows the safety team to check whether logging failures are linked to a particular model version (DI-A557AE91). A separate system component allows authorised staff to check the audit trail without accessing the full clinical record. This supports oversight while protecting patient privacy (DI-09E26C1D). The clinical safety committee reviews audit trail completeness reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Retired code not remapped before update activated
title_new: A retired clinical code is not replaced before the update goes live
hazard_old: Code retirement not flagged before activation
hazard_new: Clinical codes are updated regularly by NHS Digital. When a code is retired, it must be replaced with a current one before any update is switched on. If this step is missed, the AI workflow may still try to use the old, retired code. The system could then fail to record a diagnosis or condition correctly in the patient record.
hazardous_situation_old: Code retirement not flagged before activation
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews a patient and the AI tool that reads notes identifies a condition. The system tries to save this using a retired clinical code that is no longer valid. The condition is not recorded correctly in the patient record. The clinician does not see a warning. The patient's record shows the condition as missing or unconfirmed.
harm_old: Code retirement not flagged before activation
harm_new: The patient's condition is not properly recorded. A future clinician reviewing the record may not know the condition exists. This could lead to the wrong treatment, a missed follow-up, or a harmful prescribing decision. For a serious condition such as heart failure or cancer, this delay or omission could cause serious harm.
mitigation_new: Before any code update is switched on, the team runs a formal impact analysis. This checks every ICD-10 and OPCS code in the update to find any that have been retired. The clinical informatics team runs this check for every scheduled NHS Digital release. Any retired code must be remapped to a valid replacement before the update is allowed to go live (DI-337D44DE). In addition, before activation, the AI workflow is run in test mode against a copy of real data. This dry run checks that all codes resolve correctly and flags any errors. The clinical safety team reviews the dry-run results before sign-off. No update is activated until the dry run passes (DI-ACB587DD). The clinical safety committee reviews both controls every quarter to confirm they are being followed and are working as intended.

title_old: Dashboard shows stale currency status - overdue item not flagged
title_new: Dashboard shows out-of-date information — an overdue item is not flagged to the clinician
hazard_old: Dashboard query caches stale data
hazard_new: The dashboard stores a saved copy of its data and does not always refresh it. This means the information a clinician sees may be out of date.
hazardous_situation_old: Dashboard query caches stale data
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician checks the dashboard to see whether clinical content — such as a guideline, reference range, or care pathway — is current and approved. Because the dashboard is showing old, saved data, an item that is overdue for review appears to be up to date. The clinician does not realise the content needs checking and acts on it as though it is still valid.
harm_old: Dashboard query caches stale data
harm_new: The clinician uses clinical content that should have been reviewed and updated. This could lead to a patient receiving care based on out-of-date guidance — for example, an incorrect reference range or an outdated treatment pathway — which could cause the patient serious harm.
mitigation_new: Four controls are in place to reduce this risk. First, the system requires that any piece of clinical content can only be marked as current if it is linked to a completed review event. The system then automatically marks content as overdue once its review deadline passes, based on the type of content involved. This happens without anyone needing to trigger it manually (DI-2F157317). Second, a currency dashboard shows the review status of all clinical content, including reference ranges, in one place. Clinicians and reviewers can export this information as evidence that surveillance is taking place (DI-E5609239, DI-E7609DD8). Third, the system displays a queue of items that need review. Reviewers can sort and filter this queue. The system sends notifications to reviewers and escalates items that are overdue, so nothing is missed (DI-636D331A). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and dashboard reports each quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Deprecated guideline still referenced in active pathway rule
title_new: An out-of-date clinical guideline is still being used to guide patient care
hazard_old: Dependency enumeration query incomplete
hazard_new: The system can continue to follow a clinical guideline that has been withdrawn or replaced. When a guideline is retired, the care pathway rules that depend on it are not automatically updated. The system may therefore keep giving clinicians advice based on out-of-date guidance without any warning.
hazardous_situation_old: Dependency enumeration query incomplete
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician follows a care pathway recommendation without knowing it is based on a withdrawn guideline. The recommendation may no longer reflect current best practice. The clinician has no way to tell that the guidance is out of date.
harm_old: Dependency enumeration query incomplete
harm_new: A patient receives care that does not follow current clinical guidelines. This could mean a missed diagnosis, the wrong treatment, or a delayed referral. For a patient with a serious condition, this could cause significant harm.
mitigation_new: Six controls are in place to reduce this risk. First, when a guideline is withdrawn, the system automatically tells all clinicians and teams who were using it and keeps a permanent record of the change (DI-FC4CA3C1). The clinical safety team checks these notifications are sent every time a guideline is retired. Second, when a guideline is marked as withdrawn, the system blocks any care pathway rules that depend on it from continuing to run until they are reviewed and updated (DI-F1A768AE). The system does this automatically at the point of withdrawal. Third, when a clinical code linked to a guideline is corrected, a trained reviewer checks all related pathway rules and clinical codes to make sure they are still accurate (DI-1B8AC856). This review is carried out by the clinical informatics team each time a correction is made. Fourth, authorised clinical leads can update the set of guideline rules used in care pathways without needing a software release, so corrections can be made quickly (DI-AA8014F9). This is available at any time and does not require IT involvement. Fifth, before any guideline update is approved, a reviewer sees the old and new versions side by side, can trace back to the source document, and sees a list of every care pathway rule that will be affected (DI-1E8D8678). This check is completed by a named clinical reviewer before each update goes live. Sixth, before any updated guideline is moved into live use, the system checks for conflicts with other guidelines and marks any guideline still under review so that it remains available but flagged (DI-48ACD153). This check runs automatically each time a guideline is staged for release. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and incident reports for this risk every quarter to confirm all controls are working as intended.

title_old: Guideline staged without valid source reference
title_new: A clinical guideline is approved for use without a valid source reference
hazard_old: Source reference field not validated before staging
hazard_new: The system allows a clinical guideline to be approved and made available to clinicians before checking that it has a valid, traceable source reference. A guideline without a proper source cannot be verified as accurate or up to date.
hazardous_situation_old: Source reference field not validated before staging
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician follows a guideline that has no verified source. The guideline may contain incorrect or outdated clinical advice. The clinician has no way to check where the advice came from or whether it is trustworthy.
harm_old: Source reference field not validated before staging
harm_new: A patient receives care based on incorrect or unverified clinical advice. This could lead to the wrong treatment, a missed diagnosis, or a harmful medicine decision. The harm could be serious.
mitigation_new: The system requires every guideline to have a source reference entered before it can be approved. Authors cannot complete the approval process without linking a source (DI-80579DCC). A separate, independent check reviews each guideline for source completeness and safety before it goes live. A named reviewer carries out this check every time a guideline is updated (DI-F3EFEA88). The system also checks for conflicts between guidelines before approving them, and keeps the previous version available while any issues are resolved (DI-48ACD153). When the AI tool that reads notes suggests new guideline content, it always includes a reference to the source section of the document it used, so the origin of every suggestion can be traced (DI-147C8EF0). Any reference ranges added to guidelines must include a mandatory source entry, so traceability is maintained throughout (DI-340279C1). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of guideline approvals every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Mandatory NICE obligation not identified as time-bound
title_new: A NICE obligation with a deadline is not flagged as time-sensitive
hazard_old: Time-bound flag not set on TA with contractual deadline
hazard_new: The AI tool that reads clinical notes may not recognise that a NICE Technology Appraisal (a formal NICE ruling on a treatment) carries a mandatory deadline. If the deadline is not flagged, the system treats the obligation as routine rather than urgent.
hazardous_situation_old: Time-bound flag not set on TA with contractual deadline
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews the system's output and sees no time-sensitive alert. They do not realise the practice must act by a specific date. The NICE obligation is not acted on within the required timeframe.
harm_old: Time-bound flag not set on TA with contractual deadline
harm_new: A patient who should receive a NICE-approved treatment by a set deadline does not receive it in time. This could mean delayed access to an effective treatment, leading to avoidable harm or deterioration in the patient's condition.
mitigation_new: The system uses a structured NICE assessment prompt to check every NICE Technology Appraisal for mandatory obligations. If an obligation does not apply, the clinician must record a reason why. This runs automatically each time a relevant appraisal is processed (DI-6B085C04). The system also runs countdown timers against each NICE Technology Appraisal and Quality Standard. These timers alert the clinical team when a deadline is approaching. The team reviews these alerts on an ongoing basis (DI-44802DF3). A per-pathway NICE alignment report is produced regularly. This report shows which obligations are on track and which are at risk of being missed. It can be exported for post-market safety review (DI-ED0D477A). The rules the AI follows to detect mandatory obligations can be updated by the programme team without a full software release. This means the team can act quickly if a new NICE deadline is issued (DI-AA8014F9). The clinical safety committee reviews all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Rule promoted to active without mandatory review decision
title_new: A clinical rule goes live before a clinician has reviewed and approved it
hazard_old: Review gate not enforced before promotion endpoint
hazard_new: The system can make an AI-suggested clinical rule active without a clinician first making a formal review decision. There is no enforced check that stops this from happening.
hazardous_situation_old: Review gate not enforced before promotion endpoint
hazardous_situation_new: A clinical rule that has not been checked by a clinician becomes active in the system. Clinicians then follow that rule when caring for patients, not knowing it was never reviewed.
harm_old: Review gate not enforced before promotion endpoint
harm_new: Patients receive care based on an unreviewed rule. The rule may be wrong or unsafe. This could lead to missed diagnoses, wrong treatment, or serious patient harm.
mitigation_new: The AI tool that reads clinical guidelines produces structured rule candidates and records exactly which section of the source document each one came from (DI-147C8EF0). This gives reviewers a clear audit trail before any decision is made. A mandatory review queue holds every AI-suggested rule and blocks it from going live until a clinician makes an explicit approve or reject decision. Every decision is linked back to the original source (DI-F94EB13F). The authoring process requires a source document to be linked before a rule can move through any stage toward publication (DI-80579DCC). A hard gate in the system prevents any AI-generated rule from being published unless a reviewer has recorded a decision against it. The system will not allow this step to be skipped (DI-604767B1). Every review decision is saved to a tamper-evident log that can be exported for audit. This log shows who decided what and when (DI-0A5CC384). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and gate enforcement quarterly to confirm all controls are working as intended.

title_old: Context rule change activates without impact test
title_new: A change to how the AI reads clinical notes goes live without safety testing
hazard_old: Test gate not enforced before activation
hazard_new: The AI tool that decides if a condition is present, absent, or possible follows a set of rules. These rules can be changed. If a rule change goes live without being tested first, the AI may start reading notes incorrectly. It could mark a condition as present when it is absent, or absent when it is present.
hazardous_situation_old: Test gate not enforced before activation
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician uses the system to review a patient's conditions. The AI has applied an untested rule change. It now incorrectly records a condition as present or absent. The clinician sees wrong information and does not know it is wrong. They make a clinical decision based on that wrong information.
harm_old: Test gate not enforced before activation
harm_new: A patient receives the wrong care because their record shows incorrect information. For example, a serious condition may be missed, or a treatment may be started that the patient does not need. This could cause serious harm or death.
mitigation_new: Before any rule change goes live, the system runs an automatic check. It tests the change against a set of notes that have already been reviewed by an expert. It shows how the change would affect results across those notes. This check must be completed and reviewed before the change can be activated (DI-48C13EB6). The system blocks any rule change from going live unless a test run has been completed and approved. No one can bypass this gate (DI-DFAF200B). A separate check compares the results from the AI tool that reads notes with the results from the AI tool that decides if something is present or absent. This check runs automatically after every change and flags any differences for review (DI-F298AE65). The AI tool that reads notes also gives a confidence score for each finding it identifies. Clinicians and the safety team can use these scores to spot when the AI is less certain than usual (DI-48AD06E5). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of all rule changes and test gate outcomes every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Validation check misses quality issue in episode
title_new: A quality problem in a patient episode is not caught by the checking rules
hazard_old: Validation rule set not comprehensive
hazard_new: The system checks each patient episode for quality problems before using it in reports. The set of checking rules may not cover every type of problem. Some quality problems could pass through undetected.
hazardous_situation_old: Validation rule set not comprehensive
hazardous_situation_new: A patient episode with a quality problem is not flagged. It is included in clinical reports or pathway decisions. Clinicians act on information that is incomplete or wrong.
harm_old: Validation rule set not comprehensive
harm_new: A clinician makes a care decision based on a flawed patient record. The patient may receive the wrong treatment, miss a needed referral, or have a serious condition overlooked. This could cause serious harm.
mitigation_new: First, any episode the system marks as having a quality problem is blocked from reports until a clinician or administrator resolves the problem. This happens automatically every time an episode is processed (DI-A0579B64). Second, the system checks each episode for unusual durations, missing steps, and events recorded in the wrong order. These checks run automatically on every episode (DI-1206D9E8). Third, the system flags any part of a record it is not confident about, and highlights where clinical codes within the same episode contradict each other. This runs automatically during every episode review (DI-C7A810AA). Fourth, clinical teams can update the set of checking rules for their programme without needing a software release. A named administrator applies updates whenever guidelines change (DI-AA8014F9). Fifth, the system tells the reviewer whether each episode was classified by fixed rules or by the AI tool that reads notes, so the reviewer knows how much to rely on the result. This is shown automatically on every episode (DI-8C236A1A). Sixth, when a clinician corrects a clinical code, the system checks that related codes and terms are still consistent. This check runs automatically at the point of correction (DI-1B8AC856). Seventh, the system compares the clinical codes produced by the AI tool that reads notes against those produced by the AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible. Any disagreement is flagged for review. This runs automatically on every episode (DI-F298AE65). Eighth, before any new set of checking rules is switched on, the system runs a test pass on real data without making any changes. A named administrator must approve the results before the rules go live (DI-ACB587DD). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and flagging rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Incorrect benchmark comparison displayed
title_new: The system shows a clinician an incorrect benchmark comparison
hazard_old: Wrong denominator or population mismatch
hazard_new: The system may compare a practice's results against the wrong group of patients. For example, it might compare a small rural practice against a large city practice. The figures shown would then be misleading.
hazardous_situation_old: Wrong denominator or population mismatch
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews a dashboard showing how their practice performs against a national benchmark. The benchmark is based on the wrong patient group. The clinician believes their practice is performing well when it is not, or vice versa.
harm_old: Wrong denominator or population mismatch
harm_new: The clinician makes a care decision based on misleading figures. For example, they may not act on a gap in care because the benchmark wrongly suggests performance is acceptable. Patients may miss a review or treatment they need. The harm is likely to be minor because a clinician will usually notice other signs that something is wrong.
mitigation_new: The system displays benchmark comparison charts in audit exports so clinicians can check the underlying figures themselves (DI-916BD8C8). The charts use clear colour coding, plain labels, and show the difference between the practice result and the benchmark, making errors easier to spot (DI-7C53CC70). Population pathway dashboards show national benchmark overlays alongside practice data so clinicians can see both figures at once (DI-BA2C8F3E). The system shows a confidence level next to each AI-generated figure so clinicians know how much to rely on it (DI-DA7584D8). A guided research workspace uses plain English to describe which patient group is being used for comparison, so clinicians can check the scope is correct (DI-DD67ACFF). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and dashboard outputs every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Console shows stale AI loop status
title_new: The screen shows an out-of-date AI processing status to the clinician
hazard_old: Cache not invalidated after model event
hazard_new: The AI workflow stores a snapshot of its current status to speed up the screen display. If that snapshot is not refreshed after the AI finishes or changes state, the screen continues to show the old status. A clinician looking at the screen sees a status that no longer reflects what the AI is actually doing.
hazardous_situation_old: Cache not invalidated after model event
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician checks the screen to confirm the AI has finished reviewing a patient's notes. The screen still shows the AI as running when it has already stopped, or as complete when it has failed. The clinician believes the AI result is ready and acts on incomplete or missing information without realising it.
harm_old: Cache not invalidated after model event
harm_new: The clinician makes a clinical decision based on an AI result they believe is current and complete. In fact the AI did not finish correctly. The clinician may miss a diagnosis, overlook a medicine problem, or send a patient down the wrong care pathway. This could cause the patient serious harm.
mitigation_new: A central status dashboard shows the live stage and next required action for the AI workflow. This gives every clinician and administrator a single, up-to-date view of what the AI is doing. The system updates this view automatically whenever the AI changes state (DI-BE09736F). A visible indicator appears on every administration page whenever the AI is actively learning from new examples. This means no one can miss that a learning process is under way and the results may not yet be final (DI-5E7E8CEF). When the AI classifies a patient encounter, any correction made by a reviewer is recorded immediately and linked back to the original information the AI read from the notes. This creates a permanent, tamper-proof record so the status shown always matches the most recent human review (DI-4F67189B). When a reviewer corrects an AI classification, that correction is fed back into the AI and recorded in the model registry. This means the displayed status reflects the latest agreed result, not an earlier automated one (DI-0ADE6A8E). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of status mismatches every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Research results presented without data quality caveats
title_new: Research results shown without warning about incomplete data
hazard_old: DQ status not surfaced alongside research output
hazard_new: The system shows research results to a clinician without telling them how complete or reliable the underlying patient data is. The AI tool that reads notes may have missed diagnoses or medicines in some records. The clinician has no way of knowing this from the results alone.
hazardous_situation_old: DQ status not surfaced alongside research output
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician uses the research workspace to review a group of patients. The results look complete. The clinician does not know that data quality is poor for part of the patient group. They make a clinical or service decision based on figures that do not reflect the true picture.
harm_old: DQ status not surfaced alongside research output
harm_new: The clinician acts on misleading research results. They may change a care pathway, allocate resources incorrectly, or miss a group of patients who need follow-up. This could lead to patients receiving the wrong care or being overlooked entirely, causing serious harm.
mitigation_new: The research workspace shows a plain-English guide that helps clinicians scope their search carefully before they run it. This reduces the chance of a poorly defined query producing misleading results (DI-DD67ACFF). The workspace displays a data coverage indicator next to every set of results. When coverage is low, the system shows a clear advisory warning so the clinician knows the results may be incomplete (DI-93162C3C). Every AI-generated interpretation shown in the workspace includes a confidence level displayed alongside it. This tells the clinician how certain the AI tool is about what it has found (DI-DA7584D8). When a clinician exports results, the export includes method details and notes about data coverage automatically. No extra steps are needed from the clinician (DI-58988BF2). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and user feedback every quarter to check these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Dashboard uses incorrect population denominator
title_new: Dashboard counts the wrong group of patients as its baseline population
hazard_old: Denominator query does not exclude ineligible patients
hazard_new: The dashboard works out how many patients should be on a care pathway by counting all registered patients. It does not remove patients who are not eligible for that pathway. This means the baseline number used for all calculations is wrong from the start.
hazardous_situation_old: Denominator query does not exclude ineligible patients
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews the dashboard to check how well their practice is managing a care pathway. The baseline population figure is too large because ineligible patients have not been removed. The percentage of patients meeting targets looks better than it really is. The clinician believes care is on track and does not act.
harm_old: Denominator query does not exclude ineligible patients
harm_new: Patients who need review or treatment are not identified. The clinician does not follow up with them. Those patients may miss timely diagnosis or treatment, leading to serious harm from delayed care.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the dashboard shows national benchmark figures alongside the practice figures so clinicians can spot when their results look unusually good or bad compared with peers across the country. The development team sets this up at build and the clinical safety committee checks it is working each quarter (DI-BA2C8F3E). Second, the dashboard includes a deprivation analysis panel that breaks down pathway performance by local deprivation level. If the denominator is wrong, the breakdown will look inconsistent and prompt investigation. The clinical lead reviews this panel at each monthly governance meeting (DI-94359E76). Third, the waiting-time performance panel highlights breaches and lets clinicians drill down into individual patient lists. If the denominator is inflated, breach rates will appear lower than expected and the drill-down will reveal patients who should not be included. Clinicians use this panel during weekly operational reviews (DI-35494904). Fourth, the guided population research workspace lets clinicians build their own plain-English searches to cross-check the dashboard population against their own criteria.
