Any mismatch between the dashboard count and the clinician's own search will flag a denominator problem. Clinicians can run this check at any time (DI-DD67ACFF). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and benchmark comparisons every quarter to confirm all four controls remain effective.

title_old: Failed encounters not surfaced in operational view
title_new: Failed patient encounters not shown to clinical staff
hazard_old: Error status not written to Neo4j or dashboard query misses it
hazard_new: When the AI workflow processes a patient encounter, it may fail silently. The system may not record that the failure happened. The monitoring dashboard may then show no problem, even though patient data was never processed.
hazardous_situation_old: Error status not written to Neo4j or dashboard query misses it
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician checks the dashboard before a clinic. The dashboard looks normal. The clinician does not know that some patient encounters failed to process. The clinician sees incomplete or missing information for those patients and may not realise it is incomplete.
harm_old: Error status not written to Neo4j or dashboard query misses it
harm_new: The clinician makes a clinical decision based on incomplete patient information. A condition may be missed or a care pathway may not be started. This could lead to delayed or incorrect treatment for the patient.
mitigation_new: First, the system automatically tracks how many encounters succeed or fail for each programme and displays this on a live monitoring dashboard that refreshes without anyone needing to act. The clinical informatics team reviews this dashboard daily (DI-067E471A). Second, the system keeps a separate list of every failed encounter, showing the reason for failure. Any authorised team member can re-queue a failed encounter for reprocessing with a single action. The clinical informatics team checks and clears this list every working day (DI-69CE20C1). Third, the clinic preparation view shows the processing status of every patient on the list alongside their pathway information. The clinician can see at a glance if a patient record has not been fully processed before the appointment (DI-CF03E4EA). Fourth, if the AI workflow cannot complete its checks reliably, it automatically records a failed verdict rather than producing a result that may be wrong. This means a failed encounter is always flagged rather than silently passed through (DI-9D967259). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and dashboard reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: DQ rule not triggered on episode
title_new: Quality check not run on some patient episodes
hazard_old: Rule engine not invoked on all episode types
hazard_new: The system runs automatic quality checks on patient episodes to spot missing or incorrect information. If the quality check is not triggered for every type of episode, some episodes will not be checked at all.
hazardous_situation_old: Rule engine not invoked on all episode types
hazardous_situation_new: A patient episode that contains missing or incorrect clinical information passes through the system without being flagged. The clinician reviewing the episode does not know a quality check was skipped. They may act on incomplete or wrong information.
harm_old: Rule engine not invoked on all episode types
harm_new: A clinician makes a clinical decision based on incomplete or incorrect information in a patient episode. This could lead to the wrong diagnosis, a missed diagnosis, or the wrong treatment being given. The patient could come to serious harm as a result.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the quality check engine runs a configurable set of rules against every episode and records whether each episode passed or failed. It also stores a recommended action for any episode that fails. This runs automatically each time an episode is processed (DI-FC80B65A). Second, a live dashboard shows pass and fail rates for every rule, grouped by programme and organisation. It highlights trends so that a drop in coverage is spotted quickly. The clinical safety team reviews this dashboard regularly and can export the data for further checks (DI-E6A32FF5). Third, the system tells the reviewing clinician how each episode was classified, including whether a standard rule or a fallback method was used. This means the clinician knows if an episode was handled in an unexpected way (DI-8C236A1A). Fourth, when changes are made to an episode, the review screen shows a clear before-and-after comparison of every change. This helps the clinician spot anything that looks wrong before they approve it (DI-BC39B803). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data from the dashboard and incident reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Incorrect cohort definition produces wrong patient population
title_new: Wrong patients included in or excluded from a care cohort
hazard_old: Inclusion/exclusion rule logic error
hazard_new: The rules that decide which patients belong to a cohort may contain an error. This means the system could include patients who should not be there, or leave out patients who should be. Clinicians would then act on a list that does not reflect the true patient group.
hazardous_situation_old: Inclusion/exclusion rule logic error
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician uses the cohort to plan care or review a pathway. Because the patient list is wrong, some patients receive unnecessary interventions. Other patients who need care are missed entirely and receive no follow-up.
harm_old: Inclusion/exclusion rule logic error
harm_new: Patients left out of the cohort may miss timely diagnosis or treatment, leading to serious harm from delayed care. Patients wrongly included may receive unnecessary tests or medicines, causing avoidable side effects or distress.
mitigation_new: First, the cohort builder lets clinicians set clear inclusion and exclusion rules using clinical codes, pathway stage, and patient demographics. This makes the rules visible and reviewable by any authorised clinician at any time (DI-FE3FFE50). Second, every time a clinician edits a cohort, the system automatically saves a new version and links it to all reports that used it. This means the team can always see exactly which rules were in place when a report was run (DI-14AE0A4C). Third, population pathway dashboards show how the cohort compares with national benchmarks. A clinician reviewing the dashboard can quickly spot if the numbers look unexpectedly high or low, which may signal a rule error (DI-BA2C8F3E). Fourth, a guided plain-English workspace helps clinicians scope their cohort before it is finalised. This reduces the chance of a rule being set incorrectly in the first place (DI-DD67ACFF). Fifth, a safety netting worklist lets clinicians filter outstanding cases by severity, days waiting, and cohort. This provides a secondary check that no high-risk patients have been missed (DI-520A8674). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of cohort changes and dashboard outlier alerts every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Cohort version not tracked on run
title_new: Patient list version not recorded when the AI runs
hazard_old: Cohort version not captured on job record
hazard_new: When the AI tool runs a search or review, it does not record which version of the patient list it used. This means no one can tell afterwards whether the list has changed since the run.
hazardous_situation_old: Cohort version not captured on job record
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician acts on results from the AI tool without knowing the patient list has since been updated. Patients added or removed after the last run may be missed or wrongly included. This could affect who receives a clinical intervention or recall.
harm_old: Cohort version not captured on job record
harm_new: A patient who should have been included in a care pathway is missed, or a patient who should have been removed is still contacted. Either outcome could lead to a missed or delayed clinical action, causing minor harm.
mitigation_new: Every time a clinician or administrator edits the patient list, the system automatically saves a new numbered version and links that version to every AI run that uses it. This means the exact list used for each run is always recorded and traceable (DI-14AE0A4C). The patient list is built using clear, rule-based criteria covering clinical codes, pathway stage, and patient demographics, which reduces the chance of unintended changes going unnoticed (DI-FE3FFE50). Any proposed change to the patient list joins a risk-scored queue and cannot go live until a named reviewer approves it, acting as a check before the updated list is used in a real run (DI-7C5EC850). Before any updated AI workflow goes live, the system runs a dry-run check to confirm the configuration is valid and the correct patient list version is linked (DI-ACB587DD). Every result returned by the AI tool includes a version label for the AI component that produced it, so the clinical safety team can trace exactly which version of the tool was active during any given run (DI-0D26BE1B). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of patient list versions and run records every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

title_old: Non-standard component introduced without architectural review
title_new: A new system component is added without a safety check
hazard_old: Architecture gate not enforced in CI or design review
hazard_new: A new part of the system can be added without anyone checking it is safe and fits with the rest of the system. There is no automatic check in the build process to catch this.
hazardous_situation_old: Architecture gate not enforced in CI or design review
hazardous_situation_new: If an unchecked component is added, it may behave in unexpected ways. It could affect how the AI tool reads notes, codes diagnoses, or saves information back into the patient record. Clinicians may not know the component is there or that it has not been reviewed.
harm_old: Architecture gate not enforced in CI or design review
harm_new: A patient could receive the wrong diagnosis code or be placed on the wrong care pathway. A clinician acting on incorrect information could make a treatment decision that harms the patient.
mitigation_new: The build system runs automatic code quality checks on every change, including checks for code style and length limits, so poor-quality additions are caught before they reach live systems (DI-932C270C). The build system also scans for exposed passwords and access keys, and stops the build if any are missing or unsafe (DI-6EBF12F1). All AI model settings are stored as structured records rather than fixed values in the code, so any change to a model is visible and traceable (DI-2C56591B). All workflow logic runs through a single controlled process, which means a new component cannot quietly take over a task without being noticed (DI-A90B19EB). All coding and workflow jobs run through one shared execution path, reducing the chance that an unchecked component runs separately and undetected (DI-3FDBB57B). The AI tool that reads notes must pass a minimum accuracy threshold on a set of examples checked by an expert before any change goes live (DI-12015DBC). The shortlisting step must also meet a minimum accuracy threshold on expert-checked examples (DI-10BB41E9). Patient data must always be de-identified before it reaches the AI language tool, and this check cannot be switched off (DI-F66A7239). Long-running tasks follow a consistent tracked pattern so any unexpected behaviour is visible to the team (DI-693FFEEA). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and quality gate results every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: SOUP record incomplete
title_new: Software component record not kept up to date
hazard_old: SOUP record not updated when new dependency added
hazard_new: When a new software component is added to the system, the record of all software components is not updated. This means the safety team does not have a complete picture of what the system relies on.
hazardous_situation_old: SOUP record not updated when new dependency added
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician uses the AI tool without knowing it depends on an unrecorded software component. If that component has a known fault or is out of date, the AI tool may give incorrect information. The clinician may not be warned that the output could be unreliable.
harm_old: SOUP record not updated when new dependency added
harm_new: The clinician acts on incorrect information from the AI tool. This could lead to a wrong clinical code being saved in the patient record or an incorrect care decision being made. The patient may receive the wrong care or experience a delay in receiving the right care.
mitigation_new: The system records a version identifier in every response it sends, so the safety team can always trace which software components were used for any given output. This check runs automatically every time the system responds (DI-0D26BE1B). Published documentation of all system components is kept up to date and all interactions between components are logged. The safety team reviews this documentation when any change is made (DI-5E721A71). A detailed log of all component interactions is kept for at least ten years. The safety team can query this log at any time to check which components were active and when (DI-7D9096CA). When a clinical code is reviewed or corrected, the system checks that all related components and terminology are still valid. A trained clinician carries out this review (DI-1B8AC856). If the system detects that data used to produce a clinician-facing output is incomplete or unreliable, it flags this clearly to the clinician before they act on it (DI-88F20177). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and component records every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: Breaking change introduced without deprecation notice
title_new: A software update silently changes how the system works, breaking connected systems
hazard_old: Versioning policy not enforced in CI
hazard_new: The system that checks clinical software updates does not enforce version labelling rules. A new version of the software can be released with changes that break other connected systems. No warning is sent to the teams who rely on those connections. Clinical systems that feed patient information into care pathways may stop working correctly without anyone knowing.
hazardous_situation_old: Versioning policy not enforced in CI
hazardous_situation_new: A connected clinical system silently receives a breaking update. It begins to pull incorrect or incomplete information from patient records. A clinician reads the output and sees missing diagnoses, wrong medicines, or outdated care pathway information. The clinician does not know the information is wrong because no alert is shown.
harm_old: Versioning policy not enforced in CI
harm_new: A clinician acts on incomplete or incorrect patient information. A serious diagnosis may be missed or a wrong medicine may be given. The patient could be harmed as a result of a clinical decision based on information the system presented incorrectly.
mitigation_new: A version labelling policy requires every software release to be clearly numbered and any planned changes to be announced in advance before they take effect. The software development team applies this to every release (DI-DC8465F1). When a part of the system is due to change or be retired, the system automatically sends a warning notice to all connected teams and displays a sunset header so they can prepare. The software team manages this for every affected connection (DI-B0832A64). A dependency check runs automatically before any change is released. It confirms that no connected clinical rules or pathways will break. The software team runs this check on every release (DI-F1A768AE). Before any change that affects how information is displayed or recorded goes live, it must pass a review in a test environment, receive sign-off, be correctly versioned, and have a rollback plan ready. The software team and a clinical reviewer complete this before each release (DI-9FD54AD6). Every week, the system updates its list of clinical organisations and checks whether any of those updates would break existing connections. Any breaking change is blocked until it is resolved. The software team runs this check weekly (DI-634258FE). A permanent record of every change to patient information is kept for at least seven years. This record cannot be altered. The software team enforces this automatically for all records (DI-080A2454). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and test results for all these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

title_old: Job status not surfaced or incorrect
title_new: The system does not show the correct status of a running task
hazard_old: Progress events not published to Service Bus or polling endpoint broken
hazard_new: The system component that sends task progress updates stops working or sends no updates. The clinician's screen does not show whether a task is still running, has finished, or has failed.
hazardous_situation_old: Progress events not published to Service Bus or polling endpoint broken
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician starts a task, such as pulling information from patient notes. The screen shows no progress or shows an old status. The clinician does not know the task has stalled or failed. They may act on incomplete or missing results without realising the information is not ready.
harm_old: Progress events not published to Service Bus or polling endpoint broken
harm_new: The clinician makes a clinical decision based on incomplete results. For example, a diagnosis or medicine review may be based on missing information. This could lead to a delayed or incorrect decision for the patient, causing minor harm.
mitigation_new: The system uses a consistent, well-defined way of tracking and reporting task progress at every stage. This means the clinician always sees a clear status, including how long the task has been running, which step it is on, and an estimated finish time. The system component that manages this is built to a documented standard and supports cancellation if needed (DI-AAF6635D, DI-693FFEEA, DI-A2EF241F). The system shows partial results as each step finishes, so the clinician is not left waiting with no information (DI-CB07829F). All interactions with the system are recorded so problems can be traced and reviewed (DI-5E721A71). When the system is updated, a clear version history and plain-English reference guide are published alongside each release so clinicians and support staff know what has changed (DI-DC8465F1, DI-DD2307E8). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

title_old: API spec incorrect or out of date
title_new: System component instructions become incorrect or out of date
hazard_old: Spec not regenerated or validated on each release
hazard_new: The instructions that tell different parts of the system how to share information may not be updated when the system changes. If these instructions are wrong or out of date, parts of the system may send or receive information incorrectly.
hazardous_situation_old: Spec not regenerated or validated on each release
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician uses the system after an update. The system component instructions have not been refreshed. The system silently passes wrong or incomplete information between its parts. The clinician sees results that appear normal but are based on faulty data transfer.
harm_old: Spec not regenerated or validated on each release
harm_new: The clinician receives inaccurate information about a patient. This could lead to a missed or delayed clinical decision. The harm is likely to be minor, but a patient could receive suboptimal care if the error is not caught.
mitigation_new: First, the system automatically produces a machine-readable description of how each part of the system communicates, and this is updated with every release so instructions stay current (DI-D31B359D). Second, a plain-English guide and a list of changes are published alongside every release so clinicians and support staff can see exactly what has changed and when (DI-DD2307E8). Third, every response from the AI tool includes a version label, so the support team can trace exactly which version of the system produced any given result (DI-0D26BE1B). Fourth, when clinical codes are updated, the system flags any differences and blocks the update from going live until a clinician or the support team has reviewed and resolved each change (DI-B193C816). Fifth, before any update to procedure or diagnosis codes takes effect, the team carries out an impact review and must actively approve activation (DI-337D44DE). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and version records each quarter to confirm all five controls are working as intended.

title_old: Real patient data in sandbox
title_new: Real patient data copied into the test environment
hazard_old: Sandbox provisioning copies from production without de-identification
hazard_new: When the test environment is set up, it may copy real patient records from the live system. Those records are not stripped of patient details before copying. Real patient data then sits in a test environment that has weaker security controls.
hazardous_situation_old: Sandbox provisioning copies from production without de-identification
hazardous_situation_new: A developer, tester, or other non-clinical member of staff can view or change real patient records inside the test environment. They may not realise the data is real. The data may also be shared more widely than a live record would be, for example in bug reports or log files.
harm_old: Sandbox provisioning copies from production without de-identification
harm_new: A patient's confidential health information is seen by people who have no right to see it. This is a serious breach of patient privacy. It could cause distress, damage to reputation, or harm if sensitive information such as mental health or HIV status is disclosed without consent.
mitigation_new: The test environment is built using only artificial, made-up patient data. No real patient records are ever copied into it. This is enforced automatically each time the test environment is set up (DI-99A33896, DI-B8674FBF). The test environment is kept completely separate from the live system. Each part of the system stores patient information in its own dedicated, isolated area, so data cannot leak between environments (DI-AF5A1668, DI-84F44836). If the test environment is missing data for a particular area, a warning is shown to the person running the test so they know the results may be incomplete (DI-93162C3C). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and environment build records every quarter to confirm that no real patient data has entered the test environment.

title_old: Error exposes internal system detail
title_new: System error message reveals internal technical detail to the user
hazard_old: Exception not caught and sanitised before response
hazard_new: When the system encounters an unexpected error, it may show a raw technical error message instead of a safe, plain-language response. This could expose internal workings of the system to whoever is viewing the screen.
hazardous_situation_old: Exception not caught and sanitised before response
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician or patient sees a raw technical error message on screen. The message may contain internal system detail that is confusing or misleading. The clinician may not know whether the action they attempted was completed or not.
harm_old: Exception not caught and sanitised before response
harm_new: The clinician is unsure whether a clinical action such as saving a diagnosis or updating a medicine was completed. Acting on this uncertainty, they may repeat or skip a step. This could lead to a minor error in the patient record. The risk of serious patient harm is low because the error is visible and prompts the clinician to check.
mitigation_new: Three controls reduce this risk. First, the system uses a fixed, versioned list of error categories to classify every error into one of three groups and direct the development team to the correct fix. This list is maintained by the development team and reviewed whenever the system is updated (DI-990C0AFA). Second, every error the system returns is wrapped in a standard, consistent format with a readable error code. This means the clinician always sees a clear, structured message rather than raw technical detail. The development team applies this format to all system components at build time (DI-6654FB0E). Third, the system allows the error category rules to be updated at any time without restarting the system, and each change is tracked with a version number. The development team manages these updates as needed (DI-770FD74A). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of error messages each quarter to confirm that raw technical detail is not reaching clinicians.

title_old: Non-conformant FHIR resource breaks downstream product
title_new: A patient data message in the wrong format breaks a clinical system that relies on it
hazard_old: FHIR profile validation not run in CI
hazard_new: This system sends patient information to other clinical systems using a standard data format called FHIR. If the system sends a message that does not follow the required format rules, the receiving clinical system may fail, show wrong information, or silently drop the data.
hazardous_situation_old: FHIR profile validation not run in CI
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician using a downstream system receives incomplete or missing patient information. They do not know the data is wrong or absent. They make a clinical decision based on that incomplete picture.
harm_old: FHIR profile validation not run in CI
harm_new: A clinician acts on missing or incorrect patient information. This could lead to a wrong or delayed diagnosis, an unsafe medicine decision, or a missed referral. The patient could come to serious harm as a result.
mitigation_new: First, the system automatically checks every patient data message against the required UK format rules before it is sent. This check runs every time a software change is made, without any manual step needed. This is the automated format checker built into the development process (DI-BDFF6DA7). Second, patient findings, care milestones, and audit results are each sent in a defined, structured way so receiving systems always know what to expect. The development team sets these rules and they apply to every message the system sends (DI-710D5213). Third, before any change to the AI workflow goes live, the team runs a dry-run test to confirm the new setup produces correctly formatted messages. This happens before every activation (DI-ACB587DD). Fourth, every message the system sends includes a version label for the AI component that produced it. This lets the receiving system and the safety team trace exactly which version of the AI created a given message, making it easier to spot and fix problems quickly (DI-0D26BE1B). Fifth, when a formatting or coding problem is found, a structured review checks all related messages and fixes any errors in the clinical codes used. The clinical safety team runs this review whenever a problem is reported (DI-1B8AC856). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs from the automated format checker and any reported formatting failures every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

title_old: meta.source omitted from FHIR resource
title_new: Patient record saved without a source label
hazard_old: meta.source population step skipped
hazard_new: When the system saves a clinical finding to the patient record, it must attach a label showing where that finding came from. If this labelling step is skipped, the saved record has no source information.
hazardous_situation_old: meta.source population step skipped
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician reviews a finding in the patient record but cannot tell whether it came from the AI tool that reads notes, a manual entry, or another system. The clinician has no way to judge how reliable the finding is.
harm_old: meta.source population step skipped
harm_new: The clinician may act on a finding without knowing its origin or reliability. This could lead to a wrong or delayed clinical decision, causing serious harm to the patient.
mitigation_new: First, the system checks every saved record against approved UK clinical record standards and rejects any record that is missing required fields, including the source label. This check runs automatically every time a record is saved (DI-BDFF6DA7). Second, the system is designed so that every clinical finding, care milestone, and audit result must include a source label before it can be saved to the patient record. This rule is built into the system and cannot be bypassed (DI-710D5213). Third, population-level dashboards show clinicians a summary of patient findings. If source labels are missing, these dashboards will show incomplete data, making the gap visible to clinical staff who review them routinely (DI-BA2C8F3E). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and dashboard reports every quarter to confirm that source labels are being saved correctly on all records.

title_old: Programme activated before all prerequisites confirmed
title_new: Programme starts before all required setup steps are complete
hazard_old: Onboarding gate not enforced before programme activation
hazard_new: The system may allow a clinical programme to start before all required setup steps have been signed off. This means the programme could run without the correct settings, rules, or approvals being in place.
hazardous_situation_old: Onboarding gate not enforced before programme activation
hazardous_situation_new: If the programme starts too early, it may process patient records using incomplete or incorrect settings. Clinicians could receive wrong or misleading information about patients. They may act on that information without realising the programme was not ready to run.
harm_old: Onboarding gate not enforced before programme activation
harm_new: A clinician could make a clinical decision based on incorrect or incomplete information produced by the programme. This could lead to a patient receiving the wrong care, a missed diagnosis, or a delayed referral. The harm could be serious.
mitigation_new: A six-step setup checklist must be completed before the programme can start. The system records each step as it is finished and blocks the programme from starting until all six steps are done (DI-1987BCF5). If setup is interrupted, the system saves progress so no steps are lost. An admin dashboard shows which steps are complete and which are outstanding, so the team can see at a glance what remains (DI-C58E5515). If any reference ranges are changed, the system blocks the programme from restarting until an approval record is in place. This is checked automatically each time a change is made (DI-C5A523A7). Before the programme goes live, the AI workflow runs a test check of its own settings to confirm everything is configured correctly. The programme cannot start if this test check fails (DI-ACB587DD). Any changes to the rules the AI follows must be tested in a safe trial run before they take effect. The programme is blocked from starting until this trial run passes (DI-DFAF200B). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all these controls are working as intended every quarter.

title_old: Automated episode quality-check rule fails to catch incorrect coding
title_new: Automated quality checks miss incorrectly coded clinical entries
hazard_old: The automated episode quality-check RULE SET has coverage gaps; incorrectly coded entities pass the rule layer and enter episodes without being flagged for human review.
hazard_new: The system uses automated rules to check that clinical codes in patient records are correct. These rules have gaps. Some incorrect codes pass through the checks without being flagged for a clinician to review.
hazardous_situation_old: The automated episode quality-check RULE SET has coverage gaps; incorrectly coded entities pass the rule layer and enter episodes without being flagged for human review.
hazardous_situation_new: A patient's record contains an incorrect clinical code. The automated quality checks do not catch it. The code enters the patient's care record without any clinician reviewing it. Clinical decisions or care pathways may then be based on wrong information.
harm_old: The automated episode quality-check RULE SET has coverage gaps; incorrectly coded entities pass the rule layer and enter episodes without being flagged for human review.
harm_new: A clinician makes a clinical decision based on an incorrect code in the patient's record. The patient receives the wrong treatment, misses a needed treatment, or is placed on the wrong care pathway. This could cause serious harm.
mitigation_new: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the system blocks any flagged episode from being used in reports until a clinician has reviewed and resolved the flag. This runs automatically every time an episode is processed (DI-A0579B64). Second, a human-review gate stops any unreviewed episode classification from being used in audit reports. The clinical team manages this gate as part of routine reporting (DI-BD696225). Third, the system automatically checks coded patient encounters against clinical guideline rules. This runs each time a new coded entry is saved (DI-2AFF691F). Fourth, the programme team can update the guideline rule set at any time without needing a software release. This means gaps in the rules can be fixed quickly when found (DI-AA8014F9). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

title_old: Human reviewer approves a wrong replacement code during coding correction due to terminology-expertise gap
title_new: A reviewer picks the wrong clinical code when correcting a patient record
hazard_old: A human reviewer selects an incorrect SNOMED replacement during a coding-correction workflow because they lack terminology expertise or clinical context for ambiguous terms.
hazard_new: When a clinician reviews and corrects clinical codes in a patient record, they may choose the wrong replacement code. This can happen when the correct code requires specialist terminology knowledge they do not have, or when the original note is ambiguous.
hazardous_situation_old: A human reviewer selects an incorrect SNOMED replacement during a coding-correction workflow because they lack terminology expertise or clinical context for ambiguous terms.
hazardous_situation_new: A clinician approves an incorrect clinical code during a coding correction review. The patient record then holds the wrong diagnosis or condition code. Future clinical decisions, referrals, or medicines may be based on that wrong code without anyone realising the error.
harm_old: A human reviewer selects an incorrect SNOMED replacement during a coding-correction workflow because they lack terminology expertise or clinical context for ambiguous terms.
harm_new: The patient's record contains the wrong diagnosis or condition. A doctor or nurse reading the record may make the wrong clinical decision. This could lead to the patient receiving the wrong treatment, missing a needed treatment, or being referred along the wrong care pathway. The harm could be serious.
mitigation_new: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the system checks that any proposed replacement code is consistent with related codes already in the record and flags conflicts for the reviewer to consider before approving (DI-1B8AC856). This check runs automatically every time a coding correction is reviewed. Second, the AI tool that reads clinical notes is designed to preserve important detail such as whether a condition is confirmed, suspected, or ruled out, so the replacement code options shown to the reviewer reflect the correct clinical meaning (DI-6A0B55A4). This runs automatically during every AI workflow. Third, the system checks that any proposed replacement code is current and valid in the clinical coding system before showing it to the reviewer, so out-of-date or retired codes cannot be selected (DI-26CBDB16). This check runs automatically for every proposed code. Fourth, the review screen shows the reviewer how often each code has been used historically for similar patients, giving useful context to support the decision (DI-22F4E3CE). This information is displayed automatically on every coding correction review page. Fifth, the AI workflow can use two independent AI models and only suggests a replacement code when both models agree, reducing the chance of a misleading suggestion reaching the reviewer (DI-80DD8A47). This is configured by the system administrator and runs during every AI workflow. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and reviewer feedback every quarter to confirm all five controls are working as intended.
